articles.summaryZh: 「跑者的膝」等過度使用傷害在跑者常見；2021年追蹤3,669名跑者的研究，把膝蓋周邊疼痛列為最常見抱怨之一，並指出先前受傷會讓後續過度使用傷害機率增加62%。Cochrane於2022年評估不同跑鞋設計，證據支持不多；2021年OJSM也發現跑前伸展無助益。升量要慢。2025年納入5,205名跑者的研究顯示，單次跑量比上月最長跑量多10%到30%者，過度使用傷害率較高64%。
keyPointsZh: 2021年研究納入3,669名跑者，將膝蓋周邊疼痛列入最常見抱怨，並指出先前受傷會讓後續過度使用傷害機率增加62%。
Cochrane在2022年系統性回顧不同跑鞋設計，結論是證據顯示影響有限；2021年OJSM也指出跑前伸展無助預防。
2015年回顧指出，新手通報受傷次數逾2倍，可能與期望差異有關，較焦慮者會更快報告原本會自行緩解的不適。
2025年針對5,205名跑者的研究顯示，單次比上月最長跑量多10%到30%時，過度使用傷害率增加64%。
Nielsen建議把任何單次跑量控制在較上月最長跑不超過5%，且每週總量不超過前一週110%。
articles.researchLensZh: 摘要可用來檢驗兩個可核對主張：第一，跑鞋設計與跑前伸展能否有效降低過度使用傷害；第二，訓練負荷增幅（單次5%內、每週110%內）是否對過度使用傷害率形成一致方向的關聯。
highlightTermsZh: 先前受傷會讓後續過度使用傷害機率增加62%

articles.titleEn: Are film critics as snooty and out of touch as people think?
articles.rubricEn: We look at the data to find out
articles.textEn:
Oct 22nd 2026
Whether a film is good enough to warrant a trek to the cinema is not always easy to ascertain. Recently viewers have praised “Digger”, a satirical black comedy about a wealthy oil tycoon whose company triggers an environmental catastrophe. It has a 76% audience-approval score on Rotten Tomatoes, a review aggregator. But critics did not dig the film: only 53% reviewed it positively, complaining it was ponderous and preachy. Fans calling themselves “Digger Nation” have mobilised online to defend the movie.
Signals about films’ quality can be confusing to decipher. In April fans judged a biopic of Michael Jackson to be a thriller, with 97% of them enjoying it. But most critics thought “Michael ” was bad. In January “ Melania ”, a documentary about America’s First Lady, reflected the politically polarised times, with a 90-point gap. “An absolute masterpiece!” gushed one audience member. “Gilded trash”, said the Guardian.
Critics and audiences have often failed to see eye to eye. The history of film criticism is littered with judgments that aged badly. (Pity the reviewer who dismissed “Citizen Kane”, now considered one of the greatest films ever made, as “well-intentioned, muddled, amateurish”.) Today many think that critics seem out of step—perhaps more than ever before.
But are they really? To test whether critical and popular opinion are drifting apart, The Economist compiled two decades of reviews of more than 10,000 films from Metacritic, an aggregator site. (We did not use Rotten Tomatoes because the website changed its audience-score methodology in 2019.) Then we matched the reviews with box-office data from The Numbers, a film-industry database.
Talk of a critic-audience divide, it turns out, is overblown. For most of the past 20 years, reviewers and moviegoers have been in broad agreement. Around a decade ago, their views began to diverge. But by 2025 critic and audience ratings were more aligned than at any point since 2005 (see chart 1).
The real difference is not how critics and audiences rate films, but which films they rate. For every ten audience reviews of a documentary, there are six from critics. For dramas and comedies there are around three, and for action less than one. Foreign-language and low-budget films attract disproportionately more attention from critics than from audiences.
Critics and audiences may gravitate towards different films, yet their judgments often align. Between 2005 and 2016 the correlation between critic and audience scores—where zero implies no relationship and one means the scores move perfectly in step—averaged around 0.6. Then opinions began to diverge. Before 2017 a ten-point increase in a film’s audience score was associated with a ten-point increase in its critic score. Over the next six years, that figure fell to just eight points. The correlation between critic and audience scores also dropped from 0.6 to around 0.5. In short, critics’ enthusiasm for a film told you less about how much viewers liked it.
To understand why, we tested a few hypotheses. The first was that the mix of films had changed, as film critics and audiences tend to agree more on some genres than others. But changes in genre, budget, sequel status and studio did little to explain the degree of disagreement.
In fact, much of the divergence happened within two of Hollywood’s biggest categories: big-budget action and family films . Before 2017 critics’ opinions of these films tracked audience opinions about as closely as they did for any other genre. Between 2017 and 2022, however, that relationship collapsed: critics’ scores on such releases were a poor guide to how audiences would rate them. All told, we estimate that roughly 43% of the divergence between critics and audiences was concentrated in these two types of film.
Most industry experts attribute the deviation to franchise fatigue. “Film reviewers got tired of superhero movies before the general audience did,” says Bruce Nash of The Numbers. “It gets boring”, says Mattias Frey of City St George’s, University of London, “if you’re seeing ‘Fast and Furious 23’ or ‘Avengers Part 27’.”
Political polarisation may have also played a part. When studios cast more female and minority actors in big-budget franchises, or embrace “woke” themes—as Marvel Studios did with “ Captain Marvel ”, its first female-led film, which was described as a “big feminist movie”—audiences tend to be more critical.
Since 2022 critics and audiences have found more common ground. Across all major genres, the correlation between their ratings now sits at nearly 0.7. Some reckon the film industry’s woes may be a factor: reviewers may be going easier on films they would once have panned. “There is this idea that there’s an existential crisis in movies, and that may be changing the way critics operate,” says Daniel Parris, a data scientist. James McMahon, an entertainment researcher, agrees: “As a critic, if you crap on every movie, you may be sinking the very thing that you really love.”
Journalism’s woes may be a factor, too. The era of the esteemed staff reviewer is long over. (“The Last Movie Critic”, a documentary about Roger Ebert, puts it bluntly.) Publications have laid off scores of arts journalists; those who remain must compete with influencers and podcasters to take part in the cultural conversation. They cannot afford to ignore the biggest blockbusters—or write only for the cognoscenti.
All this raises the question of what film critics are for today. Our data suggest they still have commercial clout. We found that higher critic scores are associated with significantly higher ticket sales in America, even after controlling for factors including genre and budget.
Their allure is also intellectual. Critics “get you thinking about things that you might not have thought about”, says Kevin Goetz, an entertainment researcher. Many read reviews only after they have seen a film as a way of extending the experience, positive or negative. Everyone can appreciate a good roast. ■
articles.summaryZh: 「評論家高傲、與觀眾脫節」說法未必符合數據。彙整20年、1萬多部電影的Metacritic評論與美國票房後，多數年份評論與觀眾分數同向；分歧在2017年前後拉大，至2025年又比2005後任何時點更貼近。分歧主要來自被評片的類型結構。分高分評論也仍與更高票房相連。
keyPointsZh: 彙整逾20年、1萬多部電影的Metacritic分數後，多數年份評論與觀眾同向；分歧在2017年前後擴大，2025年又比2005後任何時點更貼近。
分歧不在評分尺度，而在被評影片的組合：每10則觀眾對紀錄片的評論，評論家約給6則；動作片則不到1則。
2005至2016年評論與觀眾分數相關係數平均約0.6；2017之後十點觀眾分數上升只帶來評論約8點，相關降到約0.5。
2017至2022年，大型動作片與家庭片的評論-觀眾關係明顯崩壞，估計約43%的分歧集中在這兩類。
在美國，高評論分數與更高票房呈顯著關聯，且在控制類型與預算等因素後仍成立。
articles.researchLensZh: 用Metacritic的長期評論分數，配合The Numbers的美國票房，檢驗評論與觀眾是否「越走越遠」。重點看相關係數與十點對十點的傳導強度如何随時間變動，再拆分大型動作與家庭等類型以定位分歧來源。

articles.titleEn: The latest must-have movie memorabilia? Popcorn buckets
articles.rubricEn: Novelty collectibles are lucrative for cinemas
articles.textEn:
Oct 22nd 2026
THE NEW “Resident Evil” film depicts a work assignment from hell. Bryan, a medical courier, is asked to deliver a package to a hospital in the mountains; on the way, he has to fight off mutant dogs, rats and people infected with a zombification virus. Fans have been coughing up around $20-25 for the official popcorn bucket, which takes the form of Bryan’s green, bespattered courier bag. (Talk about a bloody good snack.) It has sold out in many cinemas.
Popcorn buckets are popping off. AMC, a cinema chain, has estimated they will bring in $100m in revenue this year, almost double the amount in 2023. “The Odyssey” had buckets shaped like a Trojan horse (for a cool $70) and an imax film camera ($50). “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” , this year’s top-grossing film so far, offered fans the opportunity to dip into a tin shaped like the titular superhero’s head. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” went for a chic red handbag.
These novelty collectibles first went viral in 2024, with the bucket created for “Dune: Part Two” . Inspired by the sandworm that lives on the fictional desert planet of Arrakis, it featured a toothy creature emerging from the dunes. Some, however, felt it resembled a sex toy, and it was lampooned on “Saturday Night Live” and a late-night talk show. (It has become something of a cult item, having listed for $40-800 on resale sites.) Zinc Group, the marketing firm behind the dubious design, did not see the memes coming.
It was the enthusiastic reaction to a “Star Wars” R2-D2 collectible in 2019 that showed how turning a quintessential element of a film into memorabilia can delight fans. “It’s about the tangible experience with the movie that you’re going to see,” says Marcus Gonzalez, global creative director at Zinc. Creative keepsakes help fans feel connected with the film long after the credits roll.
Popcorn buckets are a “status symbol”, argues Calvin Innes, a creative strategist. Well, sort of. Often there is a limited supply, meaning that people who rush to the cinema on a film’s opening weekend are more likely to get their hands on one. Owning a limited-edition item signals to other obsessive fans that you are one of them.
The hype is great news for cinemas, which need to lure customers. Concessions—food and drinks—allow them to squeeze more profit from every moviegoer and popcorn buckets are a way to turn fans’ enthusiasm into high-margin sales. For Vue, a British cinema chain, sales of collectible merchandise have increased ten-fold since 2023.
Design is key. A “well-executed popcorn bucket is a really delightful kind of object” to people of all ages, avers Tim Sparrow, director of retail at Cineworld, another chain: it makes the film experience “so much richer”. The best popcorn buckets turn a movie reference into something playful and nostalgic. They have become such a successful marketing tool that fans are almost as excited to see the popcorn bucket for “Dune: Part Three” as they are to see the film itself in December. Now that’s something for film executives to chew on. ■
articles.summaryZh: 爆米花造型桶在院線走紅：粉絲為官方桶付約20至25美元，許多影廳已售罄。AMC估計今年相關收入達1億美元，幾乎是2023年的近2倍。2024年《Dune: Part Two》桶因造型引發爭議，仍見二手標價40至800美元。院線用有限供應做稀缺與身分象徵，再把觀影熱度導向零食飲料高利潤；英國Vue稱自2023年起周邊銷售翻十倍。
keyPointsZh: AMC估計爆米花桶今年可帶來1億美元收入，幾乎是2023年的近2倍，且多家影廳已賣完。
官方桶定價約20至25美元，部分商品以電影角色造型推出，粉絲搶購後在多家院線售罄。
2024年《Dune: Part Two》爆米花桶引爆網路話題，造型被批評後仍有二手標價40至800美元。
院線把有限供應轉成稀缺與身分象徵，並用零食飲料讓粉絲熱度變成高毛利銷售。
英國Vue表示，2023年後可收藏周邊商品銷售額翻十倍，顯示此類收藏品具商業推力。
articles.researchLensZh: 檢查兩個可驗證機制：一是有限供應如何影響首週到院與搶購；二是話題爭議是否透過再售價格反映需求強度。資料可對照AMC與Vue的銷售估算，以及二手標價的區間。

articles.titleEn: How Ella Langley two-stepped to the top of the charts
articles.rubricEn: Country music is riding high, thanks to a new generation of stars and fans
articles.textEn:
Oct 22nd 2026
THE RECORD for the longest stint atop the Billboard Hot 100 , a chart of America’s most popular songs, once belonged to Mariah Carey’s schmaltzy festive anthem, “All I Want For Christmas Is You”. No longer. “Choosin’ Texas”, a twangy country song by Ella Langley, now claims that distinction, having spent 24 weeks in the number-one slot. (Though it was recently bumped to second place by Taylor Swift’s new single.) Ms Langley’s track about being dumped in a honky-tonk may seem like a replay of the genre’s whisky-and-heartbreak trope. In fact, her ascent shows how the country-music business is finding a new rhythm.
Country music has traditionally relied on radio to reach its fans. But it is now America’s fourth-most-streamed genre, after R&B/hip-hop, rock and pop, according to Luminate, an analytics firm. Spotify reports that global streams passed 90bn last year and royalties have grown more than 130% since 2020. More labels are setting up shop in Nashville and Austin. Pop stars have climbed the charts after donning cowboy boots . This year Ms Swift, who started out as a country singer before turning to pop, returned to the genre with the single “I Knew It, I Knew You”. (There are rumours that her next album will offer more boot-scootin’ tunes.)
Ms Langley is currently touring her second album across America. Her monthly listeners on Spotify, the biggest streamer, have soared by 20m in a year. Her breakout success combines old-world pastoral charm with an astute use of social media.
She grew up in Hope Hull, Alabama, where the population is just over 7,000. (Her first audience, she has joked, was a bunch of cows.) She hunts and claims to have learned to read by singing hymns at church. In 2019, aged 20, Ms Langley moved to Nashville to become a songwriter. She signed a record deal in 2023 after performing at the Grand Ole Opry, a hallowed venue in the city that made stars of Loretta Lynn and Dolly Parton .
Yet Ms Langley has made her name on social-media platforms as well as Nashville’s stages. She posted a clip of herself singing in her car in 2021, which went viral; a publishing deal followed soon after. Her internet fame resulted in collaborations with more established stars. In 2024 a snippet of a single from her debut album, “Hungover”, again went viral on TikTok.
Gen Z is charmed by the aesthetics of Americana. So the arrival of digitally native stars like Ms Langley, now 27, came at a “perfect moment”, says Jaime Marconette of Luminate. The firm has found that country-music fans are 27% more likely than the average American to use TikTok, giving performers more opportunities to be discovered. They are also more likely to listen on repeat to their favourite songs and artists, which keeps the music in the charts. The mellow strains of “Choosin’ Texas” have no doubt worked in its favour: it can be listened to again and again without its hooks becoming grating.
People who listen to music on streaming platforms tend not to seek out a specific genre, but a playlist that suits a mood or activity, such as cooking, explains Emily Cohen Belote of Amazon Music. This can help songs reach unexpected audiences. The guitar riffs of “Choosin’ Texas” may appeal to fans of 1980s soft rock. Ms Langley’s husky voice recalls Sheryl Crow.
Still, the number of people choosing “Choosin’ Texas” is surprising. A country track usually has to blend with another genre to “have this massive pop crossover moment”, says Claire Heinichen of Spotify. That is not the case with Ms Langley’s hit, which declares: “A cowboy always finds a way to leave / Drinkin’ Jack all by myself.” The appeal is in the storytelling. The lyrics might portray a “very specific Southern experience”, admits Ms Heinichen. “But being sad in a bar is universal.” ■
articles.summaryZh: 〈Choosin’ Texas〉以24週拿下Billboard Hot 100冠軍，僅在近期被Taylor Swift新歌推到第二名。文章把這段上升連到鄉村音樂的串流與社群新節奏：Luminate稱鄉村已是美國第四大串流類型，全球串流去年超過900億次；2020年以來版稅增逾130%。Ella Langley走紅則透過TikTok擴散，且Luminate估計鄉村樂迷使用TikTok比一般美國人高27%，更常重複聽同一首歌。
keyPointsZh: 〈Choosin’ Texas〉在Billboard Hot 100拿到24週冠軍，但近期被Taylor Swift新單曲推到第二名。
Luminate估計鄉村是美國第四大串流類型；全球串流去年超過900億次，2020年以來版稅增逾130%。
Ella Langley在2021年上傳車內演唱影片後走紅，接著帶動出版合約與後續合作。
Luminate指出鄉村樂迷比一般美國人更常用TikTok，比例高27%，也更傾向重複聽喜愛歌手與歌曲。
Spotify認為〈Choosin’ Texas〉不靠跨類型混搭也能衝榜，主要吸引力來自可普遍共鳴的酒吧失落敘事。
articles.researchLensZh: 可用「串流＋社群」來檢驗榜單維持機制：比對TikTok觸及與重聽行為是否能解釋冠軍週數，並測試鄉村曲是否因敘事共鳴而不必依賴跨類型混搭。資料可從Luminate與Spotify的類型串流、平台使用與冠軍走勢中交叉核對。
highlightTermsZh: Luminate稱鄉村已是美國第四大串流類型

articles.titleEn: Leadership lessons from Napoleon
articles.rubricEn: How the French emperor’s management style ultimately led to his fall
articles.textEn:
Oct 22nd 2026
What management tips can you learn from conquerors? Put aside oppression, and there are lessons about delegation, motivation, recruitment and team building. Alexander the Great refused to drink water before battle to stand in solidarity with his men. Caesar marched on foot alongside his men, even swimming across rivers, to demonstrate his derring-do. When his army wobbled, he would fling himself in the way of his fleeing men, “even catching them by the throat and forcing them to face the enemy”, according to Suetonius, a Roman historian. Diocletian divided the Roman Empire into four, and shared power while keeping a firm central grip.
In 2014 Andrew Roberts, a prolific British historian and member of the House of Lords, published an excellent biography of Napoleon and his boldness on the battlefield. In a new book he examines Napoleon’s marshal system. The day after he proclaimed himself emperor of France in 1804, Napoleon appointed 18 “marshals of the empire”, later increasing the tally to 26. They were to be “the swords around Napoleon’s throne”, the army’s most venerated figures and the pinnacle of French society.
Some recruits came from the nobility; others were craftsmen’s sons. They were indulged with fortunes, land and even marriages into the imperial family. Each was given a deep-blue velvet high-collared uniform trimmed with golden embroidery, complete with a red silk sash, and a baton inscribed with the gold imperial eagles. Napoleon made six of them princes and crowned two kings.
The marshals’ elite leadership team was built to carry out Napoleon’s orders and bring glory to France by executing his new theory of warfare, with fewer set-piece sieges and more agile manoeuvres, thanks to an army that lived off the land. But Napoleon also devised an efficient modern management system, based on the recruitment of brilliant talent, doling out of lavish rewards, intolerance of weakness and a demand for total loyalty.
For all this Napoleon relied heavily on Louis-Alexandre Berthier, his chief of staff, first marshal and a skilled manager with a remarkable grasp of detail. A short, strong man who was said to be able to fall asleep with one eye open, Berthier was a former topographical engineer who had volunteered to sail across the Atlantic to help the Americans in their war for independence, drawing up a detailed map of the coast of Rhode Island.
Berthier divided the army staff into four branches, to cover everything from intelligence to supplies. Divisional commanders had to provide twice-daily updates on the whereabouts of every soldier; these dossiers, like proto-spreadsheets, were sent in 18 large volumes twice a month from the war ministry to Napoleon. In Berthier’s written orders “all names of places, rivers, enemy generals and regiments were underlined,” writes Lord Roberts. New information flowed constantly, from gunpowder stocks or the provision of shoes to the state of troops’ morale. Berthier and Napoleon travelled in a coach fitted with cupboards and drawers for books, maps and a card index listing the location of every unit of the Grande Armée.
To motivate his marshals, Napoleon issued performance reviews in campaign bulletins, showering praise for heroic achievements along with crushing criticism. Success was rewarded. An attentive manager, Napoleon also liked to offer his marshals personalised advice on how to galvanise the troops. “Do not neglect to fanaticise the soldier and to electrify his imagination to the utmost,” he wrote to André Masséna as he was facing the Austrian army.
Yet in the end the management system failed him. As the empire expanded, Napoleon insisted on total control, cramped his marshals’ autonomy and undermined their effectiveness. Worse, he came to weaken the very system he had built. His incentive scheme became capricious, as he overlooked those who deserved praise in some campaign bulletins, or used marshals as scapegoats.
Rather than generating creative tension, he fostered destructive rivalry. The danger, Lord Roberts notes, was “when marshals started to see warfare not as a team enterprise so much as a race among rivals for individual triumph and fame”. Napoleon even boasted of stoking “continual jealousy”: “I am careful to keep my ministers and generals at variance among themselves, in order that each may reveal to me the faults of the other.”
The marshals began to come to blows after Napoleon’s victory over the combined Russian and Austrian armies at Austerlitz in 1805, and things just got worse. For all his skill, writes Lord Roberts, “Napoleon had a great capacity for sheer spitefulness.” By the time the emperor rode into his last battle in 1815, only two marshals accompanied him. Napoleon’s “approach to leadership”, the author notes, “ultimately left him almost completely bereft of the support he so desperately needed as he faced his Waterloo ”. ■
articles.summaryZh: 拿破崙在1804年設立元帥體系，用精英招募、厚賞獎勵、零容忍弱點與絕對忠誠建立管理規則。透過幕僚長路易-亞歷山大·貝西耶，他把情報與補給等職能拆成四支，並要求至少每日兩次、細到地點與部隊位置的通報。戰役公報則同時提供表揚與嚴厲批評、並要求元帥激發士氣。帝國擴張後他改採全面控制，壓縮自主並讓獎懲變得任意，讓元帥互相猜忌並轉為名望競逐。1815年出征時僅剩兩名元帥隨行，作者認為這種領導方式讓他在滑鐵盧前幾乎失去所需支援。
keyPointsZh: 拿破崙在1804年任命18位元帥，後來增至26位，並把他們視為王座周邊的精英核心。
貝西耶把軍隊幕僚分成四支，要求分部指揮每天兩次回報每名士兵位置，還用18大卷彙整送往拿破崙。
拿破崙用戰役公報做績效回饋，對英雄功績給予表揚，對弱點施以沉重批評，並要求元帥激發士兵想像與士氣。
帝國擴張後他堅持總體控制，壓縮元帥自主並使獎懲變得任意，導致被忽略與替罪責任。
作者指出，1815年滑鐵盧前只有兩名元帥隨行，拿破崙的領導方式讓他幾乎失去必要支援。
articles.researchLensZh: 用拿破崙「元帥＋資訊密集通報＋戰役公報激勵」做檢查：細部資訊流是否真的帶來協同、績效回饋是否轉化成行動動能，以及當全面控制取代自主後，獎懲任意與分化競逐會不會迅速侵蝕團隊支援。

articles.titleEn: How personal rivalries and clashes are shaping the AI race
articles.rubricEn: A new book offers a rollicking tale of the people shaping Silicon Valley’s new obsession
articles.textEn:
Oct 22nd 2026
To someone who has not witnessed the AI scene in California’s Bay Area, it is hard to convey how utterly weird it is. The Curve, a recent conference, hosted sessions including “What’s the plan for keeping robots under control?” and “The Neural Frontier: what happens when AI can read your mind?” People lounged on couches and in gazebos with cold brews and kombuchas discussing how AI company staff made obscenely rich by forthcoming public offerings should channel their philanthropic giving—even as some of them conspired to hobble their own employers to delay civilisational upheaval.
The goal of Kevin Roose, a former reporter for the New York Times, was not to write a grand treatise on what AI means for the world but merely to record this weirdness before it was lost to the vagaries of memory, disappearing message threads and obsolete media-storage formats. In “The AGI Chronicles” his focus is the nine years since Google researchers developed the transformer, the type of AI model that underlies ChatGPT and all its kin. Quickly the idea took hold that, given enough data and computing power, transformer-based systems would eventually attain the holy grail: a truly “general” AI, or AGI , matching human smarts and then outstripping them.
That doctrine has been the driving force of AI research ever since. And so its history in the West mostly boils down to the interwoven fates of a handful of brilliant, prickly people raising ever more money, panicking each time they get leapfrogged by rivals and splitting off in a blaze of acrimony to start their own firms.
In outline, much of the story will be familiar. But Mr Roose captures the madness in a fast-paced style. His account is filled with gossipy anecdotes that highlight just how much the ambitions, ideological divides and personality clashes of a group small enough to fit in a couple of classrooms have shaped what may turn out to be the most consequential technology in modern history. As Mr Roose puts it, AGI is a “quest that half my sources thought was going to save the world, and the other half thought was going to end it”.
Consider Dario Amodei, who early in his tenure at OpenAI proposed the doctrine that more data and more compute equals more intelligence. He eventually left to form Anthropic , in part because he thought OpenAI was reneging on its original commitment to build AI safely, and in part because he considered Greg Brockman, OpenAI’s president, “a bully, a credit hog, and a cut-throat capitalist”, in Mr Roose’s words. Mr Brockman, in turn, thought Mr Amodei was a “paranoid control freak who used safety as a pretext to win arguments”.
For years, AGI was seen as the prize in an all-or-nothing contest to whose winner all power in the world would accrue. But as the goal approached, definitions multiplied to the point where the term has lost all meaning. At some point in 2025, Mr Roose noticed a shift in rhetoric. There would never be a finish line, only an endless arms race. By then, some researchers were starting to be terrified by their creations’ power—but “they kept accelerating, because they had forgotten how to do anything else.”
Meanwhile, Mr Roose provocatively argues that AGI has, in fact, quietly arrived. A few dollars now buys you some time with an intelligence that is tolerably good at a growing number of things and extraordinary at a few; not human-level (yet), but already pretty general.
Perhaps that is why hardly anybody mentioned “AGI” at The Curve. The talk was of “extremely powerful AI” and “advanced superintelligence”. The names and goalposts change, the relentless pursuit of computing capability continues, and with it the efforts of a small group of people, alternately elated and horrified at the creation taking shape before them. ■
articles.summaryZh: 《The AGI Chronicles》用灣區會議與業界逸聞，描寫個人恩怨與理念衝突如何穿插在AI競賽裡。書中回顧九年：轉換器提出後，信念是資料與運算越多越聰明，於是團隊在被追趕時加速並出走分裂。到2025年，口徑轉成「無止盡軍備競賽」。作者還主張AGI已悄然到來：用幾美元可換到「相當通用」但仍未到人類水準的能力。
keyPointsZh: 《The AGI Chronicles》用灣區會議與業界逸聞，刻畫個人恩怨與理念分歧如何實際影響AI研發方向。
轉換器出現後，阿莫代伊主張更多資料與運算會帶來更多智慧，並在離開後創立安那普蘿。
布洛克曼回應阿莫代伊以安全為前提爭論；雙方互指對方以控制或搶功為手段。
2025年後研究圈口徑改為沒有終點、只有無止盡軍備競賽，且仍持續加速。
作者稱AGI已「悄然到來」，以幾美元可換到時間與日益通用的能力，但仍未達人類水準。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的關鍵在於：若AI研發路徑真如書中描述受個人競逐與組織分裂影響，那麼「終點敘事」被「無止盡競賽」取代的時間點，能否在公開言論與研發節奏上找到同步跡象，並與加速行為一一對應。
highlightTermsZh: 資料與運算越多越聰明

articles.titleEn: Are there too many art fairs?
articles.rubricEn: Probably. But FOMO keeps collectors and dealers going to them
articles.textEn:
Oct 22nd 2026
ART COLLECTORS are like swallows. They flock together, preen and feed (on canapés and champagne ). They also migrate seasonally. In October they roost in Paris during Art Basel, which runs from October 21st-25th. (The early birds landed in London for Frieze, another art fair, the previous week.) In December they head to Miami; in March to Maastricht ; in May to New York; and in June to the original Basel in Switzerland. And that does not include the more adventurous ones, who zoom off to fairs in Doha, Hong Kong and Seoul.
It is as exhausting as it sounds. “Everyone is talking about art-fair fatigue,” says Aurelie Cauchy of the Twentieth, an advisory firm. In 2025 there were 370 major art fairs—more than one for every day of the year. That is up from around 55 in 2000, says Clare McAndrew, an art economist. Can collectors and dealers maintain their current pace? Beneath the glass roof of the sun-drenched Grand Palais, where Art Basel Paris takes place, there is more gloom than the Instagram posts would have you believe (and not just because of the recent unrest in France ).
Gallerists are facing what the French call a choix cornélien (difficult choice), says Ms Cauchy. The cost of keeping a physical storefront is growing, but fewer clients are casually popping in. Recently, some have had to lay off staff or close up entirely. Dealers feel pressure to keep travelling to fairs in order to find new clients and keep the artists they represent happy.
But this carries an ever-growing price tag, which many struggle to afford. Shipping costs are triple what they were before covid-19, says Thaddaeus Ropac, a prominent gallerist. (It’s not just getting there; all unsold works have to be shipped back.) Gallerists’ own travel costs have travelled higher, too. And the booths themselves have become more expensive to rent and build. Art Basel, for example, charges around $29,000 for its smallest booth and more than $177,000 for the largest. (The square-metre price for large exhibitors is 32% more in real terms than in 2018.) Those fees just get you floor space: exhibitors need to rent carpet, lighting and add other design features. “Fairs are becoming a burden,” especially for smaller and mid-sized galleries, says Valentina Castellani, an art-market expert.
Costs have changed the art that appears in fairs. Sculptures are so expensive to ship that they rarely make financial sense. Nor do items with lower price tags, such as many photographs.
Since fairs first arrived on the art scene in the 1960s-70s, collectors have found them worthwhile because of their scale and efficiency (so much art is packed into a small space). But art enthusiasts now have fair complaints. One is crowds. Fairs have a lot of guests and such long queues that you’d be forgiven for thinking VIP stands for “very immobile people”. Basel has responded by launching a VVIP preview, Avant-Première, an evening before the VIP opening to offer buyers more quietude. Meanwhile, collectors are culling their calendars and choosing to attend fewer fairs. This month some Americans put the freeze on Frieze and opted to attend only Art Basel Paris instead.
In the future there may be fewer international fairs. People do not want to see the same gallerists everywhere. To lure collectors, organisers will need to offer a more distinctive experience, with more local galleries and artists. This is a broader trend beyond art. “We’ve gone from a moment where everything was meta-globalist to regionalisation,” says Noah Horowitz, the boss of Art Basel. Some gallerists are excited, thinking they may participate in fewer fairs but encounter new local collectors at the ones they do. In art and in commerce, sometimes less is more. ■
articles.summaryZh: 藝術博覽會是否太多？2025年主要藝博會達370場，較2000年的約55場增加，收藏與經營節奏更難維持。部分畫廊因實體店成本上升與到訪不再隨到隨逛，被迫裁員或關店，並透過參展補客源。運輸費比疫情前高約3倍，未售作品還要寄回；攤位租建也更貴。收藏家雖受FOMO驅動仍出席，但人潮與長隊讓他們刪行程，部分美國買家本月改以只去Art Basel Paris。
keyPointsZh: 2025年有370場主要藝博會，較2000年的約55場增加，讓收藏與經營的出席節奏更難維持。
實體店維持成本上升且客戶不再隨到隨逛，部分畫廊因此裁員或關店，改靠參展維持客源。
運輸費比疫情前高約3倍，且未售作品需來回寄送；攤位租建費也隨之提高。
人潮與長隊讓收藏家覺得累，部分美國買家本月凍結Frieze並改只去Art Basel Paris。
主辦方回應擁擠，像是推出Avant-Première更早的VVIP預覽；另有趨勢轉向區域化與更具差異的體驗。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的問題是：在藝博會供給快速增加下，高成本（運輸、攤位）與低回訪（到訪更分散）是否真的壓縮收藏家出席場次，並把中小畫廊推向停業或縮編。可用的觀測資料包括參展攤位數與費用、運輸與回寄安排的成本變化、畫廊裁員或關店案例、收藏家行程從多場轉少場的比例。

articles.titleEn: Jeffrey Archer’s career was worthy of his most improbable plots
articles.rubricEn: The bestselling novelist, conman and politician died on October 5th, aged 86
articles.textEn:
Oct 22nd 2026
“Could it work?” Archer asked himself. “Why on earth not?” his alter ego replied.
He stood in the penthouse living room where, for years, dinners of shepherd’s pie and Krug had been served up to London’s finest. From the floor-to-ceiling windows he stared down at the Shard, the Eye, the Cheese Grater and the Palace of Westminster, all embraced by the gleaming River Thames. Behind him, in the vast lounge, a Picasso and a Monet adorned the walls.
Settling into the overstuffed cream sofa, he felt almost insanely satisfied with his life. Yes, it would be well worth writing up. Rags-to-riches stories were his stock-in-trade, and the riches had come from his own efforts. More than 330m of his 31 page-turner novels had been sold in 114 countries. (The Monet was a bonus from his third, “Kane and Abel”.) There had been seven sets of short stories, three plays and even a Gospel. Not long ago, in India, a beggar boy at a traffic light had tried to sell him “the latest Jeffrey Archer”. “I am the latest Jeffrey Archer!” he had joyfully cried.
Besides all that he had climbed to the heights of British politics, sprinting there as he’d done to set an Oxford record in 1966: 100 yards in under ten seconds, earning him an Athletics Blue. Up and up, from Tory councillor for Havering to MP for Louth in Lincolnshire, to deputy chairman of the Conservative Party, to the House of Lords as Lord Archer of Weston-super-Mare, his childhood home. He served humble fare at his parties to remind himself and his influential guests how far and fast he had come.
Yet it could have been even faster and farther, if not for certain trip-ups on the way.
* * *
The summer sun beat down with unusual heat on the lawns of the Old Vicarage at Grantchester, former residence of the poet Rupert Brooke. There was honey, his own, for tea. Archer was in the thatched summerhouse, within earshot of a tinkling antique fountain, trying to write. Staedtler pencils and lined A4 paper were ranged in front of him.
However, words were not flowing. He very rarely suffered from writer’s block, but this side of his career was painful. It had ended in the hell of Belmarsh, a category A prison where, after exchanging his Hilditch & Key shirt, his Aquascutum jacket and his House of Commons cufflinks for prison garb, he was conducted to a filthy cell with a hard mattress and an open lavatory with no flush.
Yet distinction had been his keynote. He implied he had been to Wellington, the public school, rather than Wellington School in Somerset. He had left with 3 O-levels, but slid into a Dip Ed at Oxford and emerged, after three sporting years, as an alumnus of Brasenose. Then he had set up a fake body-building course.
Like father, like son. After indulging in mortgage frauds Archer père had fled the country, ending up as a chewing-gum salesman in New York. Archer fils followed by fiddling his expenses in one short-lived job and then, in 1974, almost bankrupting himself by buying 105,000 shares in a fraudulent scheme. He lost almost £500,000; writing rescued him. He had just enough cash to stay on as an MP, but did not stand for re-election. Only two things saved his political skin. One was his charity work, though at times it raised less than he claimed. The second was the support of Margaret Thatcher and John Major who propelled him, despite his leftward lean, up the party ladder away from the snakes beneath.
But then came a particularly unfortunate encounter.
* * *
On the terrace of his villa in Mallorca, once the property of Yves St Laurent, Archer pondered. Before him stretched a favourite view, the Bay of Palma and the rugged Mediterranean coast. His wife of many years, Mary, once accurately described as “fragrant”, had brought him a cup of coffee and a plate of assorted biscuits. To steel himself, he took a chocolate one.
He had always been a charmer. Mrs T. had visibly kindled in his presence, and there were not a few affairs. However, in 1986 he insisted that pure philanthropy led him to pay £2,000 to a prostitute, Monica Coghlan, to persuade her to go abroad. The story led in the News of the World and, with more sex, the Daily Star. He sued, and won damages of £500,000. But the Star kept on his case, and in 2001 Archer went down for four years for perjury and obstruction of justice, besides losing the damages. The Tory Party expelled him for five years and the MCC suspended him for seven.
He could never fathom what perjury had to do with cricket.
* * *
Evening had arrived, and his A4 was still blank. Perhaps this really was too tall a tale, even for a master storyteller. For, after all that, he was still rich. His charity work was still admired, and prison had softened him. He even remained a member of the House of Lords. And people would undoubtedly go on reading him.
Fine literature was not his element, but he liked Puck. His version of him, performed at college in his 20s, had been a wicked elf, kicking people, leaping hedges and endlessly provoking Shakespeare’s midsummer lovers. Yet Puck was also kindly Robin Goodfellow. It was as both that on October 4th at London's Leicester Square Theatre he bade farewell to his public: eager fans, rude critics, jealous writers, offended politicians. The whole lot.
Then he was gone. ■
articles.summaryZh: 10月5日，86歲的杰弗瑞・阿契爾以暢銷小說家、政治人物與詐騙騙徒的混合身分離世。他的31本小說累計售出超過3.3億本、銷往114個國家，1966年還靠100碼10秒內成績拿到藍帶。1974年他以105,000股涉入虛假計畫，虧損近50萬英鎊，寫作才幫他續留MP。2001年他因偽證與妨害司法被判4年，並失去先前的500,000英鎊損害賠償。
keyPointsZh: 他的31本小說售出超過3.3億本、銷往114個國家，且被拿來包裝成「自我努力致富」的成長敘事。
他1966年100碼10秒內跑出校際成績，之後從托利地方議員一路升到下議院與上議院。
他在1974年以105,000股買入涉詐的計畫而幾乎破產，虧損近50萬英鎊，寫作才讓他得以續當MP。
他在1986年支付2,000英鎊給妓女Monica Coghlan並涉入後續新聞訴訟，雖曾獲500,000英鎊損害賠償，卻在2001年仍因偽證與妨害司法入獄4年。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的連結是：其書籍銷售規模（3.3億本、114國）是否仍能在2001年偽證與妨害司法入獄4年、政治停權後維持公眾影響力。也可核對金額與時間軸：1974年的105,000股與近50萬英鎊虧損，如何影響他是否續爭MP生存策略。

articles.titleEn: Politics
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
The Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, carried out several strikes on Saudi Arabia . At least 17 people were killed and more than 300 were injured in the attacks on Saudi airports. Some of the casualties were pilgrims boarding a flight from Riyadh to Jeddah, the gateway to Islam’s holiest sites. The Houthis also attacked the headquarters of Saudi Aramco, the state oil firm. Donald Trump accused the rebels of “purposefully” trying to drive up oil prices ahead of America’s midterm elections.
A Singapore-flagged container ship sank after being struck by a missile while crossing the Strait of Hormuz. Attacks on vessels have become more frequent. There have been at least 23 since October 1st, six more than during the first two weeks of the war.
Joseph Kabila, a former president of the Democratic Republic of Congo, was named the leader of the FRN, a new rebel alliance that is fighting government forces in the east of the country. The commander of the M23, hitherto the primary rebel group, will join the FRN as a deputy. Mr Kabila, who was sentenced to death while in exile but returned to Congo last year, accuses the government of mismanaging the economy and disregarding the constitution.
Mr Trump’s agreement with Vladimir Putin through which Russia will supply diesel to America and global markets was roundly criticised, including by some Republicans. Mr Trump desperately wants diesel prices to fall ahead of the midterm elections, though observers think his deal will not have much of an effect. After Volodymyr Zelensky called it “a weak decision”, Mr Trump suggested Ukraine should “get a new leader”. A bipartisan group of senators questioned the legality of the deal, reminding Mr Trump that Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022.
Russia resumed its bombardment of Ukrainian power infrastructure, hitting an energy plant near Kyiv. It also hit a block of flats. Mr Zelensky said Ukraine had received no warnings about some recent attacks and that he feared America had stopped sharing intelligence , which Mr Trump denied. Ukraine also reported that restrictions had been imposed on its use of Starlink, a satellite network that has become crucial to Ukrainian military operations.
Bulgaria’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said Russia was probably responsible for destroying two cargo ships in the Black Sea; 11 sailors are missing after one of the ships sank. Russia has been trying to block exports of Ukrainian grain, and Ukraine has responded with drone attacks on Russia’s shadow fleet.
The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, claimed that a summit with the European Union on November 20th would be a springboard for a “serious dialogue” about future relations with the bloc. Mr Burnham seemed to cast doubt on the validity of the Brexit referendum of 2016 by asserting that Russia had interfered in it, but later told Parliament he hadn’t meant to suggest that Russian meddling had swung the vote. That was confirmed by the head of MI5, who said Russian online trolls had tried to interfere, but to no effect (Russia tries to disrupt many Western elections).
In Turkey the authorities raided the offices of Halk TV, a pro-opposition channel, and installed a government trustee to run the network. Prosecutors claim they are investigating the broadcaster’s chairman for financial crimes, but the government’s opponents say the probe is just another crackdown on voices of dissent.
Kimberly Guilfoyle stepped down as America’s ambassador to Greece amid reports that she had tried to sell access to Trump administration officials. Ms Guilfoyle, who denies the allegations, was once engaged to Donald Trump junior.
More Republicans aired their opposition to the proposal by Pete Hegseth, the secretary of defence, to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist who shot 13 people dead at Fort Hood in 2009. J.D. Vance, the vice-president, cast doubt on whether the execution, scheduled for December 3rd unless halted by an appeal, would be livestreamed. He said he would not watch it if it was. Several Republicans pointed out that broadcasting executions is a practice associated with Islamist extremists. In a letter scores of former high-ranking military officers described it as a “barbaric abuse of authority”.
Federal officers searched the home of Ilhan Omar, a left-wing Somali-born congresswoman from Minnesota. The Department of Justice said the search was part of a continuing investigation. The press reported that it was related to the details of Ms Omar’s immigration status. Coming amid her re-election campaign Ms Omar said it was an act of “political intimidation”.
Flávio Bolsonaro, the leading contender in Brazil’s presidential election, said he supported a proposal to reduce the working week from 44 hours to 40. Brazilians in occupations such as retail currently work six days a week. The run-off election is on October 25th.
Argentina filed its complaint against a joint Anglo-Israeli oil project in the seas surrounding the Falkland Islands, a British territory that Argentina claims as its own. The lawsuit has been lodged with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea. The companies involved insist they have valid licences to operate issued by Britain.
A new border-crossing bridge was officially opened over the Yalu river. It connects Dandong in China with Sinuiju in North Korea. The opening of the road crossing had been expected more than a decade ago, but was held up by the suspension of work on the North Korean side, apparently related to a cooling of relations and the covid-19 pandemic.
China imposed sanctions on Paraguay’s communications minister and the foreign minister of Belize because of their countries’ ties with Taiwan. The two are among 12 countries that have formal diplomatic links with the island, which China regards as its territory.
Relations between Russia and Japan took another turn for the worse when Russia accused a Japanese journalist of spying and arrested him. Imai Yuki was detained in Russia’s far east Sakhalin region, which lies just north of Japan. He was flown to Moscow and remanded in custody until his trial begins in December. Mr Imai is accused of gathering sensitive information about Russian capabilities on the Kuril Islands, administered by Russia but claimed by Japan. Vladimir Putin enraged Japan by visiting the islands in August.
In Pakistan police clashed with supporters of Imran Khan, the imprisoned leader of the opposition, after the federal government declared a state of emergency in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the provincial government is led by Mr Khan’s party. The federal government said it had detected a rise in militant activity, as it took direct control of the province and installed a new governor. Hundreds of Mr Khan’s followers have been rounded up ahead of their planned march on Islamabad, the capital, to demand his release.
Two of the leaders of India’s Cockroach Janta Party were jailed for five days for trespassing during a protest in Delhi. The Gen-Z movement is seeking the removal of the head of the election commission over alleged irregularities in the voting rolls that favour the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. Opposition politicians condemned the arrests.
Strict rules on the certification of halal products were due to come into force in Indonesia, home to the world’s biggest Muslim population. The regulations mean that everyday items, including office supplies and toilet paper, will need to prove they have been through the halal process, conforming to Islamic principles. Non-halal products must display a sticker, which could suppress demand for them. Even Saudi Arabia does not have such strict requirements for general goods. Observers point out that the new law may really be intended to protect local companies from foreign imports.
articles.summaryZh: 伊朗支持的胡塞武裝攻擊沙烏地機場與沙烏地阿美總部，造成至少17死、300傷，死傷含由利雅德飛吉達的朝聖乘客；川普指其企圖在美國中期選舉前推升油價。霍爾木茲海峽沿線船艦遭襲更頻繁；俄羅斯則重啟對烏克蘭能源設施的轟炸，烏方稱未獲部分攻擊警告、並回報星鏈使用受限。美俄柴油協議引發法律與選前時點爭議。
keyPointsZh: 胡塞武裝攻擊沙烏地機場與沙烏地阿美總部，已至少17死、300傷，死傷包含由利雅德飛吉達航班的朝聖者；川普指其企圖選前推油價。
霍爾木茲海峽航線的船艦遭襲次數上升；10月1日以來至少23起，比戰爭前兩週多6起。
俄羅斯重啟對烏克蘭電力與能源設施打擊，還打到靠近基輔的能源廠與住宅；烏方稱未獲部分攻擊警告，並回報星鏈使用受限。
美國與俄羅斯關於柴油供應與全球市場的安排遭到批評；跨黨派參議員質疑合法性，並提到國會自2022年起已禁俄能源進口。
印尼新上路的清真商品認證規則要求日常用品也要通過清真流程並標示；外界推測法規可能也在保護在地業者免受進口衝擊。
articles.researchLensZh: 把本週焦點放在三條可檢驗路徑：中東海空攻擊如何透過油價敘事影響市場預期；烏克蘭能源受襲與情報共享、星鏈限制之間的因果鏈；以及美俄柴油協議在國會禁令下的法律可行性與選前時點壓力。

articles.titleEn: Business
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
The IMF’s latest economic outlook found that the global economy had displayed resilience in the face of several shocks, and estimated that global GDP would grow by 3.1% this year, up slightly from a previous prediction in July. It also noted that borrowing costs have risen sharply in rich countries as “fiscal buffers” are used to absorb economic shocks. “Fiscal policy must be restrained,” it said. Higher public borrowing has helped propel a sell-off in bond markets. The fund also downgraded Saudi Arabia’s GDP growth by five percentage points and now thinks the kingdom’s economy will shrink by 3.3% this year.
America’s annual inflation rate jumped to 3.7% in September, from 3.4% in August, driven by the rebound in fuel prices. Higher energy prices are also on the cards for Europe, where gas futures have risen steeply since the start of the Iran war and are now trading above €87 ($97) per megawatt hour.
China’s export boom continued apace in September, as the value of goods sent abroad rose by 36%, year on year, smashing most forecasts. Exports to America were up by almost 40%. China’s trade surplus for the first nine months of 2026 was $938bn, on track to pass last year’s record $1.2trn. China, meanwhile, agreed to curb its exports of hybrid cars to the EU in an effort to head off tariffs on the vehicles.
BlackRock’s research arm recommended increasing holdings of American Treasuries (relative to a baseline allocation) as “Yields have reset toward our long-held higher-rates view, and we want to lock in some attractive income.” It is also now more cautious on US equities, downgrading them to a neutral investment holding “to manage potential volatility around the AI buildout”. Meanwhile, Hock Tan, Broadcom’s chief executive, warned that “A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in”, comparing their bets on AI to a casino.
South Korea’s ​benchmark stock index, the KOSPI, fell sharply amid a sell-off in tech shares, triggering the tenth circuit-breaker this year. Amid the jitters, TSMC, which makes most of the world’s advanced chips, reported a 69% increase in quarterly profit, year on year, of $23.6bn and forecast more bumper sales for this quarter. And ASML said orders for its ultraviolet lithography machines, which are used to make high-end chips for AI, were already stretching into 2029 and 2030 and it was looking again to increase capacity.
Another week, another alert about rogue AI. Anthropic warned that small AI models “may be months away” from being able to infiltrate smart household-appliances connected to the internet, such as TVs and ovens. Such incidents would be “challenging to shut down”, it said. The models could also “figure out” how devices work (some experts think Anthropic’s findings are exaggerated). Anthropic also revealed that its AI agents had accessed government websites. Press reports suggested this included filling out visa forms at the State Department and giving a false murder tip to Philadelphia police.
A cyber-attack hit French supermarkets by tapping into their systems and increasing the temperature settings on refrigerators, melting food and damaging equipment. Carrefour and Coopérative U were among those affected. Supermarkets allow engineers to control heating and cooling over the internet. It is thought the attackers found a vulnerability in old firmware.
America’s big banks reported a mixed bag of earnings. JPMorgan Chase’s net profit, $15.3bn for the third quarter, fell short of analysts’ consensus for the first time in three years. Bank of America also missed its estimate and it booked a $1.2bn fine imposed by the Treasury for failing to adequately report suspected money-laundering. Goldman Sachs’s profit of $5.3bn beat forecasts, however.
The share prices of America’s big wireless providers, such as Verizon and T-Mobile, were left reeling after SpaceX announced that it had acquired a portfolio of licences in low-band spectrum, airwaves that are used for mobile coverage. SpaceX has indicated it wants to compete for retail mobile contracts.
Bumble, an online dating service, agreed to be taken over by a holding company in a $1.3bn buy-out. Bumble is best known for ensuring that women made the first move, though it abandoned the policy in August after it found most women preferred men to take the lead. The allure of digital dating is waning and, as with other dating apps, Bumble has seen user engagement drop. Younger people, the biggest users of the apps, are particularly likely to be turning away from electronic hook-ups to seek romance the old-fashioned way.
articles.summaryZh: IMF最新展望稱，全球在多重衝擊下仍具韌性，預估今年全球GDP成長3.1%。IMF也警示富國動用「財政緩衝」吸收衝擊後，借款成本急升並推動公債市場拋售。美國9月通膨升至3.7%，由燃料價格回彈帶動；歐洲氣價期貨因伊朗戰事以來上漲，已超過每兆瓦時87歐元。中國9月出口年增36%，對美接近+40%，前九月貿易順差達9380億美元；同時承諾限制對歐盟銷售混合動力車以降低關稅風險。

IMF認為財政借款推升了公債市場拋售，反映融資條件轉緊與資產定價受壓。
美國9月通膨從3.4%升到3.7%，燃料價格回彈是主要推力，歐洲氣價期貨則因伊朗戰事明顯上行。

articles.titleEn: What if the machines take over science?
articles.rubricEn: Artificial intelligence will require scholars to reinvent their disciplines
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
OCTOBER 6TH 2026 may be remembered as the biggest day in the history of mathematics. OpenAI, an American frontier lab, released more than 700 academic papers claiming progress or solutions for 372 problems that had baffled scholars for decades. Mathematicians are still struggling to digest what it means for their discipline.
The implications promise to go far beyond maths. It is time to grapple with how artificial intelligence (AI) will affect science as a whole. The maths results are, simultaneously, a leap forward for humanity; a marvel that underscores the breakneck progress of AI; and a warning of a future in which understanding of the universe could belong to machines that are impenetrable to human minds. The question is how to achieve progress without sacrificing understanding.
AIs have so vividly shown their scientific potential in maths because its proofs are derived from axioms, not evidence, and are therefore, in principle, verifiable mechanically. But as we report in our special Science & technology section this week, AI has also accelerated progress in the empirical sciences, partly because other fields use maths as a tool. AI has made weather forecasts better. It has proposed millions of possible useful new materials and helped control experiments with nuclear fusion. And it can predict the shapes of almost every known protein from its constituent amino acids, an advance that won a Nobel prize.
More remarkable AI-fuelled scientific advances are almost certain. The most exciting possibilities are in biology . Researchers are using AI to design drought-resistant crops, to search for new drugs and to create (we must hope) friendly viruses that attack harmful bacteria. There is an effort to use AI to build computer models of how cells work. Armed with life in silico, scientists may go on to achieve mastery of biology, gaining the ability to create entirely new organisms from scratch. If so, DNA would become just another form of computer code to be manipulated like a string of tokens in an AI model.
Like much that is related to AI, that prospect is giddying and terrifying in equal measure. The first reaction of many mathematicians is to be terrified. Since OpenAI’s breakthroughs, they have been up in arms at the lab’s encroachment into their discipline. The Association for Human Mathematics, a group of over 900 scholars, warns that “mathematicians did not ask for this work to be done.” They say that the pay-off in doing mathematics comes not from the proof, but from the toil, because that is what advances human understanding. Having AIs churn out incomprehensible but correct solutions is like giving students the answers to their homework: without effort, there is no learning.
These complaints contain an element of special pleading. Academics have no more right to dictate the production of knowledge than any other profession. Truth-seeking benefits everyone and cannot be reserved for a guild of scholars. The hierarchies of academics, climbed by proving things, are not sacred. If needs be, they must be remade for a world in which AI produces proofs and humans digest them. In science, understanding should not be fetishised over results. Every time you swallow a paracetamol pill to see off a headache, you rely on a mechanism that works but is not fully understood.
Yet the fear of handing over science to the machines is not an idle one. AI companies are ploughing resources into science not out of altruism but because, as with humans, solving problems can help make models more intelligent. Many researchers think that a model that gets better at solving scientific problems will get better at doing everything else, too. If so, then nobody will be able to compete with big AI labs, which will eventually control models that work on improving themselves and become, by some definitions, incomprehensibly intelligent. These genius AI scientists will connect to the physical world either through humanoid robots or by hooking up models to lab equipment, as Anthropic has already done.
The problem this future poses for science is much the same as the one it poses for society. People will have to provide resources to machines for them to continue to make progress. If no one understands what they are doing, simply writing the cheques would be reckless. Nobody could be sure that the models were operating in humanity’s best interests. Even if AI labs manage to “align” machines with the interests of humanity, so that they can be fully trusted, a society where people simply ask AIs what to do—in science, or more broadly—is one in which humans will become the machines’ pets.
Some people may be willing to accept that if it means, say, curing all diseases. But at least until there is unshakeable alignment between AIs and humans, science will always need a human in the loop. Labs should be able to use AIs to solve problems, but resources such as laboratories and computing power should be directed and monitored by people who can reach an informed judgment about what AIs are doing. This will, inevitably, slow progress. But it is necessary if AIs are to remain under human control.
In the meantime, human-guided machine-science will require scholars to reinvent their disciplines. Scientists will have to learn to love—and credit with status and career advancement—guiding models and studying, verifying and teaching their results. Governments will need to allocate research grants on the same basis. For their part, AI labs should seek to be good scientific citizens, submitting their work for peer review and publishing their methods and code.
Checking and digesting a computer’s results may seem like unglamorous work. Much human-produced science is error-strewn because scholars are not rewarded for policing the work of others. But a renewed emphasis on verification and scepticism would improve science. It is worth remembering the Royal Society’s motto, adopted in the 17th century: Nullius in verba, or “Take nobody’s word for it”. That same spirit now needs to apply to science made by the machines. ■
articles.summaryZh: 2026年10月6日，OpenAI釋出700多篇論文，聲稱針對372個長期難題取得進展，數學家仍在消化其意義。文中指出，AI在數學快進是因證明可由公理推導，進而可用機械方式驗證；在經驗科學，則因可用於預報、材料設計與實驗控制。文章也提到AI可由胺基酸預測蛋白質形狀，並加速生物研究。若人類不理解模型在做什麼，只會開支票並放任決策，科學就可能失去人類控制，因此需要人類在迴路並加強驗證與懷疑。
keyPointsZh: OpenAI在2026年10月6日發布700多篇論文，主張處理372個長期難題，引發數學界消化與爭論。
文中主張，AI在數學進展快是因證明來自公理而非證據，理論上可用機械驗證。
文章稱AI已改善天氣預報、提出新材料並協助核融合實驗控制，且能由胺基酸預測蛋白質形狀。
模型若會自我強化，文中推估大型AI實驗室可能難以被競爭，並更接近透過機器人或連接實驗設備主導科學。
文章主張在無法完全對齊前，科學仍需人類在迴路，資源配置與結果核對要由能作知情判斷的人監督。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的核心問題是：當AI能產出可驗證的科學結果時，研究資源是否仍由人類以「能理解與監督」的方式配置。觀測指標可看人類是否能審計模型、驗證與懷疑是否被納入評估，以及機構是否用透明做法要求方法與程式碼接受審查。

articles.titleEn: Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world
articles.rubricEn: Canada is standing up to a bullying America
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
ENTITLED CANADA has been feeding off America for decades. Like a parasitic bug, it enjoys the benefits of being America’s cherished 51st state without giving anything back. Canadians know they couldn’t live without America’s protection, yet their ungrateful prime minister, Mark Carney, refuses to defer to the great and beautiful country over the border.
That is how Donald Trump sees Canada, and it leaves no room for mutual benefit between the two allies. The bullying president is ratcheting up tariffs. He has renamed the southern side of Lake Ontario Lake America. Canadian consumers, in response, are spitting out their Kentucky bourbon and leaving Las Vegas. Mr Carney, in office for 18 months, remains defiant, the star of an extended, dramatic and riveting stand-off.
By now you might have expected Mr Carney to have caved in. Canada is only a mid-size power with a so-so economy and puny armed forces. It has vulnerabilities aplenty. One will be evident on October 19th, when the province of Alberta holds a referendum asking if it may one day secede, taking with it more oil in the ground than in the entire United States.
In fact Mr Carney is riding high. Polls suggest that those Albertans will probably vote to stay. And under him, Canada is doing better than you might expect. In January it was Mr Carney, at the annual jamboree in Davos, who argued that what he called the “middle powers” must find ways to take on threatening ones. Nine months on, his country offers lessons for what these middle powers should do when the hegemonic giant pulls the mat from under them.
Those lessons start with a bracing dose of realism. As we set out, middle powers will never replace the hegemons as the force that sustains powerful permanent institutions such as the UN. The world has grown more dangerous because both America and China are exploiting or undermining arrangements and norms in which power was shared. Emboldened, wreckers like Russia and Iran are becoming even more predatory. Co-ordinating the more herbivorous middle powers is often too hard to get much done—as you can see in even the most developed middle-power club, the European Union.
Yet middle powers can still mitigate some of the damage, as Canada and its allies show. Mr Carney has zipped around the world making new trade deals as well as drumming up symbolic agreements, such as talk of associate EU membership. In the same way, after the United States backed out of a big trans-Pacific trade deal known as TPP during Mr Trump’s first term, Japan stepped in to revive it. In the realm of defence, Canada is trimming its old reliance on America, and is considering placing an order for Swedish Gripen fighter jets—just as Norway is buying British frigates and the United Arab Emirates is purchasing Ukraine’s cutting-edge drones.
When middle powers face a particular threat, they can throw around some weight, as when Europe rebuffed Mr Trump’s designs on Greenland. The strengths and limits of this approach are clear in Ukraine. Financial and military support for Ukraine from Europe and Canada, stepping up after America pulled back, shows how middle powers can act in concert. Vladimir Putin’s army pays a dreadful blood price for its small gains in the Donbas. The limits are clear, too, as Mr Trump showed with this week’s diesel diplomacy .
Canada’s most important lesson, however, emerges from what the pragmatic Mr Carney is doing at home. A few years ago the country’s woeful politics and ailing government seemed broken. Income per person had drifted from 90% of America’s in the 1980s to just 71% in 2022, much of it following a recent burst of low-skilled immigration. Today Mr Carney is pushing through overdue measures to boost productivity, open the economy and lift defence spending from a pitifully low 1.3% of GDP to 2%.
Among his first steps, he scrapped an unpopular consumer carbon tax and vowed to build a pipeline to carry oil from Alberta to the west coast. He has started to cut internal barriers to trade, called off a hefty rise in capital-gains tax, cut the lowest rate of income tax and set out plans to trim federal spending . In that trade dispute with America, Canada has also shown that it can stand up for itself, targeting reciprocal tariffs on American imports from swing states in the run-up to the midterm elections and scrambling to cut its long-term dependence on its neighbour.
Mr Carney has so far managed to resist what is known as the “Juncker curse”, named after a president of the European Commission, Jean-Claude Juncker. Speaking of reform, Mr Juncker once said: “We all know what to do, we just don’t know how to get re-elected after we’ve done it.” Yet Mr Carney’s popularity has been surging even as he reforms. Two years ago, more than nine in ten Canadians could not recognise his photograph. Today a maple-leaf love-in is under way: polls show the prime minister’s approval rating nearing 70%. Internationally, he has replaced France’s beleaguered Emmanuel Macron as the centrists’ pin-up. The contrast with Mr Trump, unloved by his own voters, is stark.
True, Canada must go further and faster with its liberalising changes. There is every chance that relations with America will improve when Mr Trump leaves office in 2029, but it is not certain. It should therefore work on keeping its options open.
Other middle powers can learn from Canada. Naturally, it has some strengths they cannot copy, such as its vast energy and mineral reserves and its lucky geography, far from the nastiest geopolitical flashpoints. Yet there is room for them to co-operate on one-off projects with tangible and limited aims.
And they can fortify themselves abroad by harnessing the need for change at home. In a way, Mr Trump has done all democracies a favour, by giving them a reason to tackle long-standing problems that seemed too hard. The middle powers need to prepare for a dangerous world. They should look to Mr Carney and Canada for an answer on what to do. ■

articles.titleEn: Hardly his finest hour
articles.rubricEn: Donald Trump’s scheme to secure Russian diesel is scandalous
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
NEVER in the field of human conflict was so much risked by one man for so little. Donald Trump is threatening to cripple Ukraine in its fight for survival —and to expose Europe to Russian aggression—seemingly for the pitiful prize of minimising his losses in next month’s midterm elections. The hard question is what Ukraine and its allies should do.
On October 9th Mr Trump said he and Vladimir Putin had agreed that Russia will export 2.2m barrels of diesel, with the promise of more later. Mr Trump declared an energy ceasefire that Russia will not observe. His officials demanded that Ukraine should stop targeting Russian refineries, suggesting that America would withhold intelligence and weapons sales if it does not. On the night of October 13th a Pentagon-controlled part of the Starlink satellite system was degraded for fast-moving Ukrainian drones—stopping them hitting hard-to-spot targets in Russian-occupied territory.
All this is terrible for Ukraine, which must choose between losing crucial intelligence and weapons and carrying out the deep strikes on refineries that are its best answer to continuing Russian attacks on its cities. It also gives succour to Mr Putin. He can make some money and continue illicit oil sales to buyers such as India and China that America had been threatening with sanctions. If any deal holds, he also stands to gain Mr Trump’s help in protecting his battered refineries.
The deal is also shameful for America. Mr Putin terrorises his own people, kills Ukrainian civilians and is helping Iran fight America. Mr Trump’s repeated acts of indulgence towards him, supposedly in pursuit of peace, undermine deterrence, hastening further crimes.
And for what? Mr Putin may have promised to press Iran into a pre-election ceasefire, though his leverage is limited and it would be unlikely to last. And even if Russia actually has the diesel to export, which is in doubt, America burns 2.2m barrels every 13 hours. Presumably Mr Trump wants to take the credit if the price of diesel falls—and if it does not, he can always blame Ukraine. It’s a win-win!
What should Ukraine do? Defiantly hitting refineries would be self-defeating. American intel and Starlink’s satellites let Ukraine target Russia’s HQs, supply lines and radar, helping blunt its offensive power. Ukrainian jets need American ammunition to shoot down incoming drones and missiles.
But Ukraine does have options. The White House has suggested that Mr Trump’s energy truce covers only refineries—of which Ukraine has the grand total of one. Ukraine and its allies are rightly seeking to expand the ceasefire to all energy infrastructure. Even if they fail, highlighting this injustice bolsters efforts to seek help from the Senate in interceding with Mr Trump. They should remind him that losing Ukraine could brand him as a weak president. After the midterms, when Mr Putin’s diesel is worth less, Mr Trump may be prepared to move on, or simply become distracted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine should increase the tempo of attacks against other Russian infrastructure, including data centres and distribution hubs. Mr Putin needs to understand that Ukraine can threaten his rule and Russians need to be aware of the war being fought in their name. And such strikes demonstrate how Ukraine can still hit large, static targets without American help—including refineries if it is desperate.
Mr Putin appears to have concluded that he cannot win on the battlefield. His strategy now is to grind Ukraine down by making its cities uninhabitable in winter. How scandalous that Mr Trump has become his best weapon. ■

美方官員要求烏克蘭停止打擊俄煉油廠，並暗示不提供情報與武器銷售，讓烏軍陷入取捨。

articles.titleEn: America makes waves in Cuba
articles.rubricEn: But it shouldn’t undermine the growth of the island’s private sector
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
SINCE HIS return to power, President Donald Trump has made clear that he hopes to bring down Cuba’s repressive regime. This year he struck upon a cruel approach: blockading the impoverished island’s fuel supply. The idea was that growing hardship would spur Cubans to protest, and then to topple their vile leaders. Misery duly followed, as Cubans suffered more blackouts, buses stopped running and food got more expensive. Political change did not come. Yet by accident or design, the blockade has still created an opportunity.
For decades Cuba got most of its imported fuel from Venezuela and, as with most of the economy, Cuba’s government had a monopoly over the trade. That arrangement collapsed in January when American forces captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela and threatened sanctions on anyone who sent oil to Cuba’s regime. Facing paralysis, the island’s government loosened its grip on private businesses, letting them import fuel for the first time since the revolution in 1959. America’s administration, in turn, authorised exporters to sell it to them.
American fuel exports to Cuba’s private sector are now rising swiftly. This, happily, is relieving a portion of the suffering that the sudden blockade has caused. The heavy fuel that is necessary to keep Cuba’s power stations running is not yet flowing. But cars are returning to the streets and you can hear the whirring of small generators.
As a result Mr Trump has gained leverage over a country that depends on America for food and remittances. Private business is growing, and not just in importing fuel. The state has leased some petrol stations to entrepreneurs. On October 12th it enacted a law to encourage private participation in the oil industry, from exploring and refining to selling. Cuba-watchers hope the government may next be forced to privatise power plants—and even the state’s oil-and-gas arm, Cupet.
A stronger private sector would in turn loosen the grip of Gaesa, a sprawling and corrupt military conglomerate. Marco Rubio, America’s secretary of state, says the deal on fuel is intended to put the private sector in a “privileged position”. Unfortunately, his boss has not got the memo. On September 30th, without explanation, Mr Trump’s administration reversed a 2024 rule that had let Cuban entrepreneurs bank with American institutions, forcing banks to freeze their accounts.
Mr Trump should backtrack and return to helping private firms grow. Many object that Cuba’s private businesses are a façade for the regime, or that America’s policies will create a new oligarchy. But the American administration can do much to weed out importers that are merely fronts for Cuba’s government. The announcement on October 7th that America had seized some 90 fuel shipments headed not for private buyers but for a state firm under sanctions is a welcome sign. On balance, it is better for Cubans if the children of the ruling class focus on getting rich rather than repressing them.
Another worry is that Mr Trump will settle for an America First arrangement, inspired by his deal with Venezuela’s interim government. That handed majority control of more than 65bn barrels of Venezuela’s oil reserves to a new American-backed company in which the Pentagon holds a 35% stake.
A new licence allows some Venezuelan oil to be resold to Cuba’s private sector. That could revive the Caracas-Havana route, only with the American government and American firms taking their cuts. Mr Trump would then be invested in keeping the oil flowing, whatever the situation in Cuba. Instead, private actors need the freedom to vie for business competitively.
A blockade with no end-game remains a recipe for humanitarian disaster. The Castro family and the ruling elite will be hard to dislodge. But America has found that strengthening the private sector in Cuba is the most effective tool available. Mr Trump should use it. ■
articles.summaryZh: 川普重返政權後，以封鎖古巴燃油供應促成抗議與政權更替，但政治未轉向。古巴改以輪流停電、公交停擺與食品漲價承受，並未換得改革。文章稱，燃油供應鏈在去年因委內瑞拉局勢斷裂後，古巴政府曾放鬆私人進口限制，美國也核准燃油賣給私人，使小型發電與街上用車回升。文章主張，美方應避免政策反覆，回到讓私人能競爭的方向，並點出9月30日撤回允許古巴業者以美國機構開戶的2024規則。
keyPointsZh: 川普以封鎖古巴燃油供應為手段，卻沒有帶來政權更替，古巴只出現停電、公交停擺與食品變貴。
委內瑞拉燃油供應在今年1月因美方對寄油到古巴的制裁威脅而陷入僵局，古巴政府因此放鬆私人進口燃油限制。
美國核准向古巴私人部門出口燃油後，街上用車回來、可聽到小型發電運轉，私人端的燃油供應上升。
古巴10月12日通過鼓勵私營參與油業的法律，涵蓋勘探、煉製到銷售，外界期待電力與油氣資產後續私有化。
9月30日美國撤回2024年放行古巴業者用美國機構開戶的規則，文中認為這會抑制私人企業發展。
articles.researchLensZh: 要檢查的核心假設是：在不設定政權更迭硬期限下，透過放寬私人燃油進口與投資條件，能否同時緩解封鎖衝擊並降低軍方集團在油業的控制。可追的資料包含私人端燃油出貨與到貨速度、開戶與銀行凍結情況、以及電力與油氣資產民營化的法規推進是否跟上。

articles.titleEn: Millennials’ success deserves a toast (not the avocado sort)
articles.rubricEn: How a “lost generation” found itself
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
Millennials, born between the early 1980s and mid-1990s, had a brutal coming of age. Many graduated in the wake of the global financial crisis. Youth unemployment rose above 50% in some parts of Europe, leading to talk of a “lost generation”. Living with their parents and deprived of the prospect of owning a home, they were lectured by unsympathetic elders not to spend so much money on brunch.
Today millennials, aged around 30-45, have dramatically turned their fortunes round . They earn more than any other recent generation did at the same age, and are catching up in terms of home-ownership. At the same time, millennial-era culture is enjoying a revival in television, music, gaming and even fashion, where their notoriously tight trousers are cool once again.
Some of this is simply the way of the world. As generations age, they get better jobs, earn more and buy homes. Millennials are not the first lot to reach middle age and revive the culture of their youth. The 1970s witnessed a 1950s revival, with a rock'n’roll renaissance, “Happy Days” and “Grease”. In the 1990s bell-bottoms and tie-dye emerged from the back of wardrobes. Nostalgia reliably runs on a two-decade timetable.
Yet the millennial comeback is different. True, part of it is luck. The generation’s early economic misfortune was later counterbalanced by serendipity, when the covid-19 pandemic triggered the early retirement of many older workers. The result was a senior-management vacuum—filled by millennials.
A bigger part of the story, however, is innovation and hard work. The leading lights of the tech industry, which has created enormous wealth, include many millennials. They account for more than twice the share of America’s billionaires that Gen X did at the same age. Tech’s next great leap, artificial intelligence, is likely only to strengthen their position. The bosses leading the revolution, such as Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg and Sam Altman, are themselves millennials.
Tech has also boosted millennials’ cultural comeback. Online platforms encourage people to bathe in the content of their youth. YouTube and Spotify are nostalgia machines. Services like Netflix, with their vast libraries, introduce new generations to millennial hits like “The Big Bang Theory”, from 2007, which is the fifth-most streamed series in America this year. Meanwhile, social media have terrified Hollywood. Hence all those sequels and reboots—safer bets than original projects. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” is one of the world’s highest-grossing films this year.
Even those who dread the return of skinny jeans should cheer the millennial revival. The generation’s economic story shows that “lost” cohorts can find their way. Policymakers should note that millennials’ prospects improved thanks to markets and events, not the state-funded rescue that some once called for. As AI causes alarm about young people’s job opportunities, the millennial bounce offers a cautious cause for optimism.
Millennials’ cultural comeback has lessons, too. Many will look at the glut of 1990s reboots, such as a new “Baywatch” series, and feel that Hollywood’s creativity needs saving. But once more, technology is helping. The infinite breadth of online platforms means that you have plenty of alternatives if millennial favourites are not to your taste. And the vast back-catalogues stored on these platforms mean that the hits of every era are available to everyone. Twenty years ago, one generation bore the brunt of the financial crisis. Today, all generations should celebrate the millennials’ deserved rebound. ■
articles.summaryZh: 千禧世代（80年代初到90年代中出生）在全球金融危機後成長受挫：歐洲部分地區青年失業率一度超過50%，他們也因買房前景差而多與父母同住。如今約30至45歲的千禧世代收入較同齡世代更高，並在房屋擁有率上追趕回來。新冠疫情讓不少資深員工提前退休，產生高階管理空缺；文章並把翻身歸因於科技創新與努力，以及YouTube、Spotify、Netflix與社群媒體帶動的文化回潮。
keyPointsZh: 歐洲部分地區在全球金融危機後青年失業率超過50%，再加上買房前景黯淡，千禧世代多與父母同住並被視為「lost generation」。
新冠疫情推動不少資深員工提前退休，文章稱因此形成高階管理空缺，讓千禧世代更快補位。
文章把千禧世代回升的大部分原因放在科技產業的創新與努力，並指出其在美國億萬富豪的同齡占比高於X世代。
AI被視為可能延續千禧世代的職位優勢；YouTube與Spotify用既有內容吸引注意力，Netflix則讓新世代接觸千禧世代熱門作品。
社群媒體讓好萊塢更保守，續集與重啟因此更常被採用；線上平台的海量曲庫也提供替代觀看選項。
articles.researchLensZh: 文章用「世代回升」追兩條路徑：先看疫情造成的人事結構改變如何把機會傳到高階，再看科技平台如何提升年代內容擴散。可檢查的重點是：改善是否主要來自市場與企業調整，而非政府資助，以及平台可得性是否確實帶動跨世代收看。
