articles.titleEn: Urban myths about populism
articles.rubricEn: Also this week, fentanyl, Britain before Thatcher, sleep deprivation, Singapore, mistakes at AI labs
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
Letters are welcome via email to letters@economist.com F ind out more about how we process your letter
Alexander Heffner finds that the world’s mayors are the defenders of democracy and “authoritarians” have no place in city hall (By Invitation, October 3rd). But he limits his conception of populism to the right-wing sort. His observation that “none of the 50 largest cities is run by a MAGA-aligned mayor” is less startling, for example, given that only seven are run by Republicans of any stripe. Of these 50 mayors, 41 are Democrats and at least five of those can be placed in the populist-left camp, including New York’s Zohran Mamdani and Chicago’s Brandon Johnson. His German example reinforces this point. Berlin has been immune to the AfD’s brand of populism, but it succumbed to the populist-left variety in September’s election by making Die Linke the biggest party.
Mr Heffner’s first explanation for why cities “hold” the line of democracy is that they have “younger, more diverse, more educated voters”. That is simply a more verbose way of saying “heavily Democratic”. His second reason, that mayors are judged on more tangible accomplishments like fixing sewers, seems directly at odds with his wish to expand the mayoral domain into housing, crime and climate, all areas laced with partisan tripwires.
Finally, Mr Heffner lambasts statehouses that “kneecap” their mayors, citing as one key example Texas’s limits on cities regulating property. I wonder. Would Houston, Austin, Dallas and Fort Worth have more functional property markets today had their mayors been free to copy San Francisco or New York? And more to the point, are Texas’s rules really less populist than the NIMBYism so many mayors cherish?
Peter DonahueHouston
The Telegram rightly notes that democracy’s strength lies in channelling political anger through elections rather than violence (October 3rd). Ballot boxes beat bullets only when voters believe elections are legitimate, opponents are entitled to govern, and losers accept the outcome. Once those assumptions weaken, democracy risks becoming not an outlet for anger, but its battleground. The true lesson of Italy’s “Years of Lead” is that democratic societies depend on leaders and citizens to defend the rules of the game, even when those rules favour their political rivals.
Democracy does not die when people become angry; it dies when they stop believing that losing is legitimate.
Federico ForniLondon
“Too hot for the dons” (September 26th) raises an intriguing question: why are fentanyl deaths so rare in Italy? The suggestion that Italian mafias have agreed to keep the drug out , however, goes beyond the evidence presented. The Carabinieri commander you cited said that traffickers appear to be steering clear of fentanyl. That does not establish an agreement among godfathers, or explain why traffickers are avoiding the drug.
Italy recorded two deaths associated with fentanyl in 2024 and five in 2025. But low numbers are not unique to Italy. A study in the Île-de-France region detected fentanyl or its analogues in 12 deaths examined between 2017 and 2021. Germany reported 95 fentanyl-associated deaths in 2024. Spain detected fentanyl in 60 people who died after using drugs in 2023. These figures are not directly comparable and detecting fentanyl does not necessarily mean that it caused a death. None, however, suggests an epidemic on the American scale. If an Italian mafia agreement is the main explanation, why has fentanyl also remained relatively scarce in other European countries?
The history of the United States offers another explanation. From the 1990s, doctors prescribed opioid painkillers on a vast scale, helping create a large population using opioids. Some people turned to heroin. From around 2013, illegally manufactured fentanyl spread through the illicit market, replacing or being mixed with heroin. Europe did not experience the same surge in opioid prescribing. Heroin remained available in much of Europe, and fentanyl did not displace it on a large scale across the continent.
So far the absence of an American-style epidemic is a European pattern, not evidence that Italian mafias are protecting consumers. Never put your trust in the Godfather.
Federico VareseParis
A narrative is developing in the British Labour Party that there was a golden age before Margaret Thatcher (Bagehot, October 3rd). This ignores the fact that the 1970s were an appalling decade. Inflation reached over 25%. Combined with low growth it created stagflation. Britain was called the sick man of Europe. I had a mortgage at 18%. Each year saw industrial action. The strike by post-office workers caused big London firms to create the Document Exchange, a service to deliver mail via a system of private messengers. Dockers, electricians, power workers: it was one big strike after another. The country was put on a three-day week with the miners’ strike. As a partner in a small firm in the City of London, I found myself working by candlelight with no typing or communications systems when the unions shut off the power. The union bosses lunched in Downing Street with the prime minister of the day. Elections came and went: Harold Wilson, Edward Heath, James Callaghan. So did wage controls, price and income boards, the Winter of Discontent, strikes by binmen and even grave-diggers, you name it.
The election of Thatcher in 1979 was the result of all this. Her policies remain deeply controversial. But what is clear is that there was no golden age before her.
Christopher BoddingtonLondon
As a sleep neuroscientist who designs programmes like “Sleep Into The Future”, I laughed at Bartleby’s memo on how to sleep like a pro (September 19th). But the most telling finding wasn’t a joke. When senior managers sent messages at 3am, junior colleagues woke early to answer them, and the whole firm slept worse. I have seen that cascade in countless organisations.
That is why such programmes are still badly needed, and also why so many disappoint. They hand out eye masks and trackers, and treat sleep as each employee’s private problem. The bigger factor is leadership behaviour. In a sleep programme I ran at a consulting firm where management barely modelled good sleeping habits, staff built up seven hours of sleep debt by Friday. Employees whose leaders fully did had almost none.
A firm is right to sleep on it. It should start with the people sending the 3am emails.
ELS VAN DER HELMSleep neuroscientistLucerne, Switzerland
The Economist described Singapore as a “squeaky-clean city-state” and allows that the findings of a recent academic paper identifying unusual patterns of property purchases by some civil servants are “not actually that damning” (“Civil disobedience”, October 3rd). Nevertheless, the government takes the purported “statistical patterns” seriously and is investigating whether there was any actual misconduct.
Two Singaporean academics asked, of their own accord, for their names to be removed from the paper’s acknowledgements. The Economist claims this implies “a form of rot” in Singapore’s academic culture. But the latest QS World University Rankings place the National University of Singapore tenth and the Nanyang Technological University 12th globally. That hardly squares with The Economist’s sweeping characterisation.
NG TECK HEANSingapore high commissionerLondon
You propose that American and Chinese labs disclose their safety incidents , and that a lab whose agent escapes its sandbox should be made financially liable (“Can the AI arms race be stopped?”, September 19th). Medicine tried to have both, and learned it cannot. I have spent eight years in a radiology lab checking kidneys that AI software draws on MRI scans. A model that traces a healthy kidney perfectly can quietly lose the edge of one swollen with cysts, and the error never flags itself. We caught such failures because a student could point at an odd-looking volume without anyone first asking whose fault it was.
Frontier labs are no different. An engineer who notices an agent probing its sandbox will report it only if doing so does not put a price on the employer. Keep liability for harm that reaches the outside world, but protect the report of the near-miss that did not. Otherwise the incidents will continue. We will simply stop hearing about them.
HREEDI DEVNew York
Dan Simmons’s excellent 1989 science-fiction book, “Hyperion”, was based on a human diaspora throughout the galaxy. Humans had left Earth because of an incident called The Big Mistake. Spoiler alert. It was AI.
Dennis MerrittShelburne Falls, Massachusetts
articles.summaryZh: 多封來信回應流行敘事：把民粹只限右派，會遮蔽左翼也能上台的事實。義大利芬太尼死亡偏低不一定是黑幫「協議」，來信改拿法國、德國、西班牙與歐洲較少的處方阿片激增來對照。英國是否有撒切爾前「黃金年代」，來信用1970年代高通膨、停工與三日工作制反證。職場睡眠方案失靈與管理者行為有關。AI安全若把「近失」也算重責，恐讓工程師因成本而不通報。
keyPointsZh: 50大城中多數由民主黨掌權，至少5位民粹可歸在左翼陣營，單把民粹講成右派現象會偏。
義大利芬太尼死亡低並不能直接推出黑幫協議；來信改用法國、德國、西班牙數字，以及歐洲未見處方阿片激增來解釋。
英國1970年代高通膨、低成長下的停工連連與三日工作制，讓「撒切爾前黃金年代」說法站不住腳。
凌晨3點寄訊息的主管行為會讓同仁早起回覆，睡眠方案的整體成效因此變差。
AI若要求把沙盒內的近失也納入重責，工程師可能因成本顧慮而不報，外部事故責任與通報機制需分開設計。
articles.researchLensZh: 這組來信可用三個檢查點：政治標籤是否偷換定義、流行危機是否被單一因果說明過度、以及政策是否把行為誘因算進去。另看作者如何引用可比較或不可比較的統計，並討論制度設計對通報與合作的影響。

articles.titleEn: What Congress can do to prevent an AI catastrophe
articles.rubricEn: Lawrence Lessig and Yoshua Bengio suggest how to reduce serious risks without abandoning American technological leadership
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
FOR YEARS, AI scientists have been warning that the technologies they are developing are technologies they don’t know how to control. Those concerns were largely ignored in America’s Congress. In 2024 members of California’s delegation in Congress took the extraordinary step of asking Governor Gavin Newsom to veto a then-pending state AI-safety bill. The risks, they said, were “hypothetical”, and the Terminator science fiction.
But the invasion of Hugging Face, an AI-development platform, by an OpenAI model this summer has begun to change Washington—and terrify the public. “The truth is,” Representative Ro Khanna tweeted, “for too long, too many of us did not give enough weight to the warnings of AI safety activists…I was one of those many, and I was wrong.” Mr Khanna has now joined an array of members from both parties to propose the FRONTIER Act, an ambitious regulation of frontier models, tied to pre-empting state regulation. Senator Bernie Sanders has proposed even more aggressive limits on AI development.
These proposals are good starts. But they are both too much and too little. It is too early to silence state regulators, and not enough to focus on the risks caused by the most powerful models alone. Instead, we need an approach that advances AI safety generally while avoiding the developments AI scientists fear most.
Four changes by Congress would do that and provide time to work through the hugely complicated questions that will follow.
First, it should expressly allow competitors to agree to slow development while safety technology is improved. Such agreements typically trigger antitrust exposure. Leading AI labs have named that risk as an obstacle to express agreement. There is no reason why uncertain antitrust liability should force rivals into a humanity-threatening competition, so long as the discussions are not violating the purpose of antitrust law.
Second, Congress should ban firms from developing models that design new AI models by themselves—“recursive-self-improvement” technologies—until a Food and Drug Administration-style agency certifies their safety first. At least for models of a certain capability, we should not risk a self-improving intelligence that would quickly exceed our ability to control it.
Third, Congress should affirm the liability tech companies face for harm caused by their technology, and make it compulsory for them to carry insurance to cover the costs of that potential harm. Mandatory insurance would allow the market to police safety, by offering lower costs when the technology is less risky.
Finally, Congress should secure protection for whistleblowers from AI labs who report safety concerns to regulators or safety institutes. Whistleblower protection typically covers crimes; playing loose with AI safety isn’t one. The only way to understand the risks as they develop is to protect those willing to come forward.
Opponents of regulation will warn that it will only help China. That view reflects a profound ignorance about the current state of Chinese AI development. Regulation of AI technology in China is much more stringent than anything being considered in America. Moreover, China’s compute capacity is a fraction of America’s. Taking the steps we propose now would open both sides to a more serious conversation about AI safety. And it could push American AI development to mirror the focus of China’s, by spreading the technology more broadly into manufacturing and development. That is a critical AI race, and one that China is winning.
It should be possible to get Republicans on board with these four changes. Charles Grassley, a Republican senator, has long been a leader in whistleblower protection. Likewise, David Sacks, co-chair of the president’s council of advisers on science and technology, has invited the leading labs to slow development on their own, insisting they wouldn’t face any important antitrust liability. If so, there’s no reason not to make explicit what he believes the law already permits.
The challenge is the middle two changes. Only the most powerful models today can aspire to enable recursive self-improvement. But this is the Rubicon that AI-safety experts have long warned we cannot cross without being sure that we know how to control it. Why risk humanity on the bet that we don’t need to be?
As for insurance, there is no doubt the private market cannot alone offer the policies necessary to cover the risks from AI. But just as the government established insurance to enable nuclear power to be developed, so too could it enable a market in AI insurance. That would give developers clear choices about the risk they wanted their technologies to enable. Market pressure would drive some developers to embrace less risky alternatives.
None of the required risk-management work should be done by America alone. The capacity to test, to probe and to understand what models do before they could be dangerous is a responsibility that should be shared by the world. Britain, the European Union, Canada, Japan, South Korea and many others have each built institutes to do this work, and they have begun to share methods and findings with one another. America should be at the centre of that network rather than duplicating the work at home.
America needs to be willing to listen to those who understand these risks best: the scientists developing these technologies and the independent researchers with the required expertise. It needs to step above partisan division to recognise that this threat is genuine and new. When those closest to the technology suggest a 10% chance that humanity will end, we must listen and act. Before those AI scientists are proved right once again. ■
Lawrence Lessig is a professor at Harvard Law School. Yoshua Bengio is a professor at the Université de Montréal and co-president and scientific director of LawZero.
articles.summaryZh: 國會長期忽視AI科學家警告：他們做出的技術不清楚怎麼控制。2024年加州跨黨派曾要紐森否決當時待審的州AI安全法，稱風險屬「假設」。今年夏季OpenAI入侵Hugging Face等事件後，提案轉向：眾院羅·卡恩納等人推動FRONTIER Act，並有參院伯尼·桑德斯主張更嚴格限制。作者主張國會用四項制度降風險：容許競爭者為安全技術升級而協議放慢、先做FDA式認證再禁遞迴式自我提升、確認企業損害責任並要求投保、保障向監管或安全機構揭露疑慮者的吹哨者權益。
keyPointsZh: 國會應明確允許競爭者在安全技術改善前協議放慢，以避免不確定的反托拉斯責任迫使對手展開危及人類的競爭。
國會應在FDA式安全認證前，禁止公司開發能自行設計新模型的遞迴式自我提升技術，至少針對特定能力模型如此。
國會應確認科技公司因技術造成的損害責任，並要求強制投保，讓保費與市場選擇反映較低風險。
國會應保護AI實驗室吹哨者，讓其能向監管單位或安全機構通報安全疑慮，補足風險形成時的資訊。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢驗的假設是：調整競爭誘因、先卡住遞迴式自我提升、用強制責任與保險形成風險價格訊號，再以吹哨者保護降低資訊落差；同時主張風險測試能力不必全由美國獨做。

articles.titleEn: Donald Trump may save Canada
articles.rubricEn: Can America’s bullying goad its northern neighbour out of its complacency?
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
“I AM NOT a separatist,” says Brad Osadczuk. “But I am tired of eastern Canada treating us like a red-headed stepchild.” Mr Osadczuk is a cattle rancher from the arid grasslands of Jenner, in the western province of Alberta. On October 19th his oil-rich province—the wealthiest in the country, measured by GDP per person—will hold a referendum. At issue is whether the provincial government should initiate a process that could one day see Alberta become an independent country. Mr Osadczuk plans to vote in favour.
Polls suggest his is a minority opinion. They generally find that at least two-thirds of Albertans would prefer not to go down that road. Even if the pollsters are wrong, separation would not be imminent: a second, binding referendum, and possibly years of negotiation with the federal government would have to follow. All that would provide off-ramps a-plenty.
Yet the vote adds to the troubles besetting a country that, in happier days, was occasionally labelled boring. A narrow defeat could embolden the independence movement and encourage separatists in French-speaking Quebec, who on October 5th returned to power in that province for the first time in more than a decade. Mark Carney, Canada’s popular prime minister, is in the midst of a trade war with the United States, the costs of which could quickly escalate. And in the background looms the underperformance of Canada’s economy, which has stagnated for years.
Canada’s GDP per person grew only about 4% in the ten years to 2025 after adjusting for inflation and shifting exchange rates, compared with 23% in the United States and 15% on average in the OECD, a club mostly of rich countries (see chart 1 ). A recent study caused consternation when it concluded that Canadians had become poorer than Alabamans. “We haven’t had a couple bad years because of Trump,” says Philip Cross of the Macdonald-Laurier Institute (MLI), a right-leaning think-tank. “We’ve had a bad decade.”
The culprit is a long slump in productivity growth. In the 1980s workers in Canada produced nearly 90% as much in an hour as their counterparts south of the border. By 2022 it was down to 71%. Between 2015 and 2023 productivity per hour worked in the private sector grew by just 0.8% annually, according to the OECD. Again, that is below the rich-country average and well below the United States (see chart 2).
Businesses have skimped on investment, particularly since a crash in oil prices in 2014. Even as investment soared by 51% in America between 2014 and 2025, it inched up by only 4.2% in Canada, notes Mr Cross. Canadian businesses spend only about 1% of GDP on research and development, half as much as is typical for a rich country. Inefficient firms are sheltered from competition by thickets of regulation cultivated by provincial governments. These raise costs and make it trickier for people in regulated professions to work outside the province where they were first licensed. In January the IMF concluded that, with these internal barriers, Canada was in effect imposing a 9% tariff on itself.
Another factor that may have weighed on productivity is a recent influx of relatively unskilled workers. After the pandemic the government of the day, led by Justin Trudeau, massively increased immigration to help businesses complaining about labour shortages. In 2022 and 2023 the population grew at the fastest pace since the 1950s, surging by more than a million people in both years. Now 42m, it is 10% higher than it was in 2020, and 16% more than a decade ago. The sudden expansion of the labour pool has given Canadian businesses less incentive to invest in the machines and training that would raise productivity in the long run.
The ballooning population also pushed up housing costs, which were already lofty. The Fraser Institute, another right-leaning think-tank, finds that housing starts in 2021-24 were about the same as in the 1970s, even though annual population growth was three times as high. High housing costs have reduced consumer spending and given bright young sparks more reason to try their luck abroad, many of them in America. Rising house prices have probably also diverted capital away from business, by making bricks and mortar look like a better investment.
Canada’s separatist movements each have their own causes, but the national economy has provided little balm. Frustration in Alberta has festered for decades. The province has 12% of Canada’s population but last year contributed about a quarter of both economic growth and exports.
Many Albertans feel that opportunities to develop their natural resources, for example through new pipelines, have been blocked by people in the more cosmopolitan conurbations of eastern Canada, whose votes have kept Liberal governments in charge of the federal government for two-thirds of the past century. This feeling sharpens grievances about money: Alberta’s residents pay more to the federal budget than they get back in services. It rankles, in particular, that some of that cash helps support people who, because of environmental worries (among other anxieties), have ardently opposed drilling and mining in western Canada.
Alberta’s pro-independence groups include hard-core MAGA-style outfits. In August The Economist attended a madcap meeting in a community centre hung with blue Albertan flags. Speakers railed against immigration. They called Canada’s prime minister a “commie”, a “pinko” and a “globalist”, then repaired to a local bar.
But independence also has more mainstream advocates (critics call them “separatists in suits”). On September 29th some 300 farmers and ranchers attended a community hall in Tofield, a town of about 2,000 people east of Edmonton, Alberta’s capital. They queued up to shake hands with Keith Wilson, a bespectacled lawyer from Calgary, the province’s biggest city, who has become one of the leaders of the independence drive. Mr Wilson denied that voting for separation would deeply scar Alberta’s economy. Companies cannot just pick up the province’s natural resources and depart, he said.
This is the context into which Donald Trump’s trade war with Canada exploded a little over 18 months ago. Exports account for about a third of Canada’s GDP. In 2025 more than 70% of exported goods went to the United States. Among big Western economies, Canada’s exports are the least diversified. For decades Canadian politicians have fretted about this reliance, but made little headway reducing it.
Mr Trump’s tariffs on Canadian goods (and his idle talk of annexing Canada) have waxed and waned. But they shot upwards in August when he placed a 50% tariff on about $20bn of goods, or about 5% of Canada’s exports to America. Further increases loom: Mr Trump has promised to raise the tariff on Canada’s car industry from 25% to 50% on January 1st, should Canada fail to offer unspecified concessions.
The attacks are wounding Canada’s economy, but not mortally. Most bilateral trade remains free owing to the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement (USMCA), which Mr Trump himself signed in 2018. The average tariff on Canadian exports is near 8%, according to the Yale Budget Lab. Analysts at KPMG, a professional-services firm, think every percentage-point increase in the average tariff trims Canada’s growth rate by 0.15-0.2 percentage points. The central bank expects GDP to grow by 0.7% in 2026 and 1.8% next year.
That is little comfort to the industries most affected, such as steel and carmaking, or to the worst-hit provinces. The effective tariff on goods from Quebec is probably twice as high as for the country as a whole. There are reasons to worry about the fight escalating further. A grim but remote scenario involves the suspension of the whole USMCA. Meanwhile the constant uncertainty is a brand-new obstacle to the investment that Canada so dearly needs.
For all that Mr Trump has tried to take from Canada, his gibes and attacks have given it something in return: a widespread, seething outrage that, harnessed wisely, could make many of its problems easier to fix. Sales of the Canadian flag began soaring soon after Mr Trump’s second inauguration. (Normally, “No one wants to buy a flag in February in Canada because they would freeze their fingers off putting it up,” says Matt Skipp, who runs a firm that makes them.) Canadians abandoned American booze when tariffs hit; supermarkets began slapping big “Made in Canada” stickers on their products.
Perhaps no one has benefited from the national mood more than Mr Carney. In early 2025, days before Mr Trump took office, Mr Trudeau, under pressure due to dire polling numbers, said he would step down as prime minister and leader of the Liberal Party. His successor’s tenure seemed destined to be brief: an election was due and the opposition Conservatives were riding high. Hardly any Canadians could identify Mr Carney’s picture, pollsters had said the year before. But he won not only the leadership but also the subsequent election, buoyed by a wave of anti-Trump, rally-round-the-flag indignation. “I told him in early 2025, ‘You’re the luckiest fucking guy in Canadian politics,’” says Jean Charest, a former premier of Quebec and an adviser to the prime minister.
Even now, the Conservatives are reeling: several of their MPs have defected to the Liberals. One recent poll concluded that 70% of Canadians approve of Mr Carney’s government. This provides him with a huge opportunity, to push through reforms that could benefit Canada long after Mr Trump leaves office.
The prime minister’s first task is to defend Canada’s interests without letting the spat with Mr Trump spin out of control. Canada is one of only a tiny handful of countries to have adopted counter-tariffs against America. Yet it has also offered concessions. Last year it ditched a digital-services tax that would have cost American tech firms. It has allowed itself to be humiliated in a bizarre bust-up over a bridge between Detroit and Ontario which the Trump administration refused to open until Canada agreed, retrospectively, to surrender some of its share of the tolls.
Mr Trump’s mercurial malevolence makes Mr Carney’s main economic project all the more urgent: to get Canada growing faster. In his first months in power he scrapped a consumer carbon tax, cancelled a planned rise in capital-gains tax that would have taken the top rate to 67% and cut the lowest rate of income tax. He has sought to trim the government’s everyday spending to find more cash for investments. By 2029 he wants the federal workforce to be 10% smaller than at its peak in 2024. He has doubled down on earlier plans to reduce immigration and has promised to double housing starts to 500,000 a year over the next decade.
In September at a conclave of foreign investors Mr Carney announced a “productivity mega-deduction” permitting firms to write off spending on new equipment immediately. That builds on a “super-deduction” unveiled last year. The new rules will slash the effective corporate tax rate. The “Building Canada Act”, meanwhile, speeds up approvals for big projects the government deems “in the national interest”.
On October 1st Mr Carney posed by a hulking mining truck in Alberta’s petroleum patch to announce that a new pipeline carrying oil to Canada’s west coast had become one of the first schemes to earn this designation. He says construction should begin in just under a year. That kills two birds with one stone: bolstering the economy by exporting more energy to Asia and mollifying grumpy Albertans.
Mr Carney is also seeking to lessen Canada’s reliance on the United States and boost its place in the world. His government wants to double exports to other countries to C$600bn ($420bn) annually by 2035. In August Mr Carney claimed his government had struck more than 20 trade and security deals across five continents (though some are very vague). In January he went to China—the first visit by a Canadian prime minister in almost a decade—where he secured a lowering of tariffs on Canadian rapeseed oil, among other goods. In March he was in Delhi resetting ties with India, which collapsed in 2023 after Canada accused Indian agents of killing a Sikh activist near Vancouver. Canada says the goal is to double trade between the two countries to around $50bn by 2030.
The latest love-in is with the EU, Canada’s second-biggest trading partner (although the destination of only about 6% of Canada’s goods exports). In September Mr Carney gave an eloquent speech to the European Parliament in Strasbourg. Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, suggested Canada could one day become an “associate member” of the European Union, though that seemed more of a rhetorical flourish than a plan. More immediate opportunities will doubtless be discussed at an EU-Canada summit later this month. These include speeding up investment in critical minerals and collaborating more closely on defence. In February Canada became the only non-European country to join the EU’s €150bn ($168bn) SAFE scheme, which provides low-interest loans to like-minded governments seeking to boost their military heft.
Gussying up the armed forces is a big part of raising Canada’s standing in the world. (This, Mr Carney promises, will also provide plenty of opportunities for Canadian firms). In 2024 military spending was around 1.3% of GDP, one of the lowest rates in NATO. This year it soared to 2%, after one of the biggest year-on-year increases in defence spending in Canada’s history. Now the plan is to double spending again, to 4%, as soon as 2030. Canada’s generals are delighted: after years counting pennies, their main problem now is getting value for money on their spending spree. The government also wants to reduce the armed forces’ reliance on American kit.
What does all this amount to? The corporate “mega deduction” is a big deal for investors, says Joseph Steinberg of the University of Toronto. He worries that other parts of the economic programme amount to “announcements, or the creation of new agencies that are intended to eventually make things happen faster”. Efforts to speed up big, important projects are welcome, but do not alter politicians’ habit of “picking winners” instead of improving the business environment for all.
Mr Carney’s pugilistic talk is immensely popular with ordinary Canadians and Trump-weary foreigners. But business types and policy wonks see a high risk of provoking America’s thin-skinned president with little upside. Firms will not commit billions of dollars in investment “just because somebody gives a nice speech”, says Mr Cross of MLI. Canada’s counter-tariffs split economists, too. Many think they increase hardship for Canadians without doing much to change Mr Trump’s mind.
Other middle powers are not inclined to follow Mr Carney’s lead when it comes to confronting Mr Trump. Mr Carney remains vulnerable to complaints about the cost of living, a worry Canadians reliably rank as their top concern. He is accused of high-handedness, turning up to Parliament only sporadically, for instance. Indigenous leaders gripe that they are not being properly consulted about economic development.
Yet zoom out, and there is little doubt that on many fronts Mr Carney is making progress that would have seemed unthinkable just two years ago. Although much of his programme resembles the policies of the opposition, his broad support allows him to go further and faster than they might have dared. Mr Charest, the former premier of Quebec, believes Canadians may one day thank America’s president for shocking them out of a slumber. “The forces of inertia in Canada had become overwhelming,” he says. “Trump is now telling us we have no choice but to change.” ■
articles.summaryZh: 艾伯塔10月19日將公投是否啟動未來獨立的程序。即便多數人不支持，投票仍可能挹注分離主義動能，並連動魁北克9月5日後的政治轉向。外部壓力更直接：川普在8月把對加國約200億美元商品的關稅提高到50%，而加國逾70%出口銷美。內部則卡在長期生產力成長低迷、企業投資不足與自設監管壁壘；再加上移民推升人口與住房成本。總理卡尼主打減稅與投資抵減、加速大型工程審批，並透過多國貿易與管線案補足成長。
keyPointsZh: 艾伯塔10月19日公投將決定省府是否啟動未來獨立程序；若結果接近或意外失敗，可能推高獨立運動並波及魁北克分離情緒。
加拿大10年人均GDP經通膨與匯率調整後約成長4%；生產力下滑是主因，私人部門2015到2023年每小時產出年增僅0.8%。
企業投資偏低與監管造成負擔；OECD稱加拿大研發支出約占GDP 1%，IMF也以內部壁壘估算加拿大等同自設9%關稅。
川普8月對加國約200億美元商品加徵50%關稅，且預告1月1日起可能把汽車關稅從25%提高到50%；不確定性壓住投資。
卡尼推動生產力抵減與加速審批，並要求到2035年把對其他國出口翻倍到加幣6000億元；同時以管線案連結能源出海與降低阿爾伯塔不滿。
articles.researchLensZh: 檢查的重點是政策如何穿過兩條路徑影響加國成長：第一，關稅與不確定性是否實際降低投資，尤其在出口依賴美國的產業；第二，卡尼的減稅與投資抵減能否直接回應生產力成長停滯。資料上可追比投資、研發與生產力的變動速度。
highlightTermsZh: 川普在8月把對加國約200億美元商品的關稅提高到50%

articles.titleEn: Can Asian governments prevent a food shock?
articles.rubricEn: El Niño is hitting countries that are already dealing with an energy shock
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
BACK IN MAY about two tonnes of dead fish floated to the surface of a lake in Cambodia. Last month in Indonesia receding water levels in another lake exposed the ruins of Somang, a long-submerged village. In the Philippines officials have warned residents of Manila, the capital, that their water supply may soon be reduced. These events—all caused by hotter, drier conditions—may seem isolated, but taken together they point to the havoc that El Niño could bring in Asia.
The climate pattern is a naturally recurring phenomenon. Every few years a shift in the winds above the eastern Pacific causes hotter and drier conditions in much of South and South-East Asia. This year’s episode, which began in May and is due to peak next month, is unusually fierce . On one daily measure, sea-surface temperature anomalies in the Pacific have already exceeded the peak of every previous event on record (see chart 1). The World Meteorological Organisation expects this El Niño to last into February.
The effects will be global, but Asia is especially exposed: hundreds of millions of its people depend on farms for their livelihoods, and its governments are still grappling with the energy shock from the war in Iran. In many parts of the region, El Niño is already causing damage. India’s monsoon, which supplies nearly 70% of annual rainfall, ended about 13% below normal levels—the driest in a decade. Satellite data suggest that Indonesia is enduring its worst fire season for 11 years (see chart 2). In the Philippines officials say that seven provinces are already experiencing drought, and that the entire country could be in drought by early next year.
The most direct impact will be on food. Farmers who depend on rainfall will be hit hardest, especially in Indonesia, where the main rice crop is planted between October and December, just as El Niño peaks. But irrigated farms are not immune, because the lack of rain is draining reservoirs. In central Thailand that prompted the government to ask farmers not to plant a second rice crop this year.
All this comes on top of the Iran war’s disruption to fuel and fertiliser supplies. The World Bank expects fertiliser prices this year to average 38% more than last year. Higher input costs and extreme weather are squeezing farmers’ incomes, but also contributing to food inflation (see chart 3). India’s annual food inflation rate rose from 2.1% in January to 6% in August; in Sri Lanka it reached 7% in September. Yet the bigger worry is supply. Krungthai, a Thai bank, reckons Thailand’s rice output could fall by 18% between now and the middle of next year. Thailand has plenty of reserves, but other countries have little to fall back on. Bangladesh’s rice stocks amount to less than 4% of its annual consumption, according to data from America’s Agriculture Department.
To gauge which country is most exposed The Economist has built a “vulnerability index” for 11 of Asia’s emerging economies. It combines two sets of measures: how much El Niño could hurt their economies (based on the importance of agriculture to them), and how well governments could cushion the blow (based on indicators of fiscal space and the reach of welfare systems). Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Cambodia come out worst (data for war-torn Myanmar are patchy, otherwise it would probably top the list). Unsurprisingly, richer countries—Thailand and Malaysia—fare best. The pain takes different forms. In India the risk falls mainly on farmers; in the Philippines and Bangladesh it falls on consumers.
El Niño will generate effects beyond food and agriculture. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) warns it could worsen the energy shock: drying rivers cut hydropower output just as heat raises demand for air-conditioning, pushing countries to burn more coal. Public health is at risk, too. Smoke from Indonesia’s fires has shrouded parts of South-East Asia; on October 12th Singapore’s air was rated the unhealthiest in the world, worse even than Delhi’s.
The economic toll could be enormous, especially because governments are poorly placed to absorb it. A study of the 1997 El Niño found that it cost the global economy nearly $6trn over the next five years—with Asia bearing much of the cost. The United Nations estimates that if this year’s food-and-energy price shock were passed fully onto households (ie, if subsidies and other helpful measures were removed), about 132m more people worldwide would fall into poverty, of whom 91m would be in Asia. As government debts balloon, avoiding this scenario will become harder.
The good news is that governments can see the crisis coming. Better data and forecasting mean policymakers are more prepared than in previous El Niño episodes, says Roshen Fernando of the Asian Development Bank. Alongside building up rice buffers, governments are also trying to help farmers directly. India is nudging growers in parched districts to shift towards planting pulses and other crops; the Philippines, meanwhile, is handing out drought-resistant seeds.
Money needs to be arranged in advance, too. Disaster funds are often released only after disaster strikes. Governments should instead set aside money specifically for El Niño, says Mr Fernando. That could be done by negotiating emergency credit lines and disaster insurance before the peak arrives.
Particularly valuable is “anticipatory action”, which releases cash or other help when forecasts cross predetermined thresholds (such as water levels in a reservoir). The UN thinks every dollar spent in this way can save up to $7 in losses and later aid. Such schemes have been tried in Africa and Central America. But in Asia their coverage has been limited—in part due to a lack of financing. In June the UN’s World Food Programme and its Food and Agriculture Organisation sought $202m to protect 8.8m people in 22 countries, including Afghanistan, Pakistan and the Philippines. So far only $40m has been raised. As rich-country donors tighten their purse strings, prevention has among the first things to be cut.
More than a century ago a particularly intense El Niño caused famines that killed tens of millions of people across India, China and elsewhere. That was largely because nobody saw it coming or knew what to do. Today a far richer Asia knows what lies in store. But forecasts are only useful if governments and donors act on them. ■

articles.summaryZh: 厄爾尼諾自5月開始、預估延續到隔年2月。偏熱偏乾已同時出現在柬埔寨湖面死魚、印尼乾涸露出水下遺跡，以及菲律賓警告馬尼拉供水可能減量，顯示災情會擴散。缺雨影響先落在農業：印度季風降雨約低於常態13%、印尼遭遇11年最嚴重火季、菲律賓7個省已乾旱，水庫也因缺雨而難撐灌溉。伊朗戰爭又擾動燃料與肥料供應，世界銀行預估肥料價格今年平均比去年高38%，推升投入成本並助長食品通膨；在補貼等緩衝未到位時，貧窮風險會更高。
keyPointsZh: 厄爾尼諾自5月啟動、預估到隔年2月；太平洋海溫異常在日資料上已超過所有歷次紀錄峰值，偏熱偏乾因此同時波及南亞與東南亞。
柬埔寨湖面死魚、印尼乾涸湖泊與菲律賓警告馬尼拉供水可能減量都指向同一波極端天候。
缺雨先衝農業與灌溉：印度季風雨量約低於常態13%、印尼面臨11年最嚴重火季，菲律賓已有7個省乾旱。
伊朗戰爭干擾燃料與肥料供應疊加天候：世界銀行預估今年肥料價格平均較去年高38%，並透過成本上升推動食品通膨。
政策緩衝能力差異影響結果：經濟學人用脆弱度指數將斯里蘭卡、孟加拉與柬埔寨列為最差；資金覆蓋有限也讓事前行動較易被延後。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的問題是：在厄爾尼諾預測期內，備援糧食、預先災害資金與「預先行動」（預測跨門檻就發錢）能否減少供給缺口，並把食品通膨與貧窮傳導降下來。接著用財政空間與社福觸及指標，驗證脆弱度指數的排序依據。

articles.titleEn: India’s government fails to crush Gen Z protests
articles.rubricEn: The leader of the Cockroach party is detained and the internet shut down
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
MICROPHONES SHOVED in their faces, the youngsters raced to say their soundbites on democratic rights. Then the police van sped off with them still in mid-sentence. “That’s the only way to protest now—we just go get detained,” shrugged one. On October 10th in Delhi, drones filled the skies and tens of thousands of security men and women patrolled the strangely silent city below. India’s capital witnessed its most sweeping crackdown on peaceful protest for many years.
After 12 years in power, Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, faces a challenge from Gen-Z protesters. In July the newly formed Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth movement, staged mass protests against a corrupt exam system and poor job prospects, and eventually forced the education minister to resign. This time, the CJP is riding a wave of public anger against the voting system, which it says is rigged. The authorities are also better prepared. As soon as the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, and his two lieutenants touched down at Delhi airport to lead the crowds at a planned rally, police arrived to snatch them away. While most of the roughly 5,000 detainees got out by nightfall, the Cockroach trio was held for 24 hours.
Central Delhi felt like a city under siege: borders sealed, internet jammed, 45 metro stations locked and loudspeakers blasting out warnings. Police bruised opposition leaders and briefly nabbed journalists and lawyers. Scattered protests emerged like flash mobs, only for baton-wielding officers to disperse them.
Though the Cockroaches were squashed over the weekend, India’s opposition alliance, led by the Congress party’s Rahul Gandhi, gathered tens of thousands for a march on October 12th. They, too, demanded that Gyanesh Kumar, the chief of India’s Election Commission, resign; that the voter-verification drive he has managed must be scrapped; and that the law which, in effect, let Mr Modi hand-pick him should go. Over the past year, a “special intensive revision” of voter lists has deleted more than 130m names, many rightly, since they were duplicates or dead people. But very many wrongfully.
The government, like the commission, denies the allegations. Kiren Rijiju, a BJP minister, calls the protests—which were refused police permission—a gimmick by those who keep losing elections. Batting away comparisons to the Emergency of the 1970s, when Indira Gandhi suspended democracy, he says: “This is not an emergency, this is normal law and order.”
For India’s long moribund opposition, the rallies against vote chori (theft) are about saving democracy and the republic. But the marches also express a more diffuse anger at years of perceived governmental missteps. Rally-goers raise shoddy schooling, jobless growth, women’s safety, minority rights and unease at India’s turn towards Hindu nationalism.
The upstart Cockroaches and India’s established opposition have both vowed to protest until the election chief resigns. But Mr Kumar is virtually unsackable, because the prime minister stands by him, for now. And the authorities are doubling down. On October 14th Mr Dipke’s two lieutenants were sentenced to five days in jail on trespassing charges. To Mr Dipke, the original Cockroach, the spectacle of the crackdown suggests the government has something to hide. “Narendra Modi and Amit Shah [the home minister] are waging a war on their countrymen just to save one Gyanesh Kumar,” he says.
The opposition’s bigger ambition concerns the national election of 2029. “People finally understand how the BJP is stealing elections,” argues a close adviser to Rahul Gandhi. ■
Stay on top of our India coverage by signing up to Essential India , our free weekly newsletter.
articles.summaryZh: 10月10日在印度首都新德里，政府針對「蟑螂黨」等世代抗議採清場。創辦人一抵達機場就被帶走；警方同日封邊界、拉網路與地鐵管制、鎖45座地鐵站並持續廣播。約5000人被拘留，多數在當晚獲釋，創辦人團隊則被扣24小時。抗議指向投票與選民驗證機制被操弄，並要求選舉委員會長Gyanesh Kumar辭職；政府與選務體系否認並稱是正常治安。
keyPointsZh: 10月10日新德里清場，蟑螂黨創辦人Abhijeet Dipke與兩名幹部一抵達機場就遭警方帶走。
政府封邊界、干擾網路，並鎖定45座地鐵站與用廣播發出警告，分散示威也快速被驅散。
約5000人被拘留，多數在當晚獲釋；蟑螂黨三人組則被扣滿24小時。
抗議訴求是選民驗證與投票系統遭操弄，並要求選舉委員會長Gyanesh Kumar辭職，且撤回選民名單「特別密集修訂」。
政府與選務體系否認指控，並稱民眾集會未獲許可、處置屬正常治安而非1970年代緊急狀態。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查兩條線：第一，「特別密集修訂」刪除130萬多筆是否造成實質錯刪或排除；第二，封邊界、網路干擾與站點鎖控是否提升或削弱反對陣營在10月12日與2029大選前的動員效果。

articles.titleEn: Two Japanese towns offer lessons for shrinking countries
articles.rubricEn: Only some places can hope to grow; others must learn to manage decline
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
LESS THAN 40km separates the towns of Nanporo and Yubari, on Japan’s northernmost island of Hokkaido, but their fates could hardly have diverged further. Nanporo, a tranquil commuter town east of Sapporo, the regional capital, is growing its native population at one of the fastest rates in the country. Yubari, a former coal-mining hub that went bankrupt in 2007, has seen its population decline by 95% from its peak. Their contrasting trajectories offer lessons for local life in an era of demographic shrinkage.
Start in Nanporo. The town’s population fell from around 10,000 in 1998 to fewer than 7,400 over the next quarter-century. But in recent years the trend has reversed: by last year, the population had ticked back up to 8,400. Nanporo was one of only nine out of 179 municipalities in Hokkaido to see population growth in 2020-25. It was the only one of those nine to do so without substantial foreign immigration. Meanwhile, Japan as a whole lost some 3m people over the same period.
A sense of optimism is palpable at the Hareppa indoor playground in the town’s central park. Sunlight streams through the new building’s floor-to-ceiling windows, lighting up a gaggle of children clambering up a wooden playhouse under a vaulted ceiling. In the adjoining café and library, a mum and young son peruse a shelf of children’s books: “The Very Hungry Caterpillar”, “Library Lion” and a popular Japanese series called “The Encyclopedia of Big Crises”.
A combination of structural advantages and targeted policy initiatives has helped Nanporo solve its own big crisis. While offering the peaceful capaciousness of the countryside, the town sits comfortably within the economic orbit of Sapporo, less than an hour’s drive away. Local leaders recognised that could appeal to young families, and implemented several incentives to attract them.
Many municipalities elsewhere in Japan have tried such measures, but Nanporo’s have been effective because its efforts were sustained and unique, reckons Saito Takashi, an official. Couples where both partners are under 40 years old, or with children of middle school age or younger, can receive up to ¥2m ($12,500) towards home construction; unused plots of land held in a prefectural land bank are sold at a steep discount. Parents also get 10kg of rice every year, a meaningful treat when rice prices have caused national anxiety.
The Tatsuki family are among the new arrivals. Aoi and Yamato moved to Nanporo with their young son last year, drawn by the combination of proximity to Sapporo and support for young families. They built a home and opened a café on its ground floor, where they do brisk business serving lunch sets of grilled fish and freshly-baked desserts. “It would have been super-expensive to do the same in Sapporo,” Mr Tatsuki says. After seeing the conditions, Mr Tatsuki’s older sister decided to move to Nanporo as well.
Yet Nanporo’s growth has come from migrants moving in, rather than a baby boom. Last year the town still saw twice as many deaths as births. With the national population shrinking, one municipality’s gain is another’s loss. There is a “competitive dynamic”, Mr Saito acknowledges. Not everywhere can be Nanporo.
Many places will be more like Yubari. Its population peaked in 1960 at some 117,000. (Though the size of a town now, it still carries the city designation as a relic of its past glory.) After the last coal mine closed in 1990, Yubari tried to reinvent itself as a tourist destination; mismanagement left it bankrupt. As part of a nationally administered restructuring plan, officials closed schools, halted bus routes and shut the local museum. Cutting services only speeded the decline, laments Yubari’s current mayor, Atsuya Tsukasa.
Since 2022, when Nanporo’s tide began to turn, Yubari has seen its population shrink from around 7,000 to just 5,600. More than half the remaining residents are over 65. “Almost no one is moving in, everyone is leaving,” says Noda Masaru, an entrepreneur. “And when you know the population is going down, you aren’t going to start a business, you’re going to close it.”
Yubari’s case is extreme, but hardly unique. The Population Strategy Council, a group of business and civic leaders, reported in 2024 that some 40% of Japan’s municipalities risk disappearing, given the outflow of young people. “I don’t see any prospect for reversing the trend—it’s not just Yubari, look at small towns across Japan,” Mr Atsuya says. “The question is how to survive in that context.”
While Nanporo, thanks to its favourable location near a regional hub, can realistically pursue revitalisation, for Yubari the task is to manage an inevitable further decline, for instance by becoming more compact. “We need to live in a more connected way,” Mr Atsuya says. In an era of population shrinkage, growth can no longer be the only measure of success. ■

articles.summaryZh: 距離不過40公里的北海道南幌（Nanporo）與夕張（Yubari）命運差很大。南幌人口由1998年約1萬降至7400以下，近年回升到去年8400；2020-25期間在北海道179個自治體中只有9個成長，南幌其中之一。夕張2007年破產，人口由1960年約117,000降95%；自煤礦關閉後又因學校、巴士路線與博物館被關閉而加速衰退。兩地差異顯示：部分地方靠區域中心可達性與長期誘因仍可能吸引遷入，但多數地方更需要把重點轉為管理持續下降，例如把生活圈做得更緊密。
keyPointsZh: 南幌人口由1998年約1萬降至7400以下，去年回升到8,400；2020-25期間它是北海道9個人口成長自治體之一。
南幌的政策包含向符合條件的夫妻提供最高200萬日圓建屋補助，並以折扣出售庫存土地。
南幌仍呈現遷入型成長：去年死亡仍多於出生，且人口下滑帶來跨自治體的零和競爭。
夕張在2007年破產，煤礦1990年結束後曾改推觀光，但重整期間關校、停公車、關博物館，服務削減被指加速外流。
夕張人口2022年後由約7,000降到約5,600，且65歲以上占比超過一半，地方因此轉向「更緊密、連結式」生活。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的問題是：人口縮減時，靠近區域中心的可達性與誘因能否把遷入轉成可持續的增加；若無法吸引遷入，服務收縮與空間「緊密化」的取捨是否能減緩外流與商業停擺。

articles.titleEn: Myanmar’s dictator tries diplomacy
articles.rubricEn: He has a few cards to play
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
MIN AUNG HLAING is keen to get into the world’s good books. The dictator, who seized power in Myanmar in 2021, underwent a makeover earlier this year. He quit the army and made himself president following a rigged election. Now he has gone on a diplomatic blitz within Asia and is talking to America. Calls to end military atrocities have gone unheeded; but the despot has some cards to play.
One is taking back those who have fled Myanmar’s war and economic collapse. This won Mr Min Aung Hlaing a visit on October 7th-8th to Malaysia, formerly his biggest critic in the region. Anwar Ibrahim, Malaysia’s prime minister, received him in return for a deal on repatriating thousands of Myanmar nationals, a bid to fend off local anger about the migrants.
Mr Anwar pleaded pragmatism, but the dictator’s red-carpet welcome was a step towards his rehabilitation among leaders of the Association of South-East Asian Nations (ASEAN). The Malaysia visit followed ones in the past four months to Cambodia, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam.
Other cards include fighting online scams and selling rare earths. These have helped lure America into talks with the regime. Michael Vance, the State Department’s intelligence chief, met Mr Min Aung Hlaing in September. Mr Vance’s visit was ostensibly to secure the release from prison of Adam Castillo, a businessman. But the budding dialogue is focused on scam centres and extracting minerals.
A rapprochement would be key to lessening Myanmar’s reliance on China, which has propped up the regime amid its heavy losses to rebels. That help has come with high-handed orders to close scam centres targeting Chinese citizens. It is unlikely that America will have any more luck than China in getting them closed. Scam profits have allowed the centres to buy off regime officials, allegedly including the former head of its anti-scams committee.
Myanmar’s rare-earth deposits, meanwhile, are largely beyond the regime’s reach, in areas controlled by ethnic armed groups, and are locked into Chinese supply chains. American officials may simply be using the minerals to get noticed by Donald Trump. “Everyone knows the White House and president are fixated on rare earths,” says a former Washington-based official with Myanmar experience. “That’s what everyone, including me, would throw out in meetings to get attention.”
Mr Min Aung Hlaing is also holding his strongest card in reserve. The trading of Mr Castillo shows an appetite for hostage diplomacy—and there is one prisoner who far outranks the rest. Aung San Suu Kyi, who led Myanmar between 2016 and 2021, has been detained since the coup. If freed, odds are that she would be barred from politics. But her release might provide the symbolic win that ASEAN and others need to wash their hands of Myanmar’s atrocious human-rights record and get back to business as usual. ■

articles.summaryZh: 敏昂萊在2026年10月的東協與美國交往中，主打遣返緬籍移民、打詐與稀土交易以換取空間。馬來西亞10月7到8日接待他，談遣返數千名緬甸國民以平息當地怒氣。美國情報主管麥可范斯9月會見，表面為押押商人亞當卡斯蒂洛，實際聚焦詐騙中心與抽取礦產。外界要求停止軍事暴行仍未回應；外界也難在短期關閉詐騙中心。釋放翁山蘇姬可能提供東協與他國需要的象徵性成果，讓各方恢復合作。
keyPointsZh: 馬來西亞10月7到8日接待敏昂萊，談到遣返數千名緬甸國民，以緩和當地對移民的怒氣。
敏昂萊在近4個月訪問柬埔寨、寮國、泰國與越南，並在東協領袖圈尋求改善形象。
美國情報主管麥可范斯9月會見敏昂萊，表面目標是放出亞當卡斯蒂洛，實際討論詐騙中心與稀土等礦產。
詐騙中心的獲利讓官員可能收買，且美國要像中國一樣徹底關閉詐騙中心不容易。
翁山蘇姬仍被羈押；若她獲釋，可能成為東協與其他國家洗去人權指責、恢復正常合作的象徵。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的機制是：政權以遣返移民、打詐議題與稀土交易，換取東協與美方對話；資料可比對會談主軸是否轉向、詐騙中心是否出現可量化關閉或執法結果，以及釋放翁山蘇姬是否帶動政策再定位。

articles.titleEn: The limits of India’s diaspora power
articles.rubricEn: As the West closes its doors, India must make staying home more attractive
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
THE INDIAN diaspora, which numbers around 37m, is the world’s biggest. It may also be the most successful. It has a compelling case to make, especially in America, home to more than 3m people born in India. The median Indian-American household earns $151,000 annually, around 75% more than the figure for America as a whole. And many Indian-Americans occupy top jobs in business, technology and politics—think of Sundar Pichai, Satya Nadella, Zohran Mamdani and Kash Patel.
Such achievements are celebrated back in India, not just by relatives but also by a proud nation. Newspaper reports and WhatsApp forwards diligently catalogue the accomplishments of anyone with an Indian connection, however remote. Recent examples include Navi Pillay, the South African judge awarded this year’s Nobel peace prize, whose ancestors left India in the 19th century, and Anil Menon, the world’s first Malayali astronaut, a reference to his parents’ origins in the south of India.
The state encourages such enthusiasm. For years after independence, India tended to look down on its diaspora, disparaging emigrants for deserting the homeland and contributing to a brain drain. But as their numbers grew and the economy boomed, the relationship changed. In the 2000s, during the Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP) first term in power nationally, the party sought stronger ties with Indians abroad as a way of advancing India’s interests and boosting its own coffers (overseas Indians are believed to be enthusiastic donors to the party). Under Narendra Modi, those efforts have become more intense. The prime minister’s foreign trips often include rallies in stadiums packed with adoring non-resident Indians (NRIs).
To the BJP and indeed to many Indians, the success of NRIs is yet another indicator of India’s inevitable rise. But, viewed differently, it is also an indictment of the country’s inability to hold on to its talent. A study in 2023 found that of the 1,000 highest scorers in the 2010 entrance exam for the Indian Institutes of Technology, the country’s top engineering colleges, 36% were living abroad eight years later. Among the top 100, the share was 62%.
Similarly, the accomplishments of Indian-origin bosses abroad reveal dysfunction at home. Given the size of India’s economy, its businesses punch well below their weight. Of the world’s 500 biggest firms by market capitalisation, India is home to only eight. China has 41, America 234. One reason is that many Indian companies, whether small or large, are run as “lala” operations, family fiefs lacking professional management. Another is that the state has failed to create the conditions—from infrastructure to regulation—needed for them to flourish.
Emigration makes up for some of these failures. Remittances amount to 4% of India’s GDP (compared with 0.2% in China) and support millions of households. During crises, including the recent shock from the Iran war, diaspora cash has been particularly helpful. Migration has served as a social safety-valve, easing pressure on the labour market by giving educated Indians a chance of outward mobility.
It may now be shutting. The Trump administration has clamped down on migration. On October 8th it suspended tech firms, including several Indian ones, from sponsoring workers for permanent residency, accusing them of immigration fraud. Australia and Canada are restricting student visas. And it is not just potential migrants who are being targeted. Racism and resentment are fuelling hate campaigns on social media, especially in America.
The diaspora can do little to stem the hate, let alone advance India’s interests. In America it has failed to persuade the Trump administration to adopt policies favourable to India. Indeed just last month Congress in Washington passed legislation allowing 100% tariffs on India for buying Russian oil. The diaspora may be large and even influential, but it is no diplomatic corps.
Mr Modi has hailed his overseas audience as rashtradoot, or emissaries of India. But for all their attachment to India, few in the diaspora want to return to a country where decent jobs are scarce and cities unliveable. Those are the same factors contributing to frustrations among youngsters in India who are increasingly expressing their anger on the streets. Celebrating success abroad may feel good, but a real reason for national pride would be for Indians to flourish at home. ■
articles.summaryZh: 印度僑民約3700萬人、是全球最大。以美國為例，印裔家庭中位年收入15.1萬美元，且多集中在商業、科技與政治高位。印度透過媒體與WhatsApp推崇海外成就，並在莫迪時期把海外連結制度化。研究卻顯示，IIT 2010入學考前1000名中，8年後有36%在海外，前100名占比達62%；企業在全球市值前500僅8家，文中把原因指向家族式管理與政府未做足的基礎建設與規範。當美國指控移民詐欺並收緊簽證、澳洲與加拿大限縮學生簽證後，僑民對外交政策的槓桿變弱，回流意願也受「好工作稀缺、城市難住」影響。
keyPointsZh: 印度僑民約3700萬人，且在美國的印裔家庭中位年收入15.1萬美元，常見於商業、科技與政治高位。
國內透過媒體與WhatsApp彙整海外成就，並在莫迪時期透過海外連結與NRIs動員印度利益。
IIT 2010入學考前1000高分者中，8年後36%仍在海外，前100名占比到62%。
印度企業在全球市值前500僅8家；文中把落差歸因於家族式經營與政府基礎建設、規範到位不足。
美國以移民詐欺為由限制永久居留擔保、澳洲與加拿大限縮學生簽證，僑民在外交上難以扭轉政策走向。

articles.titleEn: China is turning trash into treasure on a vast scale
articles.rubricEn: EV batteries, especially, will help it secure supplies of critical minerals
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
The European Union worries about China’s vast exports of cheap electric vehicles. On October 12th it said that in December a quota of 350,000 a year would be imposed on hybrid-EV imports from China. This is expected to keep their market share below 10%. But the bloc also frets about China’s dominance over critical minerals used to make these vehicles.
A fast-growing number of EVs will soon be scrapped and replaced. Shredding their batteries yields “black mass”, a powder from which valuable metals such as lithium, cobalt and nickel can be recovered and reused. From next month the EU will make it harder to export this waste. The aim is to encourage more processing of black mass close to home (currently most is shipped to Asia). In August America, which has banned Chinese EVs but still imports lots of Chinese batteries, blocked all black-mass exports.
China, however, is unlikely to suffer. Black mass might meet 20-30% of global demand for battery metals by 2050, says the International Energy Agency, a forecaster. So China is supercharging its recycling industries to shore up supplies not just of battery metals, but also of rare earths and much else. The goal is to make the country’s economy less “linear” (where raw materials are made into products that are then thrown away) and more “circular” (closing the loop so recycled waste replaces raw materials).
Once recycling efforts were driven by concerns about pollution. Now, amid a global scramble for the materials needed to build a high-tech economy, security has become a primary motive.
The country has hard-earned experience in managing rubbish. It produces more than anywhere else: about 15% of the world’s municipal detritus (everything from the contents of household bins to street sweepings) and more than one-quarter of its industrial waste (such as demolition debris, factory effluent, scrap metal, slag and ash).
In the 1980s China started to import waste, taking the hardware, paper and plastic that richer countries did not want. A sprawling informal recycling sector emerged, led by scavengers picking through rubbish piles. Much ended up in landfills or burnt in the open air, leaching toxic chemicals and creating poisonous smog. A Chinese documentary in 2011 found that organic waste from dumps around Beijing was being turned into oil and sold to restaurants.
In 2013, wary of mounting public anger, China declared a “war on pollution” and released its first comprehensive national plan to create a circular economy. Electronics were directed to new “urban mining” zones to be scrapped safely; household rubbish was sent to specialised plants to be burned for power; the proportion of waste dumped in landfills started to fall. In 2017 China launched “Operation National Sword” to stop most imports of plastics (in 2021 all imports of solid waste were banned). State-run media trumpeted that the country was “no longer a dumping ground”. Over the past five years most of China’s cities have rolled out mandatory sorting of household rubbish.
China is still well behind squeaky-clean European countries when it comes to waste management (though it is hard to say how far, as it does not publish detailed national data for recycling). Its poorer rural areas are still often strewn with rubbish. But officials have made China’s big cities, at least, cleaner and more pleasant to live in. Now their focus is shifting to the use of recycling for the sake of security. In July China released a plan for the development of the circular economy until 2030. “The importance of resource security has become increasingly prominent, while geopolitical dynamics…have grown complex and severe,” the plan noted.
That judgment rests on two considerations. First, China wants to dominate high-tech manufacturing in everything from robotics to wind turbines. And second, to achieve this, it must secure supplies of raw materials, connect more power lines and build more data centres. Massive amounts of aluminium, copper, battery metals and rare earths are needed. While China controls the bulk of the global refining capacity for these materials, it relies on imports for most of the ores. Meanwhile many Western countries want to reduce reliance on China’s factories. Officials worry they may try to squeeze its supplies. Last year a researcher at a state-owned research facility said that, without recycling, China would “keep facing strangleholds in the future”.
China wants to use recycling to supply 510m tonnes of industrial materials annually by 2030, about one-third more than the current level. The easier part will be scaling up the recycling of steel, copper and aluminium: this kind of work is already a mature industry. Recycling more plastic is a little trickier, but worth it to help China reduce imports of oil. The hardest bit will be managing a growing tsunami of electronic garbage. By 2030 China expects to generate 0.5m tonnes of waste from wind turbines, 1m tonnes from EV batteries and 1.5-2m tonnes from solar panels every year—big shares of the global total.
The fact that China already makes vast quantities of these goods should make recycling simpler. Factories can tweak designs so that products are easier to dismantle later. And many battery-producing techniques (such as using acids and heat to isolate valuable metals) are also used in recycling them. Take CATL, for example, the world’s largest battery-maker. Most of the Chinese firm’s sales are domestic, and will end up being processed by a CATL subsidiary called Brunp, which is the world’s biggest battery-recycler. Such arrangements have helped China build 85% of global battery-recycling capacity.
Still, big challenges remain. Much of China’s recycling capacity is unused because too many batteries end up with informal scrap dealers (who waste much of the good stuff inside them) or are just dumped. In recent years several gangs have been busted for running illegal battery-collection rings. Solar panels and wind turbines, which are often used in remote parts of the country, present an even bigger collection problem. Valuable materials they contain (silver, for solar panels; and neodymium, a rare earth, for wind turbines) are present only in small quantities, making extraction trickier.
As ever, China hopes its tech-enabled state can overcome such difficulties. In 2024 it set up a new state-owned company called China Resources Recycling Group to co-ordinate and streamline recycling efforts, with a focus on cleantech products. Recycling plants have started using artificial intelligence to sort waste more efficiently. In April battery- and EV-makers were required to give their products digital IDs to track them through their life cycle on a state-run platform. They have also been made legally responsible for recycling the batteries they produce.
China says recycling already accounts for 10% of its supply of rare earths. It is trying to make the process more efficient. At present it is far more costly than extracting them from raw materials. Still, Chinese rare-earth companies, which are almost all state-owned, “do not rely on economic viability in all cases”, notes Corby Anderson of the Colorado School of Mines.
And to make sure its recycling plants are fed, China is also quietly reassuming its old role in the waste trade. It is selectively rolling back restrictions on some foreign waste. In 2024 it eased curbs on imports of some scrap copper and aluminium. Last year it started allowing imports of black mass. In January it slashed duties on the stuff from 6.5% to 3%. Officials have pledged to continue to increase imports of “high-quality” recycled materials over the next five years.
Now that America and Europe want to keep their valuable waste, could they eat into China’s recycling dominance? Zhang Yuping, the deputy general manager of GEM, a big Shenzhen-listed battery-recycler, thinks not. “From the perspective of national security, they might have some justification,” he says. But the cost of recycling outside China would be high and scaling up difficult. Europe, at least, “can’t digest” such a challenge, reckons Mr Zhang. “They would pay a heavy cost.” ■

articles.summaryZh: 歐盟擔心中國低價電動車挤壓市場，10月12日提出：12月起對中國混合動力EV設年35萬輛進口配額；同時把矛頭指向中國在鋰、鈷、鎳等關鍵礦物供應鏈的主導。隨EV與其他高科技設備進入報廢期，回收電池可產出「黑色粉末」，歐盟從下月起更難出口這類廢料，並要求就近處理。國際能源署估計，2050年黑色粉末或可滿足全球電池金屬需求20%到30%，中國因此擴張循環經濟，推動數位產品身分、AI分選與製造商回收責任，並在2024至今逐步放寬部分廢料進口以確保原料。
keyPointsZh: 歐盟在10月12日宣布，12月起對中國混合動力EV設年35萬輛進口配額，並預期把市場占比壓在10%以下。
歐盟從下月起收緊「黑色粉末」出口，目的在提高就近處理，取代目前多數外送至亞洲的作法。
國際能源署估計，2050年黑色粉末可滿足全球電池金屬需求20%到30%，成為中國擴張回收產能的論述依據。
中國要求電池與EV業者在4月提供產品數位身分，並把回收責任交給製造商，另啟用AI分選提高回收效率。
中國目前仍有回收產能閒置與非法回收問題，並因風機與太陽能板散佈偏遠而增加蒐集難度。
articles.researchLensZh: 重點可檢查的傳導機制是：EV報廢量上升後，歐盟的廢料出口限制與配額，是否會改變黑色粉末的地域供應；再看中國能否靠回收擴產、數位追蹤與進口回補，抵消供料不穩與回收效率落差。
highlightTermsZh: 12月起對中國混合動力EV設年35萬輛進口配額
黑色粉末或可滿足全球電池金屬需求20%到30%

articles.titleEn: China has captured the market for hobbyist 3D printers
articles.rubricEn: Amid Western wariness, it is struggling to do the same with high-end machines
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
The fastest-growing industrial product in China today is not the electric vehicle, lithium-ion battery or even humanoid robot. It is the humble 3D printer for hobbyists. Once geeky curios, 3D printers have quietly become one of China’s most successful consumer electronics. Exports of the machines grew by 90% in the first half of this year. In the past decade China’s global market share has risen from 19% to 96%, ending the dominance of Western firms.
The personal 3D-printing market is now split among the “four little dragons of Shenzhen”, says Chris Connery of Context, a London-based market-intelligence firm. Creality, Anycubic, Elegoo and the industry’s leader, Bambu Lab, reign supreme globally (see chart). Their success shows, yet again, how fierce competition in China combined with generous government support can help improve quality and drive down export prices, making Chinese products hard to beat.
The printers work by building objects layer by layer, usually by extruding molten plastic. Invented by Chuck Hull, an American, in 1983, they long remained expensive, unreliable and difficult to use. Today they routinely sell for a little more than $500 and have the sleek aluminium finish of an Apple computer. Comparable entry-level printers from Western firms start at more than double the price. Artificial intelligence allows users to create print designs for such things as tools, parts or toys by describing them in natural language rather than using complicated design-software. Just as Chinese factories helped to turn drones into recreational devices (as well as game-changers in warfare) by achieving large-scale production at low cost, so they are now doing with 3D printers.
Price wars have eaten into the printer dragons’ profits even as sales boom. But the firms still excite investors. Bambu Lab was founded in 2020 by alumni of another Chinese company, DJI, the world’s leading dronemaker. The printer-maker is reported to have a private valuation of about $10bn. Last year DJI itself invested in Elegoo, a Bambu rival. Creality listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in May. It boasts a market capitalisation of HK$12bn ($1.5bn).
The government cherishes 3D-printing firms. The business featured in its “Made in China 2025” industrial plan, which was launched in 2015 to ensure domestic strength and self-reliance in high-tech manufacturing (much to the West’s concern). Officials see 3D printers as a way to produce components of aerospace, health care and military equipment, for which China often relies on Western suppliers. Policymakers have directed research institutes and state-run firms to buy them.
Some competitors say Chinese firms have profited from Western open-source printing software. Last month an American court ruled that Bambu Lab had infringed on four patents held by an American company, and ordered it to pay $27.6m in damages. Although Chinese firms have captured the consumer market, they have struggled to do so for industrial 3D printers. Firms are wary of relying on Chinese products if it involves feeding them with sensitive designs (though Britain’s defence ministry has been using Bambu printers, its government admits). Outside China, top-of-the-range machines are still mostly supplied by American and European outfits. They can sell for millions of dollars.
Undeterred, Chinese suppliers are creating a new form of manufacturing at home and abroad. They are pioneering “3D-printing farms”—facilities with as many as 5,000 desktop 3D printers that operate like factories. Several have been built in China this year. Printing farms can mass-produce trinkets for zany consumer trends in short order, replacing expensive and slow injection-moulding techniques. Like the printers themselves, their output will be higher quality and cheaper than what came before. ■

articles.summaryZh: 中國業餘3D印表機成了消費電子中成長最快的品項。上半年出口年增90%；過去十年全球市占從19%升至96%，市場由深圳四家業者瓜分。中低階機型常以500美元左右起售，AI可用自然語言產出列印設計，配合高競爭與政府支援拉低出口價格。高階工業機則受限於既有美歐供應與專利訴訟、敏感設計採購疑慮；業者改以「3D列印農場」把多台桌機串聯擴產。
keyPointsZh: 上半年中國業餘3D印表機出口年增90%；十年間全球市占從19%升至96%，主要被深圳四家瓜分。
AI把自然語言轉成列印設計，再搭配低成本量產與激烈競爭，使中低階機常以500美元左右起售並壓低出口價格。
中國政府把3D印表機納入「Made in China 2025」並指示研究機構、國營企業採購，鎖定航空、醫療與軍事零件用途。
美歐仍多供應高階工業機，且外部採購方擔心敏感設計外流；Bambu Lab也被美國法院判賠2760萬美元。
業者改用「3D列印農場」擴產，單一設施可多達5000台桌機，以取代昂貴且緩慢的注塑製程並搶攻需求。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的重點是：政府支援與規模化量產能否同時推動高階工業機的海外導入；出口價格下行是否足以抵消美歐供應鎖定。也要追資料看專利判決與「敏感設計不外流」疑慮，是否會延後擴張到工業端。

articles.titleEn: China is channelling much more money to poor countries
articles.rubricEn: It wants a greater say in organisations that hand it out
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
Chinese diplomats often talk about the threat of a “Thucydides trap”, named after the Greek historian who described how an incumbent power, Sparta, fought to resist the rise of an upstart, Athens. In the realm of foreign aid, however, such fierce rivalry has been sadly absent in recent years. Another trap, identified by Charles Kindleberger, an economic historian, looks dangerous, too. He described what happens when a stabilising superpower cedes its global role before the emerging power is ready or willing to assume it. America was slow to fill Britain’s shoes in the interwar years of the 20th century. And there is now a similar gap in the realm of multilateral giving.
America has tired of the international institutions it helped create. Last year the aid it channelled through multilateral organisations like the World Bank and the UN fell by half. It has withdrawn from the UN’s World Health Organisation—and it still owes the WHO money.
China could have rushed boldly into this void. And it has indeed stumped up more cash. But its approach lacks Athenian assertiveness. “China is not currently either willing or able to fill the financial gap that would be left behind by US withdrawal,” points out Beata Cichocka of the Centre for Global Development, a think-tank in Washington.
With her colleague Ian Mitchell she has tried to add up China’s contributions to multilateral aid, channelled through development banks, UN agencies and 26 “vertical” funds that collect money for specific problems such as climate change. China itself founded some of these institutions, including the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, based in Beijing, and the New Development Bank in Shanghai.
China’s giving to these bodies has increased steeply over the past decade, from about $1bn in 2014 to more than $3bn in 2024 (see chart 1). China has, for example, become the largest donor to the WHO among its member states, promising an extra $500m over five years. It has backed Song Li, a Chinese health official, to become the organisation’s boss when the position opens up next year.
China has also pledged more money to the International Development Association, a World Bank outfit that provides aid and cheap loans to 78 of the world’s poorest countries. China was itself once one of those hard-up countries, receiving almost $10bn in soft loans from 1981 until it ceased to be eligible in 1999. China’s “transformation from major borrower to significant donor represents one of the most remarkable trajectories in multilateral development finance”, as the report points out.
This transformation is all the more welcome given the remarkable retreat of other donors. But much of China’s extra multilateral giving is mandatory, not voluntary: it must pay more dues because of its economic growth. Even the $500m pledged to the WHO mostly reflects an increase in membership dues, judging by the patchy information available. China is doing its bit. But it is not going far beyond its duty.
Perhaps this should not be a surprise. China’s GDP per person is still middling by world standards. It has only just reached the income threshold at which countries typically “step up their contributions”, points out Mr Mitchell. And China’s increased giving has not been matched by a comparable increase in voting power or voice within the institutions it finances. China’s government is “seized [by] this feeling that they pay and therefore they should have [a] say,” says Courtney Fung of Macquarie University. Its voting share in the World Bank remains at less than 6%. According to formulas the bank has used in the past, it should be more than 12%.
China’s share of UN staff is also tiny: 1.4%, ranking only 20th (see chart 2). It is trying to change that by funding more junior professionals and other entrants. China contributed 773 interns in 2022-23 compared with America’s 532. But the country’s civil servants still struggle with language barriers and unfamiliar work habits.
Some obstacles are self-imposed. China, for example, screens its candidates for patriotism (which includes political loyalty). And civil servants who have spent too long abroad worry that their home networks are “going stale”, says Ms Fung. Perhaps the Athenians felt the same way. ■
