articles.titleEn: European museums are seeing a spike in high-value art theft
articles.rubricEn: Forget cat burglars. Today’s thieves smash, grab and run
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
LILLI HOLLEIN, the director of Vienna’s Museum for Applied Art (MAK), has just been through the toughest six weeks of her career. On August 27th two armed thieves stole a platinum necklace bedecked with 673 diamonds, designed by Van Cleef & Arpels in 1939 for Queen Nazli of Egypt, from a special exhibition at the museum. Wearing no masks, they entered the neo-Renaissance building on Vienna’s Ringstrasse, bought tickets, wandered into the exhibition and smashed the armoured display case with 41 blows from a hammer they had hidden in their clothes. Snatching the necklace, valued at more than $4m, they made off on foot through the adjacent Stadtpark.
The MAK reopened the next day, having belatedly installed metal detectors at the entrance, securing the doors long after the crooks had bolted. In subsequent weeks Ms Hollein, whose tenure as director had been extended by five years this spring, came under fire for lax security. On October 2nd an independent investigation found that the MAK and its staff behaved properly: had anyone tried to take on the thieves, they might have endangered themselves and the 104 visitors who were in the show. The museum had deployed 185 video cameras, 125 alarm sensors, special safety glass and trained guards. Yet the report concluded that such thefts by professionals cannot be prevented with reasonable measures.
That claim seems bizarre. It cannot be impossible to stop hoods from walking into museums and nicking the art. (Had someone thought of metal detectors earlier, they would have spotted the thieves’ hammer and pistol.) Rather, it seems the threat has risen and the response remains inadequate. European museum directors, Ms Hollein says, are confronted with a new type of violent and brazen theft. The robberies are often smash-and-grab attacks that last just a few minutes. It usually takes four to five minutes for the police to arrive. Global losses from art theft for museums and galleries are estimated to amount to $8bn annually.
“Art theft has always existed,” says Anthony Amore, head of security at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston, the site of the most notorious art theft since the second world war. (In that crime in 1990, 13 masterpieces worth about $500m were stolen.) Essentially every major museum in the world has been robbed, says Mr Amore, though most thefts are small. But he notes an increase in high-value robberies in Europe, where one finds first-rate art even in small provincial museums. Many European collections are displayed in old buildings that are tricky to secure. In August thieves stole four masterworks by Antonello da Messina, worth up to €80m ($89m), in a provincial town in Sicily. In September two burglars broke into the Renoir museum, in Cagnes-sur-Mer in France, and made off with two paintings valued at €4.2m.
Spectacular robberies, such as last year’s theft of jewellery worth €90m from the Louvre in Paris, can create a vicious circle. Thieves may not be cat burglars any more but many are copycats, says Arthur Brand, a Dutch art-crime investigator. Just 12 hours after the Louvre robbery, some 2,000 gold and silver coins were stolen from a museum in Langres in north-eastern France. Thieves increasingly focus on jewellery and gold coins, which can be dismantled or melted down for sale. (Renoirs or Rembrandts are almost impossible to sell, and are taken chiefly for ransom.) In 2017 a massive 100kg gold coin was stolen from Berlin’s Bode museum by members of the Remmo clan, a notorious Berlin crime family. In 2019 other clan members made off with 18th-century jewellery containing more than 4,300 diamonds from the Green Vault in Dresden, worth at least €113m.
Only around 10% of stolen art is ever found. But most of the Green Vault jewellery was recovered after Remmo clan members were arrested and confessed. And this month six people were arrested for the theft of the Renoirs in Cagnes-sur-Mer; the two paintings were recovered. French police used DNA and mobile-phone data to track down the suspects, and arrested them when one visited another museum—probably, the police said, not “simply out of love for art”.
High-tech solutions, such as display cases that drop through the floor when assaulted, are expensive. But few European museums even have metal detectors. Many do not have their own security chief; they may share one with several others. Curators tend to focus on fund-raising and high-profile exhibitions, and pay less attention to protective measures until something goes wrong. Mr Amore says they need to develop multiple layers of protection, equip guards with better communication systems and develop strong relationships with local police. AI-enabled security cameras could deliver better warnings. But there is no way to render museums entirely safe. Displaying art to the public will always make it possible for a thief to grab it. ■
articles.summaryZh: 歐洲博物館出現高價藝術品「砸毀搶走」暴力竊案。維也納MAK在8月27日遭兩名武裝歹徒以41下錘擊砸毀裝甲展示櫃，搶走價值逾400萬美元、鑲673顆鑽石的鉑金項鍊；歹徒步行逃離，警方約4到5分鐘才到。MAK隔天才補裝入口金屬探測器。獨立調查提到其後續安防配置完備，但仍認為專業竊賊靠合理措施難以完全防住。文章亦指出歐洲收藏常藏在老建築且偏向珠寶與金幣：全球每年損失估約80億美元、僅約10%可尋回。
keyPointsZh: 維也納MAK 8月27日遭兩名武裝歹徒以41下錘擊砸毀裝甲展示櫃，搶走價值逾400萬美元、鑲673顆鑽石的鉑金項鍊。
歹徒購票入館、拆毀展示並步行逃離；警方到場通常需4到5分鐘。
MAK隔天才補裝入口金屬探測器，獨立調查認為其用在場館的安防部署到位，但仍稱合理措施難以阻止專業竊賊。
文章把風險上升歸到「砸毀搶走」手法，且多數搶案只花幾分鐘完成。
全球藝術品竊盜損失估每年80億美元，且僅約10%能找回，竊賊偏好可拆解或熔售的珠寶與金幣。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查假設是：即使博物館已配置多種安防，當「砸毀搶走」時間窗縮短到幾分鐘且警方到場要4到5分鐘，現有防線是否仍難以把高價目標排除。可用MAK案例的設備與調查結論對照，並用「僅約10%尋回」與珠寶/金幣變現機制驗證誘因。

articles.titleEn: Alice Weidel would pull the plug on German support for Ukraine
articles.rubricEn: The populist-right politician says Ukraine has “already lost” against Russia and should sue for peace
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
ALICE WEIDEL, co-leader of Germany’s populist-right Alternative for Germany (afd), has good reason to think her moment has arrived. Her party has opened up a wide polling lead and stands on the cusp of running its first-ever government, in the state of Saxony-Anhalt. In the course of a 75-minute interview for The Insider in a Bundestag meeting room overlooking Berlin’s river Spree (available to watch from 6pm London time), she offers a confident and fluent performance. Nonetheless, working out what Ms Weidel stands for can prove elusive.
What she opposes is clear. Start with German backing for Ukraine’s defence against Vladimir Putin’s invasion. Futile, she says: Ukraine is “too small” and has “already lost”. Germany should apply “pressure on the Ukrainian president” to end the killing. Policy must follow “Germany first” principles, including by emulating Donald Trump’s diesel deal with Russia.
Worse, prolonging the war “endangers Germany” since it could become a target. This is plausible, as Russia’s hybrid attacks on nato allies suggest. And yet Ms Weidel is reluctant to call out Russia as a threat. Germany recently blamed the Kremlin for a failed drone attack at Leipzig airport. But Ms Weidel says she has seen no evidence that Russia was behind this “so-called attempted drone attack”. Anyway, what about the presumed Ukrainian bombing of the Nord Stream gas pipelines?
This rhetorical judo is a habit. Asked for signs that Mr Putin wants peace, Ms Weidel throws the question back: what about Volodymyr Zelensky? She accepts Russia was the aggressor in 2022, but adds, “when diplomacy is at the table, history is sitting there too.” She means that for decades the West ignored Russia’s security concerns, and must stop doing so.
Ms Weidel, a self-styled “libertarian conservative”, fulminates against Germany’s surge in spending, which she says will lead its interest payments to double in three years. Analysts say the afd’s budget proposals do not add up. But Ms Weidel insists that slashing energy subsidies, foreign aid and welfare can pay for tax cuts and debt reduction. She does not include defence, which accounts for the largest share of new borrowing. Indeed, she accepts “we will have to spend more”. But rather than offer details she simply condemns German support for Ukraine.
As for the euro, it is a “myth” that the afd seeks to leave, says Ms Weidel (though its manifesto in last year’s election in effect urged exit). Instead she wants thorough reform such that the European Central Bank stops financing “highly indebted” countries. Marine Le Pen wants “free debt financing, even though France is already in a huge debt crisis”. Europe is “certainly” headed for a bond-market crisis.
Only one question irritates her. Ms Weidel calls the suggestion that the afd harbours extremists “completely unfounded”, although countless party figures have been linked to ethnonationalist or neo-Nazi groups. On “remigration”, a slippery term beloved of the populist right, Ms Weidel says it simply means deporting failed asylum-seekers and the like. Since Syria’s civil war is over, “100% of the Syrian citizens” must return, as must Afghans and the 1m-plus Ukrainians in Germany, once the peace she claims is close takes hold. “Four to five million” will have to go.
“Professionals who want to work here”, by contrast, are welcome. “I love it! Everyone loves it in my party!” exclaims Ms Weidel. So does she disavow her colleagues in Saxony-Anhalt whose recent manifesto railed against “culturally alien skilled workers”? Not at all. Indeed, the foreign workers that Germany should aim to attract are put off by failures of integration.
Behind the bluster lurks a skilled political manager. She forcefully defends Björn Höcke, the afd’s most divisive figure, who has been fined for using a banned Nazi slogan. But she once tried to have him expelled, only to discover he commanded too much support. Ms Weidel has personally failed to capture voters’ affections (see chart). But her ability to pick her battles, suing for peace where necessary, is her most valuable political asset.
Might that extend to other German parties? All mainstream outfits exclude the afd from coalitions under the so-called Brandmauer (firewall) policy. This, Ms Weidel alleges, forces a country that votes for right-wing policies to accept left-wing governments. Yet should the Brandmauer fall, negotiating coalitions would require the afd to compromise, primarily with the centre-right Christian Democrats (cdu). And this is not to Ms Weidel’s taste. “Why should we?” she asks. “On our main points…there are no compromises to be made. The cdu has to move first. And if it doesn’t move quickly, it will perish.” ■
The interview will be available from 6pm London time on The Insider.
articles.summaryZh: 魏德爾主張德國停止對烏克蘭的防衛援助，並稱烏方「已經輸了」，要對烏國總統施壓以結束殺戮。她質疑俄方是否涉萊比錫機場無人機事件，稱未見俄方牽涉「所謂企圖無人機攻擊」的證據，並以「外交桌上也有歷史」回指西方過去忽視俄安全憂慮。她主打「德國優先」的預算取向，主張削能源補貼、對外援助與福利來降稅控債，並承認防務新增支出仍會需要但未給細節。她主張歐洲央行不應為「高負債國家」融資，並指「Brandmauer」讓afd難入聯盟；若放寬，她要求cdu先讓步。
keyPointsZh: 魏德爾主張德國停止對烏克蘭的防衛援助，並稱烏方「已經輸了」，因此要對烏國總統施壓以結束殺戮。
她在俄方威脅的判斷上設置證據門檻，稱未見俄方涉萊比錫機場「所謂企圖無人機攻擊」的證據。
她強調「外交桌上也有歷史」，用西方長期忽視俄羅斯安全憂慮來反轉討論方向。
她推動「德國優先」的財政取向，主張削能源補貼、對外援助與福利以降稅控債，但未交代新增防務借款細節。
她認為afd難以進入聯合受「Brandmauer」影響；若協商恢復，她要求cdu先讓步。
articles.researchLensZh: 可核對的問題是：她如何用「證據是否存在」來處理萊比錫無人機指控，並如何把「控債降稅」與仍須增加的防務支出放進同一套預算敘事；同時檢查Brandmauer若鬆動後，她是否仍維持不妥協的聯盟談判立場。

articles.titleEn: Europe has lots of pleasant cities but too few that matter
articles.rubricEn: A tale of too many cities
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
Is Paris a big city? It depends on whom you ask. A tourist with only a few days to take in its sights will probably find it dauntingly large. To the French it occasionally feels smothering, the bloated administrative headquarters of an over-centralised country. But after 20-odd centuries of existence, the Ville Lumière has a distinction besides that of top tourist destination or national capital: it is by some distance the European Union’s largest city, a metropolitan standard-bearer for a largely urbanised continent. And seen through that lens it starts looking rather…petite. With one-third the population of Shanghai and less than half the economic output of New York, Paris makes an underwhelming urban flagship for a union of 450m people. Europe has perfected the art of making cityscapes pleasant. Making them mighty engines of economic dynamism is another matter.
Europe’s cities are a wonder to behold. A stroll through Lisbon, Stockholm or Krakow is a fine way to while away an afternoon. The latest ranking of the best places in the world to live, compiled by the Economist Intelligence Unit, our sister company, puts Copenhagen and Vienna at the very top. (Indonesia’s Jakarta, the world’s largest city, with a population of 42m, comes in 132nd.) But what they make up for in charm Euro-cities often lack in size, and thus commercial heft. The ten biggest urban areas in America account for a third of its economic output. In the EU the figure is nearer one-sixth, according to Oxford Economics, a consultancy. Even China and India, with their vast rural hinterlands, have a bigger share of output coming out of their largest cities. Of the 82 urban areas estimated by the UN to have a population of more than 5m people, Paris (in 36th place, with just under 10m people) and Madrid (72nd) are the only ones in the EU that make the cut.
Et alors? some might ask. Who would want a Jakarta-sur-Seine, a Tokyo am Rhein? Economists might. For them, when it comes to cities, bigger nearly always means better. Cramming more humans near each other creates more opportunities to match productive workers with innovative firms. The result is the sort of economic dynamism Europe desperately needs. Doubling the population of a city is associated with a double-digit growth in productivity, according to the OECD, a club of mostly rich countries (even smaller increases make a sizeable difference). In part that is because more productive people will flock to metropolises to seize opportunities. But even accounting for that factor, bigger cities make everyone richer just by making it easier for ideas, skills and opportunities to circulate. World-class amenities, from football stadiums to opera houses, help make up for congestion, high rents and cramped living conditions.
Europeans like their cities big, but not too big—and for there to be lots of them. This is partly for historical reasons. Centuries of weak central states and municipal independence led to a dense lattice of powerful cities. Many gradually seeped out of their tiny medieval boundaries, sometimes despite planning laws designed to protect against unsightly sprawl. In time European conurbations settled into the shape and size that made sense given their respective countries (or regions, in the case of Germany, a place with lots of competing urban centres). Even a city with grand aspirations could not outgrow its immediate national confines.
What is perhaps surprising is that this pattern of urban development has so far survived the past few decades of European integration. In theory businesses and citizens ought to think of their “home” as the EU, rather than individual countries, the better to compete against rivals in China and America. A single market in workers and ideas should have resulted in a handful of megalopolises acting as powerhouses for an integrated EU economy, not just a national one. A few European cities have specialised into continental hubs of global import: Milan in fashion, Eindhoven in semiconductor-manufacturing equipment, Brussels in crafting regulations. But none has the oomph of New York and its role in global finance, for example, or Shenzhen and manufacturing.
The result is the dispersal of riches across multiple midsize cities, many of them national capitals, yet none of them quite up to global snuff (sorry, Prague). In a world of winner-takes-most globalised industries such as artificial intelligence, this is a sizeable disadvantage. A bright graduate from America’s 50th-biggest urban economy (Charleston, South Carolina) with dreams of working in tech will undoubtedly make for San Francisco, the gateway to Silicon Valley. His counterpart in the EU’s 50th-biggest city (Graz in Austria) will have many options. Should she go to Silicon Allee in Berlin, Silicon Docks in Dublin, perhaps the Silicon Sentier in Paris? Such dispersion gnaws at European competitiveness.
Europeans strolling through their souped-up towns might console themselves with two thoughts. The first is that it may be possible to replicate the advantages of metropolises by connecting lots of nearby midsize cities. Could Amsterdam, Antwerp, Cologne and Brussels—all of them a short hop away on high-speed trains—not join forces to create a mega-hub that could turn them jointly into one city of global scale? Alas not: the advantages of being in the same place seem to decay sharply over even short distances (especially if spread across different countries).
The second is that being a pleasant place might matter more than eking out that last ounce of growth. Having lots of middling cities means none is likely to disconnect from its home polities. In an age when plenty of voters feel “left behind” by out-of-touch metropolitan types, that may be worth something. With its dense thicket of wee cities, Europe has no New York or Los Angeles to dominate global industries. But neither does it have vast swathes of “flyover country” for urban elites to sneer at. ■
articles.summaryZh: 巴黎人口與經濟產出約只有上海的三分之一、紐約的一半以下，對一個450萬人口的歐盟而言，難當城市旗艦。文章用城市規模來解釋落差：歐洲更擅長把街景做得宜人，但較少產生商業厚度，因為城市間的想法、技能與機會難以高密度循環。歐洲一度可望靠市場整合催生少數跨國大都會，卻仍呈現多個中型城市分散財富，讓創新與人才較不集中。
keyPointsZh: 歐盟最大城市巴黎的人口約千萬出頭，且經濟產出不到紐約一半，作者認為難成450萬人口的城市旗艦。
城市規模被當作成長槓桿：OECD資料指出，人口翻倍與兩位數生產力成長相關。
歐盟整合原本預期形成少數跨國超級都會，但現實仍是多個中型城市分散財富，缺乏紐約或深圳等集聚力。
用高鐵把阿姆斯特丹、安特衛普、科隆與布魯塞爾連成單一樞紐的想法，仍受限於即使短距離也會快速衰退的同地優勢。
分散城市網絡讓選民較不易覺得被「拋下」，也降低城市脫離其國內政治語境的風險。
articles.researchLensZh: 核對兩個可檢查假設：歐洲多中型城市是否確實降低「同地」的想法與技能循環；以及若改成跨國都市集聚，是否能換到足以抵消歐洲偏好小而多城市的政治與生活面向成本。

articles.titleEn: Britain’s new Dad’s Army
articles.rubricEn: The government wants its citizens to prepare for crises
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
AT A DISUSED hospital in north London, Colin Harmsworth puts his army through their paces. Clad in orange berets, they learn how to strap tourniquets to bleeding limbs and operate drones. Mr Harmsworth founded the Joint Civil Aid Corps to help Britain’s emergency services during a national crisis. Its members, he says, must be uniformed and disciplined: when duty calls, it’s no good turning up in jeans and arguing.
On paper the vision is sprawling, the product of 14 years of deliberations. Mr Harmsworth, a former cavalry soldier, took inspiration from the Civil Defence Corps, which in the cold war was tasked with digging Britons out of whatever remained of bombed cities. He imagines a force of more than 80,000 volunteers, spanning the country, and a budget north of £180m ($240m). There would be roles for medics, quartermasters, meteorologists and a drum corps. For now, however, volunteers number in the low hundreds and must buy their own uniforms. Mr Harmsworth, the “commandant”, is on the hunt for a philanthropist to make his dream reality.
His beret-wearers, meanwhile, are the British state in microcosm. Once dismissed as an eccentric pursuit, the task of galvanising Britons for “whole-of-society” responses to crises now preoccupies Whitehall. Like Mr Harmsworth, officials are adept at producing long policy papers but short of cash. Whether the state is in better shape for a crisis than the Joint Civil Aid Corps remains unclear.
Government ministers are planning a flurry of “big-muscle moves” on the topic. A public-information campaign will soon encourage Britons to stockpile food, water, torches and radios in preparation for emergencies such as bad weather. Similar measures already abound in other European countries, but a government survey found that 32% of Britons have supplies for only a day or less. Next year hundreds of officials and ministers will take part in Exercise Albiston Shadow, a war game to test the state’s reaction to hybrid attacks by a hostile power. The home-defence “war books”, as classified plans are known, are being updated for the first time since 2004.
Ministers are also preparing the Defence Readiness Bill, with provisions for mobilising armed-forces reserves and industries in a crisis. An emergency communications channel, the Resilient Voice System, is being upgraded. ThinkLabour, a think-tank with close government ties, proposes a volunteer National Resilience Corps that resembles groups in the Nordic states (and Mr Harmsworth’s vision).
One threat such measures must guard against is conflict. Sir Keir Starmer, the previous prime minister, warned in the spring that Britain might be at war with a rearmed Russia by 2030. Last week in Berlin Andy Burnham, Sir Keir’s successor, said sabotage and cyber-attacks by hostile states were growing more frequent. The government thinks Iran was behind what seemed to be an attempted attack on RAF Fairford, an airbase in Gloucestershire.
Officials must also plan for natural disasters such as pandemics, floods and wildfires. And Britain’s shoddy infrastructure might give way, too. In the 2026 edition of the National Risk Register, officials updated the odds of a whole region losing its water supply from below 1% to 5-25%. The impact, they said, would be “catastrophic”.
The catastrophising was long overdue. Britain’s state used to fear citizens would scorn advice on how to meet disaster. The ridiculing of the cold-war-era “Protect and Survive” information campaign is still remembered in Whitehall, says Toby Harris of the National Preparedness Commission, a non-profit venture.
Now there has been a “sea change in mentality, at least in the Cabinet Office”, says Elizabeth Braw of the Atlantic Council, another think-tank. During the covid-19 pandemic Britons followed lockdown rules surprisingly strictly; 500,000 signed up to volunteer within 24 hours. A survey found that 84% wanted the state to tell them how to prepare for crises.
Are its plans now sound? One problem is that Britain often uses its armed forces for civilian problems such as security at the Olympic games, wildfires and public-sector strikes. In a conflict, though, all available troops might be engaged in fighting, says Ed Arnold of RUSI, yet another think-tank. And so while the state can respond well to one crisis, it is bad at planning for several occurring at once. Moreover, a “whole-of-society” plan is not much help if society does not know what it is. And here, as in so much else, Britain’s state displays a pathological inclination to secrecy.
Occasional glimpses behind the curtain are not reassuring. Consider preparations at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA) for interruptions to food supplies. Officials fear supply chains are vulnerable—to cyber-attacks on the power grid, for instance. Food is designated one of 13 “critical national infrastructure” sectors. But Defra has “very little confidence” that cross-government governance of such sectors is joined up, and a database of relevant businesses and sites is yet to cover the food industry.
Businesses, meanwhile, have not seen the “playbook” Defra has drawn up for a food crisis. The National Audit Office has observed, drily, that this means the “plans may not work in practice”. The industry has not been invited to Whitehall’s crisis exercises. Nor have Local Resilience Forums, the provincial bodies meant to manage crises, been told what to do when the supermarket shelves are bare.
Money is part of the problem. Ministers boast that Britain will next year hit a new NATO target of spending 1.5% of GDP on “resilience”. Yet it will not spend a penny more than originally planned. Defra officials deemed the cost of a full emergency food plan too steep, opting for a “minimum viable product”. Money frustrates Mr Harmsworth, too. “In my heart of hearts, I know I can make it work,” he says. But only “if I have sufficient funding to do it.” ■
articles.summaryZh: 英國政府推動「全民韌性」危機準備，規劃制服化志工、公共資訊宣導民眾備糧備水，並升級緊急通訊與國防應變制度；同時用演習測混合攻擊反應，還更新自2004年的「戰爭手冊」。落地仍有疑慮：英軍資源恐被多個民用任務分散，食品供應的跨部會與企業資料未整合，國家審計認為計畫「未必能在實務運作」。政府稱明年NATO韌性目標為GDP 1.5%，但不增支出，讓完整計畫受限。
keyPointsZh: 內閣啟動公共資訊宣導，鼓勵民眾備糧備水與應急用品；政府調查指32%英國人僅有一天或更短存量。
Exercise Albiston Shadow將測試混合攻擊下的國家反應，Resilient Voice System也正升級；分類「戰爭手冊」自2004年後首次更新。
武裝部隊常被用在民用任務，如奧運安保、山火與公部門罷工；衝突時可能同時被牽走，難以同時覆蓋多種危機。
DEFRA對跨部會治理信心不高，食品產業的企業與地點資料庫也未涵蓋；審計機關稱相關計畫「未必能在實務運作」。
政府宣稱明年達成NATO韌性GDP 1.5%目標，但不會超出原先預算，DEFRA與志工計畫因而採取「最低可行」版本。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的轉導問題是：資訊宣導與演習能否轉成跨部會、跨地方、產業可執行的作業流程。尤其要核對食品關鍵基礎設施的企業名單是否補齊、是否納入演練，以及「不增支出」是否迫使計畫縮到最低版本。

articles.titleEn: Attack drones, meet Britain’s crack clay-pigeon shooters
articles.rubricEn: An old hobby trains soldiers for a new type of warfare
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
It was a bad day to be a clay pigeon. On a misty morning in Wiltshire, British soldiers gathered for their annual shooting championship. Around 100 shot at 100 targets each—a massacre. Shotguns boomed, and neat clay discs were blasted into bright bursts of colour.
Clay-pigeon shooting was born in the late 1800s to help hunters improve their aim. In the second world war it was used to train fighter pilots. Today Peter Meager, boss of the army’s clay-target shooting team, hopes it can help prepare soldiers for drone warfare. “I think there are huge transferable skills,” he says.
Such skills are needed. Drones are behind 80% of the enemy targets Ukraine destroys. In June Britain’s Defence Investment Plan committed £750m ($950m) to counter-drone protection. Futuristic solutions include acoustic radars and direct-energy weapons.
Victorian ones might help, too. Shotguns are great for hitting aerial targets because their shells contain many projectiles, which spread out in the air. That makes it easier to catch a bird’s wing or a quadcopter’s propeller. But the army trains soldiers to shoot rifles instead.
The two are very different, says Ben Cookson, one of the army’s crack shots. Rifle shooting is about “being as still as possible”. You get in position, aim, breathe in and fire. “If you do that with a shotgun you’re doomed.” Hitting an airborne target means moving with it and judging how far ahead of it to aim. When rifle shooters come to Mr Cookson for tutoring, “we have to completely retrain them”, he says.
Clay-pigeon shooting is a good place to start. Launchers built to mimic the flight patterns of different birds can feasibly simulate those of drones, too. Most can fire clays at a drone-like speed of 50mph, and some at over 100mph.
And so, after Ukrainians told British instructors how useful shotguns were on the front line, the army started using clays to develop soldiers’ proficiency with them. But a shotgun should only ever be “a last resort”, says Mr Meager. A drone within range of one is already too close—much better to down it earlier.
Plenty of questions still hover over shotguns’ use as an anti-drone defence. Spotting the things is hard. In Wiltshire some shooters don tinted goggles to make the orange clays pop. Might whizzier versions help identify a distant, fast-moving quadcopter? Can standard lead shells take down armoured military drones? How widely should the shot be spread when targeting an incoming one?
These are questions for the nerds. At the army’s tournament the focus was on technique: the top score was 94 out of 100. Your correspondent, while not quite managing that, did at least avoid embarrassing himself in front of the troops (”a natural”, said Mr Cookson, a kind man). Spirits were high. But one cloud hanging over the day had little to do with the rain. “I hate drones,” sighs Mr Meager. ■
articles.summaryZh: 威爾特郡霧晨，英國軍方辦年度黏土飛靶射擊賽：約100名士兵各打100個靶。彼得·米格爾把這類「命中空中目標」技巧視為可移轉訓練，用來準備無人機作戰；他說英軍6月投了7.5億英鎊強化反無人機防護。文中也提到無人機攻擊在烏克蘭戰場使英方摧毀的敵方目標占比達80%，並列出聲學雷達、定向能武器等方案。軍方同時改用霰彈槍訓練，但強調必須等同最後手段，且仍卡在偵測、彈藥與射擊散布角度等可行性問題。
keyPointsZh: 威爾特郡年度黏土飛靶賽約100名士兵各打100個靶，主軸是把命中空中目標的動作訓練做成可移轉技能。
文中稱無人機攻擊在烏克蘭戰場背後占80%被摧毀的敵方目標；英國6月國防投資計畫承諾投入7.5億英鎊反無人機防護。
米格爾把黏土飛靶視為準備無人機戰的路徑，但也說霰彈槍只能作為最後手段，距離內的無人機已太近。
Ben Cookson稱步槍訓練要盡量保持靜止、點射判斷提前量；用霰彈槍則必須「完全重訓」來處理跟動與提前量。
文中列出疑問：遠距能否靠護目鏡辨識、標準lead彈能否打到裝甲無人機，以及目標來襲時應如何設定彈丸散布。
articles.researchLensZh: 把「命中高速移動目標」的技能轉移，當成可檢驗假設：黏土飛靶能否用模擬速度與軌跡，對應到偵測困難下的反無人機任務表現；並逐一檢查護目鏡辨識、提前量與散布角度的傳導機制。

articles.titleEn: Israel and Britain have forestalled a diplomatic crisis—for now
articles.rubricEn: But a once-special relationship is faltering
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
THE UNION JACK still flies in Jerusalem, over the same building it has been on for 59 years. On October 8th Israel and Britain agreed, after weeks of diplomatic wrangling, to rename this office the UK Mission rather than the Consulate-General. Both countries saved face but the fracas between them is far from over.
Their spat began soon after Britain changed its prime minister in July and appointed Ed Miliband as foreign secretary. One of his priorities has been to harden Britain’s position on Israel's brutal war in Gaza and its de facto annexation of the occupied West Bank. In some places Israeli settlers have been carrying out ethnic cleansing with tacit support from their government. Many, especially in the Labour Party, thought Britain’s government was previously far too soft on this.
On September 8th Mr Miliband announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, as did France and Canada. Previous such efforts by Western countries, targeting individual settlers and organisations, have had limited effect. The difference this time is the intention to take “action on services” and “companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlement activity”. This broad brush might paint everything from government ministries to Israel’s biggest banks.
In response, the Israeli government said it would close Britain’s consulate in Jerusalem, which serves its relations with Palestinians, and remove Britons working on Gaza’s planned reconstruction. Britain then threatened to escalate matters by expelling Israeli diplomats. The eventual compromise of renaming Britain’s consulate has cooled things for now.
Two big questions hang over Britain’s new stance on Israel. First, how far is it prepared to go? Mr Miliband has said he will need six to nine months to prepare legislation for the sanctions, and that they will target only the settlements, “not Israel”, with which Britain has “important and valued trade”. The sanctions, when they materialise, may therefore be little more than a gesture. But they may also be designed to cause serious damage. This uncertainty probably explains in part why America has not yet intervened. “It’s a game-changer,” says one senior Israeli diplomat. “Everyone understands what this can mean and Israeli banks are very worried.”
The second question is over timing. Some in Britain’s Foreign Office wanted to delay Mr Miliband’s announcement until after Israel’s parliamentary election on October 27th. Binyamin Netanyahu, the country’s prime minister, will not change its settlement policy when he needs to appeal to right-wing voters. After the election there may be a different government in Jerusalem. Mr Miliband, though, has his own political timetable.
Palestine has become a huge issue in British politics. In the 2024 elections Labour lost five seats to independent pro-Palestine candidates. This year, as in past ones, protesters waved Palestinian flags outside the Labour Party conference. But Mr Miliband’s sanctions statement nevertheless made it easier to remove the issue from the conference’s agenda—the result he was after, says one Labour adviser. His next steps might also be dictated by domestic politics, especially if the government calls an early election.
On September 30th Mr Netanyahu fired a shot across Britain’s bows. He lambasted the country in an interview with Fox News for announcing its sanctions “pretty much the next day” after Israel gave it intelligence on the “Iranian-sponsored” attack on an RAF base.
Israeli spooks were aghast at what they saw as Mr Netanyahu’s breach of secrecy. Close co-operation between the two countries’ intelligence services has long served both sides well, and the prospect of Iranian attacks on British soil gives them an obvious shared enemy. But some in the Israeli government argue that further British sanctions should be met with threats to withhold intelligence. “Ministers with political agendas could put us on a slippery slope to disrupting intelligence-sharing and harming both countries’ national security,” warns one Israeli official. ■
articles.summaryZh: 以色列與英國因加沙戰爭與約旦河西岸實質併吞議題升溫。9月8日外相Ed Miliband宣布對西岸以色列定居點制裁，擬涵蓋支援或獲利非法定居活動的服務與公司；以方隨即稱將關閉駐耶路撒冷英國機構並移走協助加沙重建的英國人員。雙方最後改以把機構改名為「UK Mission」止血。仍有兩個變數：制裁實際力度是否會觸及大型銀行，以及制裁時點是否受10月27日以色列選舉、英國國內政治議程影響。
keyPointsZh: 9月8日Miliband宣布制裁西岸以色列定居點，未來可擴到提供服務或獲利非法定居活動的公司與機構，範圍可能從部會到大型銀行。
以色列政府回應稱將關閉駐耶路撒冷英國機構、並移走協助加沙重建的英國人員；英國隨後威脅驅逐以色列外交人員，最後以改名「UK Mission」暫時降溫。
Miliband預計6到9個月完成制裁立法，且表示只針對定居點、不針對以色列，但外界仍擔心可能造成更大損害。
英國官員曾想把宣布延到10月27日以色列國會選舉後才發布，因選後可能換政府；但Miliband有自己的政治時程。
制裁發布時間也引發情報合作疑慮：內文提到內塔尼亞胡指控英方在以色列提供「伊朗支持」攻擊情報後幾乎隔天就宣布，部分以方擔心影響保密與情報共享。
articles.researchLensZh: 檢查兩個可驗證路徑：一是制裁立法的對象是否從定居點擴到提供服務與牟利的金融體系，導致政策壓力落到銀行；二是宣布時點是否被英國國內政治或10月27日以色列選舉牽動，並評估是否因此影響英以情報共享。
highlightTermsZh: 擬涵蓋支援或獲利非法定居活動的服務與公司

articles.titleEn: The City of London honours an ancient pact
articles.rubricEn: Meet the world’s most elaborate rent payment
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
In a fusty room at the Royal Courts of Justice, a man in a tricorn hat receives a payment. He is the king’s remembrancer, an office once charged with keeping track of money owed to the crown. This is the annual Ceremony of Quit Rents, held this year on October 14th. The earliest recorded one was in 1211. Each year the City of London pays a levy to the monarch for two plots of land: six giant horseshoes, 61 nails and two knives, one blunt and one sharp.
The remembrancer then inspects the wares. An official tries the blunt knife—traditionally a billhook—which should be able to bend a hazel stick without cutting it. Next he wields the sharp one, which needs to chop through the wood. Once the horseshoes and nails have been counted, the payment is accepted and the City can enjoy its tenancies for another 12 months.
In theory, at least. These days no one knows exactly where the rented land is, though some have made educated guesses. The first parcel is somewhere in Shropshire, where a man named Nicholas rented moorland before passing his tenancy on. The other is near London’s Strand, a stone’s throw from The Economist’s office. It came from a blacksmith called Walter, who paid for access to a forge (hence the horseshoes). Uncertainty over the postcodes has not stopped the crown claiming its due. In today’s Square Mile firms hire armies of lawyers to draft agreements and then wriggle out of them. But for the king’s remembrancer contracts are sacred.
The ceremony is the sort of thing Britain is famous for. In this common-law country, precedent piles on precedent and keeping up appearances is paramount. Hence the Tower of London has been locked at 9.53pm every night for 700 years, and the king has held an annual swan-counting event for even longer.
Other “quit rents” abound. For centuries the City has paid the crown £11 ($15) a year for the “town of Southwark”. In parts of East Anglia, Leicester and London people honour ancient deals by handing over roses. The Duke of Wellington hangs onto his country mansion only so long as he delivers a French flag to the king each June (something to do with Waterloo).
The autumn ceremony at the Royal Courts of Justice is the most ancient such occasion. Those watching from the public gallery admit the event is nonsense. But, says one, it is “lovely nonsense”. ■
articles.summaryZh: 英國倫敦城在皇家法院辦年度Quit Rents。2026年10月14日，「國王遺聞官」收取象徵性租金，讓倫敦城兩塊土地的租約再延續12個月；最早紀錄回到1211年。付款要清點六個大型馬蹄、61支釘子與兩把刀，遺聞官再用鈍刀與利刀測試木材。近年租地實際位置多半不明，王室仍按程序主張收款，且對此類合約維持約束。
keyPointsZh: 2026年10月14日，國王遺聞官在皇家法院收取倫敦城年度Quit Rents，租約再延續12個月。
象徵性付款包含六個大型馬蹄、61支釘子與兩把刀，遺聞官需逐一清點。
遺聞官先用鈍刀（傳統billhook）測木材可彎不切，再用利刀砍斷木材。
租地近年位置多半不明，但王室仍以合約主張收取；倫敦城對此儀式合約較難迴避。
倫敦城長期向南方克繳£11/年；東盎格利亞、萊斯特與倫敦則有人以玫瑰或附加物件履行類似quit rents義務。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢驗的問題是：在租地位置難以確認時，制度如何仍讓履約義務可被持續執行。可把文中「象徵租金＋儀式性清點與刀具驗證」視為機制切片，對照普通法先例如何把義務鎖進程序層級。
highlightTermsZh: 六個大型馬蹄、61支釘子與兩把刀

articles.titleEn: Lessons from Britain’s humiliating IMF bail-out
articles.rubricEn: Fifty years on, a fiscal crisis would play out very differently
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
The similarities between 1976 and 2026 are eerie. Then as now the spectre of decline haunted Britain, its economy troubled by energy crises, inflation and a lack of competitiveness. In both years the embattled Labour Party appointed a new prime minister, despite having won office only two years before. And both leaders then chose chancellors called Healey.
As John Healey, today’s chancellor, prepares for the budget on October 28th, he might well worry that he will suffer the fate of Denis Healey, his predecessor in 1976. On September 28th that year, the earlier Healey was about to board a plane when sterling’s freefall forced him to turn back and apply for an emergency loan from the IMF. A $3.9bn bail-out, agreed upon in December, imposed on the birthplace of the industrial revolution the sort of humiliating conditions normally reserved for the world’s sketchiest economies.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, warned last year that the government was on track once again to go cap in hand to the IMF. There are superficial echoes of 1976. Then investors revolted, refusing to buy British government bonds (or “gilts”) unless they offered much higher yields. Today’s bondholders charge Britain more to borrow than any other G7 country.
But though Britain can learn much from 1976, another trip to the IMF is unlikely. Things are nowhere near as bad today. Inflation was 13.7% in 1976; the IMF reckons it will be 3.8% this year. Ten-year gilt yields, then 15.7%, are now 5.4% (see table). And the economy was in another era. Marginal tax rates hit 98%. The government struck economy-wide wage deals with the unions. The Labour conference of 1976 passed a motion calling for the nationalisation of the country’s biggest four banks and seven insurance companies.
Most importantly, Britain managed its currency very differently 50 years ago. At the beginning of March 1976 £1 was worth $2.02; by October it had fallen to $1.57, driven by Britain’s embarrassing mismanagement of its economy. The Bank of England tried, and failed, to prop up the value of sterling by selling its foreign-currency reserves. In June it borrowed more from other central banks. And when those debts came due in December, Healey was forced to turn to the IMF.
The government is now happier to let the pound float freely on currency markets, making a repeat of the IMF drama improbable. But that does not mean Britain is out of the woods. Today a fiscal crisis would take a different form. Britain’s debt-to-GDP ratio is 95%, nearly double its level in the 1970s. Growth is much slower, leaving the country more exposed to sudden changes in market sentiment.
A crisis in 2026, therefore, might start in the gilt market. The government has two defences against things spiralling out of control: a plan for cutting the deficit and an independent central bank charged with keeping inflation down. But if either were doubted, yields could surge. This could start a vicious cycle, in which soaring borrowing costs worsened the public finances and in turn sent yields even higher. So might a jump in volatility elsewhere, since global markets are now far more complex and interconnected than in 1976.
To guard against such a crisis, Mr Healey should learn from his predecessor. The first lesson is the importance of flexibility. In 1976 it was not just that officials tried to resist changes to exchange rates. Unions refused to accept real-terms pay cuts, fuelling inflation and deepening the crisis. Flexible labour and currency markets give the economy shock absorbers.
Mr Healey also needs to ensure that investors really believe he will cut the deficit. Denis Healey grumbled that the 1976 crisis was avoidable: his spending cuts were working and only pessimistic forecasts spooked markets. He had a point, since spending came in below forecast, but the panic still caused real damage. Credibility in markets matters in itself, especially for Britain, which runs a current-account deficit (as in 1976) and relies on the kindness of flighty strangers to fund itself.
The IMF crisis wounded British pride. But it also gave Denis Healey an external constraint—the IMF—that helped enforce much-needed spending cuts against the will of many backbenchers. As Lord Macpherson, a former Treasury permanent secretary, puts it: “The only time the British state gets a grip on anything is when it is staring into the abyss.” Spending today is already 45% of GDP, as in 1976, and an ageing, sicker population will add to the strain. A crisis might be the only way to force John Healey or his successors to make tough but necessary choices. ■
articles.summaryZh: 1976年英國在能源危機、通膨與競爭力不足下承受金融壓力。英鎊在匯率操作失靈後加速貶值，英格蘭銀行用外匯存底撐盤失敗，央行間借款到期後，Denis Healey 只能向IMF求援，拿到39億美元紓困並被加上羞辱式條件。2026年雖有相似人事與投資人疑慮，但文中估計通膨3.8%、十年gilts殖利率約5.4%，再度進IMF機率較低；若危機出現，較可能先從公債市場的殖利率上升觸發連鎖反應。
keyPointsZh: 1976年英鎊因經濟失管走弱，英格蘭銀行賣出外匯存底與向其他央行借款都未能止跌，最後在債務到期後由Denis Healey改向IMF借款。
1976年通膨達13.7%，2026年被IMF估計為3.8%；十年gilts殖利率1976年15.7%而2026年約5.4%，因此文中認為再度進IMF的情境不太相同。
英國債務占GDP比95%且成長偏慢，使其更易受市場情緒改變；若市場懷疑赤字削減與央行抑通膨的承諾，殖利率可能暴衝並惡化財政。
文中把1976教訓落在兩點：以彈性吸收衝擊，並強化市場對赤字削減的信心，因為英國依賴持續融資。
文中指出支出已約占GDP 45%，再加上人口老化與健康需求，外部約束可能成為促成減支抉擇的壓力來源。
articles.researchLensZh: 回到原文檢驗三個鏈條：匯率與勞動市場彈性如何影響通膨與危機深度、2026的通膨與十年gilts殖利率水準是否真的降低「進IMF」風險、以及赤字削減與央行承諾若被質疑，殖利率如何從公債市場回饋到公共財政。
highlightTermsZh: 英格蘭銀行用外匯存底撐盤失敗

articles.titleEn: In Britain, “European” doesn’t mean white
articles.rubricEn: The country’s EU citizens are astonishingly diverse
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
To the uninformed palate, pindakaas is simply peanut butter. But some Somalis in Leicester, a city in the English Midlands, prefer the Dutch product. Jars of imported pindakaas can be bought in corner shops around the run-down St Matthew’s housing estate, near the city centre. So can Dutch oatmeal, Dutch vanilla sugar and condiments such as kruiden ketchup and romige fritessaus.
The Somalis of St Matthew’s developed a taste for such foods in the Netherlands, where many were refugees. They gained Dutch citizenship then migrated to Britain under eu freedom-of-movement rules. They are part of a large, diverse population of ethnic-minority Europeans in the country. Often overlooked, this population challenges British assumptions about immigration and Europe.
The Migration Observatory, a think-tank at Oxford University, estimates that some 800,000 ethnic-minority people in Britain hold eu passports. Most come from “old” European countries, such as France, Italy and the Netherlands, rather than the “new” countries that joined the union after 2003, such as Lithuania and Poland. Young Western Europeans in Britain are startlingly diverse (see chart).
Numbering almost 80,000, Portuguese Asians are the biggest group. Many come from the Indian state of Goa, which was Portuguese until 1961; people with deep roots in the state can obtain Portuguese passports. Espirito Roy Sequeira, a former seaman who now lives in Leicester, says that many Goans find Portugal more familiar than Britain because of its food and its Catholic churches. But Britain appeals to those who want their children to grow up with perfect English. “English is an international language; Portuguese is not,” says Mr Sequeira, rather understating the importance of Portuguese.
Abdikayf Farah, who runs a Somali education charity, spent a dozen years in Denmark. He moved to Leicester partly for its relaxed multiculturalism. The Danish government frowns on what it calls “parallel societies” and “ghettos”, and tries to break up immigrant enclaves; Britain does nothing of the kind. Education is another draw. Mr Farah says that the Somalis who migrated from the eu are especially ambitious for their children.
Those children are faring pretty well. Last year 53% of Asian pupils and 41% of black African pupils in Leicester’s schools got at least a grade 5 in their English and Maths gcse exams. The figure for white Britons was 24%. Immigrants’ children perform better than average in the pisa tests run by the oecd, a club of mostly rich countries, making Britain unusual among European nations.
Another draw is the belief that ethnic minorities find it easier to get ahead in Britain. Hielen Tekeste Berhe, an Italian citizen with Eritrean parents, speaks of a “glass ceiling” in Italy. She has created a startup called The Fair Grocer, which is inspired by Italian and east African food cultures. Attending gatherings of black entrepreneurs in Britain, she sometimes detects a familiar accent, and realises that she is speaking to another Italian.
If the population of European ethnic minorities is growing today, it is probably more a result of childbirth than immigration. Brexit has suppressed movement of all kinds. Indeed, Aké Achi, founder of a group called Black Europeans, says that many people are struggling to establish their right to remain in Britain. Ethnic minorities are over-represented among those who report problems with the scheme that allows Europeans to settle after Brexit.
A sociologist at Loughborough University, Simone Varriale, says that Britons tend to squeeze black and Asian Europeans into the post-colonial categories they are familiar with. To them, an African Italian is simply African. But some resist this flattening of their identities. “It’s not just that we have Italian passports. We are Italians!” declares Ms Tekeste Berhe. In a Leicester suburb Azim Zicar, a Mozambican Asian it worker, speaks Portuguese to his children and strives to introduce them to others who share their background.
Now that most Britons see Brexit as a failure, politicians and think-tanks have begun to probe their appetite for rejoining the eu. Because that would mean a resumption of free movement, an important question is how Britons feel about migration from Europe.
A poll by British Future, a think-tank, found that 41% believe workers from the eu should be given priority over those from elsewhere, compared with 40% who think they should be treated equally. A Cambridge University study found that Britons grew keener on European migration when they were told to imagine a nurse from Poland. Yet some migrants are both from the eu and from outside the eu. Free movement has given Britain pindakaas-eating Somalis as well as Poles. ■
articles.summaryZh: 「歐洲人」在英國不等於白人。牛津 Migration Observatory 推估，英國約有80萬名少數族裔持有歐盟護照，多數來自法國、義大利、荷蘭等「舊歐洲」國家。萊斯特的索馬利裔在荷蘭取得公民後，依歐盟自由移動規則遷居英國，並偏好荷蘭食物；他們的子女在GCSE英語與數學也不差。民意顯示41%支持給來自歐盟的工人優先，40%主張同等對待；文中另指出英國常把黑、亞裔歐洲人塞進熟悉的後殖民標籤。
keyPointsZh: 牛津 Migration Observatory 推估英國約有80萬名少數族裔持有歐盟護照，多數來自法國、義大利、荷蘭等「舊歐洲」國家。
萊斯特索馬利裔在荷蘭取得公民身分後，依歐盟自由移動規則遷居英國，並把荷蘭食品文化帶進生活。
萊斯特學校成績顯示，亞洲與黑人非裔在GCSE英語與數學達到至少5級的比例高於白人。
文中指出英國常用既有分類把黑、亞裔歐洲人簡化，部分人因此強調自己同時有歐洲護照與「真正的」身份。
英國民調顯示41%主張給歐盟工人優先、40%主張同等對待，並且想像特定歐洲移民情境後支持度曾上升。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的問題是：歐盟自由移動是否透過取得公民、定居與家庭選擇，影響少數族裔子女的教育表現；同時英國人如何把「歐洲」落到既有族群分類，會不會因為具體移民形象而改變對歐洲移民的態度。
