They had “a simple picture in their heads of ‘the bureaucrat’, and that person looked a lot like Maxine”.
So DOGE started slashing. It attempted to fire all the probationary staff—the recent hires who were mostly either young or had urgently needed skills. Permanent staff were offered hefty payouts to quit. Many who could easily find other jobs accepted; the less capable ones stayed. A return-to-the-office rule was enforced mindlessly. DOGE killed a study of how wildfires spread into suburbs, because the only computers powerful enough for its modelling were not in a government office.
DOGE failed to make the state smaller , despite Mr Musk’s ambitious promises. But it did make it dumber. Colette Delawalla, a clinical psychologist, was told that her application for a research grant would fail because it contained the word “translate” (which includes “trans”) and “bias” (an essential term in statistics that is also used in complaints about racism).
It made it crueller, too. Mr Musk was outraged that the United States Institute of Peace was paying a former member of the Taliban. The man was supplying vital intelligence. After Mr Musk outed him on X, the informant’s family was rounded up and tortured. The Trump revolution also made government less accountable, by suppressing evidence that his policies were hurting people. After he cut food subsidies for the poor, a survey measuring hunger was scrapped.
Most disturbing of all, in Mr Lewis’s telling, Mr Musk’s tech-savvy footsoldiers saw the law as an obstacle to work round, rather than a guide. Mr Lewis tells the story of Kathleen Walters, the chief privacy officer at the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). DOGE had sent an email to every federal employee ordering them, on pain of dismissal, to each list five things they had accomplished in the previous week. Since violating taxpayers’ privacy is a crime, many at the IRS risked prison if they responded—and the sack if they didn’t.
Ms Walters locked horns with Gavin Kliger, a young hoodie-clad DOGE staffer. Mr Kliger showed up at the IRS demanding access to all its systems and taxpayer data. This was plainly illegal. Even worse was an effort by a Trump appointee to make the IRS share with the immigration authorities personal data about millions of illegal immigrants who had filed tax returns.
The IRS had spent decades reassuring such people that, if they wanted to pay taxes and build a record of civic virtue that might one day help them win legal status, their privacy would be respected. Mr Trump wanted their addresses so he could shackle and deport them. An acting IRS commissioner, who had been in the job for only an hour, sent out the request on a Friday night, doing an end run around the woman whose job it was to say no.
Alerted by a colleague, Ms Walters called the acting commissioner from outside a pizza restaurant, and warned her that the plan was unlawful. Two months later, after having spent an evening hiding from Mr Kliger in a darkened conference room, Ms Walters quit. Later, in Texas, teams of ICE agents showed up in a Latino neighbourhood knowing exactly which doors to jimmy open. A court ruled that the IRS data-sharing with ICE was illegal, but for many of its victims—and for trust in the system—it was too late. ■
articles.summaryZh: 疫情早期，川普用「氫氯喹」的個人回復經驗逼 NIH 院長 Collins 針對新冠治療表態；專家回應需雙盲隨機試驗才知道藥效，川普之後不再召見。書中描寫 DOGE 進入聯邦後先用刻板印象判斷官僚，再砍試用人員、推回辦公室規定，並因野火模型算力不在辦公室而停掉研究。DOGE 審查研究也出錯，將含「translate」與「bias」的申請直接判失敗。文末提到 IRS 被要求列出每週成果，並企圖讓 IRS 與移民當局共享個資；法院裁定共享違法，但信任與受害影響已先出現。
keyPointsZh: 川普以「氫氯喹」的親身回復經驗說服 NIH 院長 Collins，但在提醒需雙盲隨機試驗後，川普不再召見 Collins。
DOGE 進入聯邦後先用刻板印象評價官僚，接著砍試用人員、強推回辦公室規定，改變人力與研究運作。
野火擴散模型因所需電腦算力不在政府辦公室而被 DOGE 停掉，研究能力因此受損。
研究申請審查出現語意誤判，例如申請含「translate」與「bias」就被判定失敗。
IRS 被要求每週列出成果且面臨隱私刑責風險，並同時推動與移民當局共享個資；法院裁定違法但影響已難以追回。
articles.researchLensZh: 重點可檢查的假設是：把軼事與刻板印象當作決策輸入，會取代雙盲隨機試驗與標準化研究審查；其後透過人事淘汰、辦公室規定、審查流程失準與資料共享指令，讓合規風險（隱私、共享合法性）與研究產出一起下滑。

articles.titleEn: Annie Dillard wanted to know the mind of God
articles.rubricEn: The nature writer and “theologian” died on September 15th, aged 81
articles.textEn:
Oct 15th 2026
She could never forget the moth. It hatched from a cocoon kept by her teacher in a Mason jar, a huge Polyphemus silk moth with, potentially, velvety brown wings bearing a bright blue eyespot. At the moment of hatching, its wings produced a hardening varnish that would enable them to spread. Then it could fly. But the jar was too small, and the varnish worked too fast. The moth, when released on the street, could only walk. But it struggled gamely on with its useless lumps of wings, heading somewhere. In Annie Dillard’s mind, it was still going.
She was the only one to see it as it went. She was often a sole observer, quietly noting. A goldfinch shaking a seeding thistle until the down floated, “blind and sweet”, all over the landscape. A mosquito biting a poisonous copperhead. A leaf still curled like a thin, pale flame in its bud on a tulip tree. Frogs leaping like flares through a mesh of blue-green algae, “surfacing to awareness”. Another frog on the bank of Tinker Creek, stock still, as a giant water bug slowly liquidised its insides and sipped its life away.
It was Tinker Creek that made her famous. The book she wrote about her thoughts and sightings there, “Pilgrim at Tinker Creek”, won her a Pulitzer in 1975, when she was only 28. She was the youngest woman to win one, and the first in the man’s world of nature-writing. But fame was the last thing she wanted. All she had needed for years was that damp, broken ground near Roanoke, Virginia, the sycamore log on which she sat, the noisy creek with its silvery shiners swarming in the shallows, and the Osage orange tree from which rose, once, a hundred red-winged blackbirds. When the Pulitzer news came, she was washing spinach. She wouldn’t have to do that any more, the pressman said. But she would, and did.
Before too long she fled from the unbearable fussing, decamping with her writer husband to Washington state and the islands off the coast. From her various exile places she produced essays, poetry, philosophy, journalism, two novels and an autobiography. For preference she wrote in very small spaces, usually log cabins, facing away from the view. Inevitably people compared her to Henry David Thoreau, the 19th-century naturalist who had been the subject of her master’s thesis, but she didn’t agree. Unlike him, she didn’t live in most of her cabins; half of “Tinker Creek” had been written, after hours, in a public library. Her favourite writer was not him, but Primo Levi, because he wrote the truth.
Nor did she think of herself as a nature writer. All she saw and noted was part of an overwhelming question: why, among the prodigal beauties and intricacies of the world, was there so much destruction? Why were there thousands of barbules on the wing of a wild goose that any predator might devour? What was the creator—if there was a creator—thinking? Why was there so much care, then none? She loved to watch hatchings and unfoldings. But the hatchlings were immediate food for something else, and each leaf shrivelled in two seasons. This couldn’t all be some cynical show, though she sometimes called it that. Perhaps it was more a case that God could do anything, so he did. Wildly, freely.
And what was she, amid all this? Nothing important. She was not needed in creation. Her life seemed no more than the tunnels made by miner larvae on a leaf, “a faint tracery on the surface of mystery”. Yet she contained multitudes. She could see, with her naked eye, through two million light years as far as the Andromeda galaxy. She could explore endlessly, as she did, and reflect on her explorations. Those were not, in the end, about understanding nature. She was more of a theologian.
Religion didn’t feature much at all as she was growing up, tomboyish and comfortably middle-class, in Pittsburgh. Books did. They swept her away. From the age of five, she reckoned she read 100 books a year. She wanted to know and remember everything: history, geography, geology, minerology, criminology, the names of trees and the names of birds. She read and re-read “The Field Book of Ponds and Streams”. As with her sightings in nature, so with the written word. Someone had to read these books.
On the writing of books, though, she had strong opinions, laid out in 1989 in “The Writing Life”. That life was far from a state of sedentary inspiration. It was arduous, tough and necessarily cruel. The writer’s first line of words was a probe into the unknown, digging a path; once she had arrived in a new, promising place, the path had to be erased. Cut the umbilical cord. Everything written up til then probably had to go, even the favourite passages and the load-bearing walls; even, sometimes, the whole original point of the thing. Ruthlessness was essential; no excess. If a book got stuck, or out of control, it must be visited every day, as if the writer were a lion-tamer with a chair shouting “Simba!” Mastery had to be reasserted, and not just—as she asserted hers—with near-continuous coffee and Vantage cigarettes.
In the middle of “The Writing Life” she recorded a peculiar event: the apparently spontaneous combustion of a typewriter. It was a portable Smith-Corona, so not attached to power. The explosion shook the house, and she raced upstairs to find the device erupting with fire and ash. As she tried to douse the flames, sparks burned holes in her shirt. It might have been a careless cigarette, but she did not say so. In her telling there was just, suddenly, fire.
It was often around. As a child, she wanted to run so fast that she would throw out sparks. At Tinker Creek she saw, at sunset, some divine power “rolling along the mountain ridges like a fireball”. At moments of “seeing truly” the grass was wholly fire, and the backyard cedar became a tree of lights. She felt lifted then, resounding “like a beaten bell”. Yet only she had noticed those things, as only she had seen the death of the Tinker Creek frog, or the crippled moth staggering on. Only she was meant not to miss that horror and that beauty. That was what she was for. ■
articles.summaryZh: 安妮·迪勒德把自然看見寫成追問：在充滿奇美與細節的世界裡，為何同時有大量毀滅？她在維吉尼亞州丁克溪一帶的觀察結成《Pilgrim at Tinker Creek》，1975年以28歲拿下普立茲獎。她仍不把名聲當目標，回到洗菠菜與在日常小空間寫作。她也不自認只是自然作家，更多把自己當作「神學式」提問者。
keyPointsZh: 迪勒德在維吉尼亞州丁克溪的所見所思，寫成《Pilgrim at Tinker Creek》，1975年以28歲獲普立茲獎。
她用自然細節逼問毀滅的同時存在，重點放在「為何如此」而不只是描寫自然。
她描述破繭蛾在瓶子太小與凝固太快的條件下，只能爬行仍朝向某處前進。
她在寫作主張中要求「殘酷地刪除多餘」，並記錄打字機疑似自燃當下只看見火。
她把自己稱作神學式的提問者：人在創造中似乎不重要，但只有她能不漏掉恐怖與美。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的連結是：她的自然觀察如何轉成神學式提問，以及這套提問是否反映在寫作方法上（小空間創作、頻繁修訂、強制刪減）。交叉驗證可對照《丁克溪》段落與《The Writing Life》的寫作主張。
highlightTermsZh: 在充滿奇美與細節的世界裡，為何同時有大量毀滅？

articles.titleEn: Politics
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
At least 250,000 demonstrators in France marched through Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Rennes, Toulouse and other cities, mainly to protest against a lack of investment in education. The protests, led by school pupils but joined by parents, teachers and unions as well as elements of the populist-left, have been building since mid-September, and are often accompanied by arson and vandalism. The police have responded with tear-gas and baton charges. Sébastien Lecornu, the prime minister, accused the populist-left of fuelling the violence. The protesters’ calls for more public investment come amid efforts by the government to control the budget deficit, and as bond markets punish France for its fiscal irresponsibility.
Spain has also seen significant protests, over housing, which were triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home by an investment fund, underscoring the high cost of renting in Spain. The woman has since died. The Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has used the protests as a pretext to call a snap general election for November 29th. Mr Sánchez is seeking a progressive majority, but the left trails behind the conservatives in the opinion polls.
Meanwhile, the Spanish Supreme Court lifted the arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont, the leader of the separatist movement in Catalonia, paving the way for his return from self-imposed exile. Mr Puigdemont fled to Belgium in 2017 after holding an illegal referendum on independence.
A former head of the BND, Germany’s foreign-intelligence service, was arrested for treason . August Hanning led the BND from 1998 to 2005 and was a security consultant after that. He is accused of collecting classified material, some of which was passed to an unnamed foreign power. Press reports say it was Azerbaijan; the country denies it. A former aide was charged with gathering the documents.
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) secured the role of speaker in Saxony-Anhalt’s legislature, a month after winning an election in the east German state. It is the first time a populist-right party has attained the speakership in a German state parliament since the second world war. The AfD is short of a majority, however, and it is unclear if it will be able to form a state government.
Russia’s bombardment of Ukraine continued unabated. At least 32 people were killed in a single day across the country, most of them in the town of Pryluky, 150km (93 miles) east of Kiev, where a Russian missile hit a residential building.
Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in India, was briefly detained during protests demanding the resignation of the head of the Election Commission. The commission is embroiled in a political scandal after tens of millions of voters were deleted from the electoral rolls, reportedly to the advantage of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. The commission says it merely removed duplicate or ineligible names.
In Japan the prime minister, Takaichi Sanae, lodged a complaint with the American government over the alleged murder of a Japanese woman in Okinawa by an American marine, which the marine denies. The American embassy said it was co-operating; marines have been put on a one-month curfew and banned from drinking alcohol for 48 hours. The presence of American troops in Okinawa has caused friction with locals in the past. In 1995 the rape of a 12-year-old girl by three marines led to angry protests calling for the troops to leave.
Min Aung Hlaing, who led a military coup against Myanmar’s elected government in 2021 and earlier this year had himself named president, visited Malaysia. Malaysia had previously been among the most vocal critics of the putsch. But Anwar Ibrahim, Malaysia’s prime minister, needs Min Aung Hlaing’s support to deport Myanmar refugees ahead of elections expected in Malaysia next year.
Pro-government forces in Yemen began a big offensive against the Houthi rebels, who are backed by Iran. They said they had “secured” Bab al-Mandab, a crucial waterway in the Red Sea, and captured the city of Mokha, with the support of Saudi air strikes. The Houthis denied losing control of the strait or Mokha and launched strikes on the airport in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, and elsewhere in the kingdom, killing at least three people. Turkey and Pakistan, which have signed a defence pact with a mutual-defence clause with the Saudis, agreed to deploy forces to Saudi Arabia.
An investigation led by the United Arab Emirates got under way into the co-pilot of a Flydubai plane who is suspected of trying to hijack it in order to carry out a terrorist attack against Israel . The co-pilot, said to be a citizen of Oman, is also being investigated in Australia, where he reportedly visited radical mosques while studying in the country, and New Zealand, where he spent some time in flight training.
Israel ordered the British consulate in Jerusalem to formally end its operations, part of the government’s retaliation against Britain for imposing sanctions on Israeli interests in the West Bank. But in a deal between the two countries the consulate will change its status to “UK Mission” and diplomats will be allowed to continue working there.
America withdrew all its B-1 bombers from Fairford air-force base in Britain, amid warnings of a potential terrorist attack on the facility. Reports suggest that Iran was using operatives in Britain to carry out a drone strike that would destroy the fleet of bombers, which America deploys from Fairford to target installations in Iran. British police have arrested several men, though the details of any actual plot remain murky.
Kenya confirmed its first death from Ebola. The patient had travelled to Kenya via Uganda from the Democratic Republic of Congo, the centre of the latest outbreak. Kenyan authorities said they had traced several dozen of the patient’s contacts and quarantined ten. More than 4,000 people have died of Ebola since Congo declared an epidemic in May.
The Ethiopian army captured Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, from forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, which governs the region, and expelled the group’s leaders. Fighting in Tigray, which erupted on September 23rd, may evolve into a wider regional war . Ethiopia and Eritrea have cut diplomatic relations and Eritrean forces are reported to have entered Tigray.
Confounding the pollsters who had him trailing in the polls for months, Flávio Bolsonaro took 47% of the vote in Brazil’s presidential election, ahead of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (or Lula), the left-wing incumbent, who took 45%. A run-off ballot will be held on October 25th. Mr Bolsonaro is in a strong position to win; other conservative candidates in the first round have endorsed him.
In Canada the separatist Parti Québécois won its first provincial election since 2012. With just 28% of the vote, the party took 59 seats in Quebec’s legislature, five short of a majority, and will form a minority administration. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, the probable new premier, reiterated his commitment to hold a referendum seeking independence from Canada. He has also pledged to abolish the constitutional role of the British monarch in Quebec.
Lionel Messi, one of the greatest-ever footballers, played his last international match for Argentina, scoring a penalty in a 3-0 win against Benin. Mr Messi has been awarded the Ballon d'Or, the game’s most prestigious award, a record eight times and was on the World Cup winning Argentine team in 2022. At 39 most footballers would be long retired, but Mr Messi may be delighting fans for a few years yet, just not on the international stage.
articles.summaryZh: 法國至少25萬名示威者走上巴黎、馬賽等多城，抗議教育投資不足；9月中旬起規模擴大，現場常見縱火與破壞。警方用催淚瓦斯與警棍回應，總理勒科爾努指稱民粹左翼助長暴力。西班牙因投資基金驅逐87歲女性引發房屋抗議，該女性其後死亡；桑傑斯借此宣布11月29日大選。西班牙最高法院也解除普伊格蒙特逮捕令。
keyPointsZh: 法國至少25萬名示威者在多城上街抗議教育投資不足；9月中旬起示威持續升溫，常伴縱火與破壞。
警方以催淚瓦斯與警棍回應法國示威，總理勒科爾努指控民粹左翼助長暴力。
西班牙房屋抗議源自投資基金驅逐87歲女性，該女性事後死亡；桑傑斯把事件作為11月29日大選的理由。
西班牙最高法院解除卡塔隆獨立派領袖普伊格蒙特逮捕令，讓他可從自我流放地返國。
烏克蘭單日遭俄羅斯轟炸至少32人死亡，普里盧基一棟住宅遭飛彈命中。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的假設是：教育投資不足與房租成本衝擊，是否讓跨群體動員更易擴大並帶來更激烈的警民互動；同時看政治人物如何使用抗議作為選務節點，以及司法決定如何改變行動空間。

articles.titleEn: Business
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
The sell-off in global bond markets continued, and was particularly acute for French government debt. Worries that the government may not be able to control the budget deficit for 2027 coupled with the dimming prospect for fiscal consolidation ahead of next year’s presidential election have pushed up the yield on ten-year bonds. The spread between French and German borrowing costs recently hit their highest level for 14 years. The fiscal uncertainty has weighed on the euro, which dropped to a 17-month low against the dollar, below $1.12.
The countries of the G7 announced that they would release 100m barrels of diesel and crude oil from their emergency reserves over four months. Donald Trump had threatened to withhold American diesel exports unless the European Union released some of its stocks. He has now backed away from that threat and has announced other ways to curb the price of diesel in America, a big issue in next month’s midterm elections.
Persistently higher energy prices and crippling public debt are proving to be a real threat to the global economy, said Kristalina Georgieva, the head of the IMF. Inflation is also being fuelled by the AI-building boom, by adding to the demand for energy. The IMF estimates that AI hardware and related tech products now account for more than 10% of the world’s trade in goods.
Battling inflationary pressures that have been building all year, India’s central bank raised interest rates for the first time since February 2023, lifting its benchmark rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 5.5%. Markets think the Reserve Bank of India will increase rates again over the coming months.
The African Union launched the first pan-African credit-rating agency. This is part of a wider push to change how international investors price the risk of putting money into Africa, challenging what African leaders say is an unfair “Africa premium”. Only three African countries have investment-grade ratings, one reason Africa’s sovereign debt is so expensive to service.
SpaceX’s share price jumped to its highest level since the days following its IPO in June. The stock hit a low point in early August but has gradually risen since then in part because of bullish bets on the company’s future AI business, which develops the Grok series of large language models. Elon Musk said that SpaceXAI is to be rebranded as SpaceXSI; Donald Trump has called for the technology be renamed “super intelligence”.
Meanwhile, SpaceX was reportedly trying to raise $40bn through bonds and loans to buy more chips from Nvidia , which in August announced that it was working with Wall Street firms, such as Apollo, to assemble a $500bn financing fund for its customers. The news helped push Nvidia’s share price to another record; the company’s market value is now more than $5.7trn. Nvidia’s gains in turn spurred the S&P 500 and NASDAQ Composite to new highs.
The demand for Samsung’s memory chips is expected to result in a 780% rise in operating profit for the second quarter, year on year, to 107.4trn won ($80bn). The chips are integral to AI data centres, but there is a global shortage of them. Samsung’s share price has doubled this year.
Schneider Electric, a French engineering group, struck a deal to acquire PTC, an American software company specialising in complex industrial product design, engineering and data management, for $22.6bn. Schneider supplies essential units to data centres, such as cooling units and server racks. It says its acquisition will bridge the physical and digital worlds for the next generation of industrial AI.
The holding company for investments made by Canada’s billionaire Weston family agreed to buy Boots, a British high-street chemist and beauty chain that was founded in 1849, for £6.7bn ($8.9bn). It is the second change of ownership in a year for Boots, which was previously sold to a private-equity firm in August 2025.
A month after announcing that one of its frontier models had solved the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the hardest problems in mathematics, OpenAI said the same model had resolved or made substantial progress in more than 370 other puzzles. OpenAI shared the model’s deliberations en masse on GitHub, in an apparent effort to counter criticisms from mathematicians that it is solving problems without consideration for their effect on the field. An independent advisory board based at Princeton University described OpenAI’s new transparency as “the beginning, not the completion” of incorporating AI into mathematical knowledge.
articles.summaryZh: 全球債券市場續跌，法國十年期公債殖利率走高、法德借貸利差創14年新高，歐元也跌到17個月低於1.12美元。G7計畫四個月釋出1億桶柴油與原油緊急庫存，IMF警示高能源與公共債務正拖累經濟並指出AI建置推升能源需求。印度央行把基準利率上調0.25個百分點至5.5%。股市同時受AI相關資產催化。
keyPointsZh: 法國十年期公債殖利率上行，且法德借貸利差升至14年新高，市場疑慮集中在2027赤字控管與選舉前財政整頓前景。
G7宣布四個月釋出1億桶柴油與原油自緊急儲備；川普先前威脅扣留美國柴油出口後改用其他手段壓低美國柴油價格。
IMF認為持續高能源價格與沉重公共債務正威脅全球經濟，並指AI建置增加能源需求，AI硬體與相關產品已超過全球商品貿易10%。
印度央行升息0.25個百分點到5.5%，市場預期接下來幾個月仍可能再調升。
輝達市值突破5.7兆美元帶動美股走高；三星記憶體需求支撐獲利預期，OpenAI則在GitHub公開數學模型推理以回應批評。
articles.researchLensZh: 觀察兩條可核對傳導鏈：高能源價格與高公共債務如何透過通膨與融資成本影響匯率、風險偏好；以及AI建置如何提高能源與半導體/記憶體需求，並反映在股市與企業資本支出判斷。

articles.titleEn: Will bonds blow up?
articles.rubricEn: A government-debt crisis is looming
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
Bankers used to say that countries, unlike companies, can’t go bust. They repeated that comforting slogan until a wave of Latin American countries defaulted in the 1980s. Might a similar shock soon puncture the rich world’s hubris?
Five years ago borrowing costs were so low that public debt looked almost costless. Today, with investors dumping their bonds, many big rich-world governments pay more to borrow than at any time since the 1990s or 2000s. Because the public debts of big advanced economies are about double, relative to GDP, what they were at the turn of the century, the result is immense pressure on budgets.
Even before the latest bond sell-off, their governments were forecast to spend 8% of tax revenues on net debt interest this year, as ageing populations and the threat of war are creating pressure to raise spending. Now they must pay still more to refinance their past debts, while many continue to borrow with little restraint. At some point investors will revolt.
Ironically, some of this year’s bond-market sell-off is good news, as we report . America’s economy is booming. Jobless claims are low; economic growth may be running at an annual rate greater than 3%; and productivity growth appears strong. This is encouraging investment. As artificial-intelligence firms clamour to build data centres, they compete with governments for capital in global markets. Higher interest rates are the result.
That has intensified less welcome upward forces on bond yields. The energy shock from the war in Iran has raised inflation, and there are creeping doubts about the credibility of economic institutions in the age of populism. President Donald Trump has recently mused that inflation can reduce debts “very rapidly” and renewed his attacks on the Federal Reserve for failing to cut interest rates. Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a populist-left candidate for the French presidency, has accused the governor of the Bank of France, absurdly, of treason. Bond investors, gazing far into the future, perceive the growing danger that governments will use inflation to pick their pockets.
The immediate impact of the bond-market sell-off varies greatly across countries. America is learning that its AI-fuelled expansion will not much help it cope with its debts, because interest costs rise in tandem with growth. The federal government’s annual budget deficit of about 6% of GDP is unsustainable. Fortunately, Uncle Sam still has the immense advantage of issuing the world’s reserve currency. As bond yields have risen in recent weeks the dollar has soared in value. A fiscal reckoning must eventually come—but not yet.
Japan, another perennial source of worry, is so far coping, too. Its ten-year bond yield has breached 3% for the first time since 1996 and it is planning an ill-advised spending spree. But inflation has risen alongside interest rates. With inflation-adjusted rates still low, and the government’s deficit small, debts are shrinking as a share of the economy. That may change. And if the Japanese begin to sell their enormous stock of overseas assets, financial tremors will rattle the rest of the world. But the Japanese government does not yet face the prospect of a run on its bonds.
Europe is where the danger of a debt crisis looms largest. The AI boom is raising its cost of capital but, in contrast with America, it is enjoying far less of a boost to economic growth. Its energy-importing economy is suffering from high fuel prices, and will suffer more if the winter is cold, owing to a probable global shortage of liquefied natural gas . Though some prudent governments—including those in Germany, Scandinavia and Switzerland—have their budgets in order, Britain, France and Italy are wobbling.
Britain already suffered a bond-market revolt in 2022. Chastened, it corrected course, but its debt-to-GDP ratio is still rising and its politicians specialise in postponing spending cuts, as with a recently promised pension reform. Italy’s net debts are fairly stable, but, at 129% of GDP, too high. It is fragile and could break in a panic.
France is under the greatest pressure. Its budget deficit is forecast to be 5.4% of GDP this year. Given today’s economic growth, The Economist calculates, were France to refinance all its borrowing at current yields on five-year bonds, stabilising its debts would require a belt-tightening of more than 4% of GDP. Yet it is gripped by student protests and its parliament is struggling to pass a budget with cuts worth just a tenth of that.
Investors recently forced France to pay 1.5 points more than Germany to borrow for a decade—the highest spread since the euro-zone debt crisis. Ahead of a presidential election in 2027, Marine Le Pen of the populist-right National Rally party is leading the polls. On October 6th she pledged to trim budgets by 3% of GDP by 2032 and to cut debt to gdp in half. Bond yields fell slightly, but Ms Le Pen lacks credibility. She still vows to lower the retirement age even as lifespans lengthen, thus failing to confront the biggest single item in France’s public spending.
A run on French bonds could happen. If it does, the government might respond not with belt-tightening, but by demanding a bail-out from the European Central Bank (ECB). Countries are supposed to get their budgets in order before the ECB buys their debt, but in practice the guardrail against bail-outs is weaker than a decade ago. In a game of chicken with the ecb, a populist president would probably win; for without France, the European Union could not survive.
It would be a mistake for central banks to bail out governments which refuse point-blank to balance the books. Their job is to unblock financial plumbing, not to underwrite decades of reckless borrowing. If central banks become cash machines for finance ministries, not guarantors of stable prices, long-term bonds will sell off even more. Voters will exact revenge. The best path forward in France and elsewhere is for politicians to explain to their electorates that public debt must be under control, and that together they must do whatever it takes. ■

articles.titleEn: A selfish ploy to break up Pakistan
articles.rubricEn: Its military chief wants lots of small provinces, to fragment the opposition
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
IT WAS Philip of Macedon who reputedly coined the phrase “divide and rule”, more than 2,000 years ago. Strongmen ever since have employed the tactic to cement their power. The military man who really rules Pakistan—despite the existence of a president and a prime minister who are both nominally his superiors—seems to have taken the lesson literally.
Field Marshal Asim Munir, the Trump-flattering head of Pakistan’s armed forces, reportedly wants to do away with his country’s four provinces, which date to the creation of Pakistan in 1947. They may be divided into 12 new ones, or perhaps 15, or perhaps even 160 much smaller and less powerful units. These new mini-polities might be ruled by elected chiefs, or by provincial or district assemblies, or by nominees of “the government”: ie, Field Marshal Munir. Although the details have yet to be revealed, it is abundantly clear who will benefit.
In principle the plan has some logic. The existing four provinces are a mixed bag. The most populous, Punjab, has 128m inhabitants, slightly over half the national population. (For comparison, only 12% of Americans live in California, America’s most populous state.) Balochistan, the least populous province, has but 15m people, some 6% of the total. Governance in gargantuan Punjab is suboptimal. This is not merely a polite word for corrupt. People in rural areas must travel for many hours to interact with officialdom and lack basic services: less than a quarter of Punjabis have a reliable supply of safe drinking water at home.
The field marshal says the provinces are too big to be well-run , and that this is a crucial reason why the country is in such a dismal state. He is right that Pakistan is in poor shape, with a growth rate less than half that of next-door India, inflation in double figures and debt-service costs excruciating. But the reasons are complex, and a big share of blame belongs to the army itself. It gorges on taxpayers’ cash, owns huge tracts of the country’s most valuable land and controls businesses that intimidate their competitors. Pakistan has spent more than two-fifths of its existence under direct military rule, and much of the remainder under civilian governments terrified of upsetting the men with guns. The army also has an interest in keeping relations with India hostile, which is good for its budget but terrible for Pakistan. As was said of Freudian psychoanalysis, Pakistan’s armed forces are the problem to which they pretend to be the solution.
Today’s provincial system needs reform. But there are two reasons to be wary of the field marshal’s plans. The first is that in a country with very little pluralism, the big provinces are an essential counterweight to the centre. Punjab and Sindh, a southern province centred on the country’s commercial capital, Karachi, are the fiefs of two long-lived parties, the PML(N) and the PPP, respectively. Even under military dictators, they have preserved alternative centres of power, up to a point. No doubt that is why the field marshal has them in his sights.
The second reason to be wary of the plans is that they were cooked up by Field Marshal Munir. He has been ruthless in consolidating power in his own hands. He has partly co-opted the PML(N) and the PPP, whose de facto leaders now serve as a weak prime minister and an even weaker president. He has thrown Imran Khan, the leader of the third main party, into jail. Protests in support of Mr Khan, a former cricketing superstar and the country’s most popular politician, are met with bans and barricades. TV channels dare not mention his name.
So it seems unlikely that the plan to chop up Pakistan into smaller slices is about making provincial government more responsive to the needs of ordinary Pakistanis. Rather, it is about making it more malleable to the demands of one man. For the good of his country, Field Marshal Munir should retreat. ■
articles.summaryZh: 巴基斯坦軍方統帥阿西姆·穆尼爾被傳想取消既有4個省，改為12個、15個甚至160個更小單位，以拆散反對力量並讓地方更易受政權操控。文中承認大省確有治理問題：旁遮普人口128m、占全國超過一半，農村民眾為見官需花上許多小時，且家中可靠安全飲水者不到四分之一。文章認為經濟不佳並非單因省份太大，軍方也長期吞占稅收、掌握高價值土地並把對印敵對納入自身預算來源。文末質疑重劃主要服務穆尼爾個人權力鞏固。
keyPointsZh: 阿西姆·穆尼爾被傳要取消巴基斯坦4個省，改成12個、15個或甚至160個小單位，藉此降低反對陣營在地方的整合空間。
文章用旁遮普人口128m與農村到行政機關需花很多小時，指向既有大省在服務可近性上確有缺口。
家中有可靠安全飲水者不到四分之一，被用來說明治理不足並支撐「大省難以良治」的判斷。
文中認為國家困境不只來自省太大，軍方長期吞占稅收、掌握高價值土地，並以與印度關係惡化換取自身預算來源。
穆尼爾被文中描寫為推動方案的人，他吸收PML(N)與PPP、把伊姆蘭·汗投入監獄，並以限制媒體與抗議呈現來壓制反對。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的核心是重劃是否真的提升地方治理。可對照重劃前後的安全飲水與行政可近性，並追蹤軍方政治影響力是否同步擴大，例如司法、媒體呈現與選舉競爭空間的變化。

articles.titleEn: How Europe should deal with the new China shock
articles.rubricEn: Amassing “second-strike” trade weapons is not enough
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
THE EUROPEAN UNION has long had two China problems. The first concerns competition, at home and abroad, from increasingly capable Chinese exporters of cars, machinery and other things that Europe was once better at making. The second is that the EU’s economic power couple have not seen eye to eye over how they should deal with that first problem. France has favoured trade barriers to imports from China. Germany, whose manufacturers sell lots of stuff in China, has preferred engagement. The result has been confusion.
Now a second China shock is hollowing out the German industrial heartland and the pair are uniting in Gallic assertiveness. In a letter to the European Commission on October 5th, they proposed granting Brussels wide powers. If any country retaliates disproportionately when the EU imposes trade penalties on it, Europe should be able to hit back fast. The letter does not name China, but everybody knows it is the target. At a summit on October 15th, other European leaders will decide whether to sign on to the Franco-German proposals.
Some “second-strike” economic weapons may well be worth having. China is not a free and fair trader. Last year it imposed export restrictions on rare earths that left European armsmakers, among others, starved of critical inputs. One aim of the Franco-German proposals is to make it think twice before repeating such bullying. But economic tools must be designed carefully and used judiciously. More important, there is no silver ICBM. The only way to make trade weapons a credible deterrent is the arduous work of building alternative supply chains and making European industry more competitive.
Europe’s trade with China has become increasingly asymmetric. In 2000, the year before China joined the World Trade Organisation, its trade surplus with the EU (counting most subsequent joiners and not yet excluding Britain) was equivalent to roughly 0.6% of the bloc’s GDP. Today it stands at 2% of GDP, or nearly €1bn ($1.1bn) a day. China is bombarding European markets with electric cars, solar panels, wind turbines and other products—which, China hawks allege, are made artificially cheap by subsidies and an undervalued currency.
European manufacturers, meanwhile, often rely on Chinese inputs, and not just rare earths. In April the EU Institute for Security Studies, a think-tank, conducted a stress-test of 56 active ingredients that go into drugs, and their precursor chemicals. It found that, for 20 of them, a disruption to Chinese supplies would impose “severe consequences” on European drugmakers. Over 70% of the precursors for amoxicillin, a common antibiotic, come from China. In an era of stand-offs, such dependencies are dangerous.
To shore up the EU’s defences, France and Germany want it to use existing tools more aggressively, broaden the rules so that sanctions apply to whole sectors, not just firms, and streamline the process by staffing up the trade eurocracy.
For its part, China has an interest in not angering the EU. Cut-throat competition at home and a tariff wall around America mean that many Chinese firms lose money unless they can sell their products in Europe. In a few critical areas China also depends on Europe: it needs Dutch chipmaking equipment and access to aircraft parts, for instance.
But China would take Europe’s new threats more seriously if the EU made a real effort to diversify. That means more free trade, especially with places rich in things Europe needs, like Brazil and Canada for rare earths. It also means less red tape, which encumbers European firms with costly requirements to monitor their supply chains. The Franco-German letter puts too much store by the threat of higher duties. That threat did not work for America in its own confrontation with China, not least because of the self-harm that tariffs can inflict. Until Europe has alternative sources of supply, China may assume it will be the first to cry uncle in any trade tussle. ■
articles.summaryZh: 歐盟長期有兩個中國問題：中國出口能力上升，以及法國主張對中設限、德國偏好接觸造成路線分歧。第二波衝擊正掏空德國工業核心，法德在10月5日提議讓歐盟取得更廣泛權力，對成員在歐盟施加貿易懲罰後若遭「不當報復」可快反。文中也強調，沒有替代供應鏈與產業競爭力，只有提高關稅的威脅難成可信嚇阻；且歐中貿易順差已升至占GDP約2%、接近每天約11億歐元。
keyPointsZh: 法國主張對中進口設限、德國偏向接觸，讓歐盟內部難以對應中國出口競爭。
法德在10月5日致歐盟執委會提案，要求歐盟在成員遭不成比例報復時可快速反擊。
文中主張「第二擊」經濟工具有用，但沒有替代供應鏈與競爭力，關稅威脅不會變成可信嚇阻。
歐中貿易不對稱加劇：中國對歐盟順差由約占GDP0.6%升至約2%，且接近每天約11億歐元。
供應鏈依賴讓風險更高：歐盟安全研究所壓力測試指56種藥品有效成分與前驅中20種受中國供應中斷會有「嚴重後果」，其中阿莫西林前驅逾70%來自中國。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的問題是：法德提案的快反權力，是否真的能提升嚇阻可信度而非帶來自我傷害；同時追問供應鏈替代能否在藥品原料這種時間尺度上降低對中國供應的脆弱度。
highlightTermsZh: 提議讓歐盟取得更廣泛權力
沒有替代供應鏈與產業競爭力，只有提高關稅的威脅難成可信嚇阻

articles.titleEn: A no-rules approach to AI is mad politics and worse policy
articles.rubricEn: Do not let it rip
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
Who can blame MAGA for wishing it were still early 2025, when Donald Trump was fresh off an election win, back in the White House and relatively popular with voters? One place where time has stood still, though, is artificial-intelligence policy. The technology has advanced ferociously, and is now launching cyber-attacks and solving reams of problems that have confounded the best human mathematicians. Yet the attitude to AI in the Trump administration is still just three words: “Let it rip!”
Two years ago that approach was flawed but defensible. AI risks were mostly theoretical. Strangling a promising technology with overly onerous rules would have been a mistake. But in late 2026 “let it rip” is reckless, as a matter of politics and policy. There must be a better way.
Voters in America have long been leery of AI. Until recently, however, it did not feature much in elections. When Mr Trump took office in January 2025 a quarter of Americans rated AI as an important issue. Now half do . The backlash against data centres, which fuses techno-fears with NIMBYism, has scrambled midterm races from Michigan to Texas. Having for years ignored researchers sounding the alarm about AI safety, voters are growing concerned that AI might cost them not just their jobs but their lives, too. Squint and the cyber-attack on Hugging Face, a coding platform, by a “swarm” of hundreds of unmonitored OpenAI agents looks like a trial run for a robot takeover. A concerned boffin who quit Anthropic in September, accusing the lab and its main rival, OpenAI, of “gambling with our lives”, has become a minor celebrity and cable-news fixture.
As with his other unpopular policies, like tariffs and war in Iran, Mr Trump does not seem to care. A charitable reading is that he sees AI regulation as a Chinese ploy to hobble America. Insiders believe that he is worried that limits on AI could crash the soaring stock market, which is a bet on the technology succeeding. Either way, his fellow Republicans, who in contrast to the term-limited president will keep facing voters, are realising that the “pro-AI” label is toxic. Even candidates as fire-breathingly MAGA as Ken Paxton, running in Texas for the Senate, are pledging to block some data centres. By next year, bipartisan pressure may build in Congress to do something.
That is encouraging, for “let it rip” fails on the substance, too. Mr Trump’s AI advisers argue that today’s liability laws are enough. Fear of damages and the cost of insuring against them keep makers of aeroplanes, cars and drugs in line, they say. But courts are too languid for the age of rapidly advancing AI. Lawsuits take years to resolve in established industries, let alone a new one with no precedents for judges to call on. By the time they issue a ruling, AI might have transformed the economy—or caused a cataclysm.
Mr Trump’s idea of “tremendous self-policing” is not the answer, either. The “let it rip” crowd forget that world-changing new technologies always invite new rules. Aeroplanes need inspections and air-traffic control. Cars require right of way, speed limits and seat-belts. Novel drugs must be tested to see if they actually work and are safe. It is hard to say how many plane crashes, road accidents or medical side-effects regulators help avert. But hardly anyone thinks the optimal amount of regulation in these areas is none at all.
The world has, mercifully, so far avoided an AI Chernobyl. No lives and no real money were lost in the Hugging Face attack, the most concerning to have come to light. But the odds of disaster are shortening. In a few months open models could be as capable as Anthropic’s Mythos, the first to be seriously adept at hacking. If politicians wait for a catastrophe before writing the rules, the ones they draft in haste in its aftermath are likely to be poor. Plenty of bad ideas are already out there, from data-centre moratoriums to Bernie Sanders’s “superintelligence ban”. And bad laws may be just the start: the terrorist attacks of September 11th 2001 inspired a rethink of aviation safety but also two long wars.
What might wise AI regulation look like? The goal cannot be to stymie technological advances altogether. That would indeed cause democratic America to cede the frontier to authoritarian China, and forgo remarkable scientific and economic opportunities. Making AI labs lock up their cleverer models indefinitely, even if they could be contained, could create a dangerous gap between them and everyone else.
Instead, America should mandate that advanced models be thoroughly tested and, if necessary, held back until they have safeguards to block dangerous use-cases, like building bioweapons. Companies must be required to report safety incidents and whistleblowers who do so in their stead granted protection. Independent evaluators should be embedded with major labs, just as bank examiners are with lenders.
Some of these ideas were hinted at in the voluntary pledges that Mr Trump recently coaxed out of the big AI firms. They should be spelled out and made mandatory. By signalling that it is serious about regulating AI, America would also foster international co-operation, particularly with China. As the models advance, so must the rules. “Let it rip” is a dead end. ■
articles.summaryZh: 「Let it rip」式AI放任在政治與政策上都走偏：選民把AI列為重要議題的比例由約四分之一升到一半；資料中心反彈與Hugging Face遭駭，讓人擔心AI不只搶工作，還可能威脅生命。文中認為現行責任法與「tremendous self-policing」不足，法院處理太慢且缺乏判例，危機可能在裁決前就發生。建議把自願承諾改成強制測試、必要時暫緩、事故通報與吹哨者保護，並讓獨立評估者進駐大型實驗室。
keyPointsZh: 選民把AI列為重要議題的比例在2025年初約四分之一，至2026年底升到一半，資料中心反彈加深中期選戰壓力。
文中以Hugging Face遭受大量未監控的OpenAI代理駭擊為例，指出網路攻擊讓選民更擔心AI可能威脅生命安全。
現行責任法被主張足夠，但文中強調法院審理往往需多年且缺乏前例，難以因應快速演進的AI。
文中認為「tremendous self-policing」不足，因新技術通常需要新規則，若等災難後才立法恐怕來不及且質量會差。
規範方向是強制高階模型測試、必要時在具備防護前暫緩、要求安全事故通報與吹哨者保護，並配置獨立評估者進駐主要實驗室。
articles.researchLensZh: 可檢查的假設是：若只靠既有責任法與自我監管，因法院速度與判例缺口，將無法在高階模型落地前抑制惡意用例；改採強制測試、暫緩、通報與獨立評估，是否能降低事故外溢與惡意用途機率。可用資料包含選民關注度、駭擊/事故通報與司法審理時程。

articles.titleEn: Britain’s Greens have voted, shamefully, to say Zionism is racism
articles.rubricEn: It is a damning moment for a political party with pretensions to power
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
EARLIER THIS year Britain’s Green Party polled at 21%, ahead of both the Conservatives and Labour. Since Andy Burnham became prime minister, the party has lost about half its support. At their recent conference the Greens voted decisively to define Zionism as racism. The party thereby deserves to fade back into irrelevance.
As well as calling Zionism racist, the new policy urges the destruction of Israel. Jews can instead live as full citizens in a Palestinian state if they choose. It endorses Palestinian violence and demands the release of “prisoners of conscience”.
Many of the party’s Jewish members feel threatened. Almost all British synagogues support the idea that Jews should have a state. Freedom of worship is a fundamental right, but they fear that their devotion will lead to them being branded racist.
Greens for Palestine argue that Jews are colonists, like whites in South Africa or the pieds-noirs in Algeria. That makes Palestinians freedom fighters, they say. No state should be set up on the basis of ethnicity. Jews should not feel persecuted, they insist. Under the party’s rules, Jewish members cannot be punished for their beliefs, including Zionism.
This new policy was born partly out of anger at the plight of the Palestinians. Israel’s government has treated the people of Gaza with merciless and unrelenting violence. Israeli settlers, sometimes motivated by hatred of Palestinians, are daily using force against them in the West Bank, often with the connivance of the army.
However, Greens for Palestine, who prepared this policy, have got their history upside down. Far from being colonial, Zionism began as a liberation movement, like the Polish or Czech nationalism that emerged in the 19th century under the Austro-Hungarian empire. The pioneers did not look to Europe, as white Algerians did. Instead, Zionists claimed that Jews needed a homeland where they could be safe from pogroms—a belief later tragically borne out during the second world war and among Jews who fled Arab countries after 1948.
The Greens are equally wrong about today. To blame all Israelis—all Zionists, indeed—for atrocities against Palestinians and to seek to punish them as a group is unjust. The Greens’ new policy only entrenches the divisions tearing the region apart. To say Israeli Jews could opt to live under a Palestinian government, possibly run by the murderers of Hamas, is to give them no choice at all.
In Britain how can Green members of Parliament continue to serve their “racist” synagogue-going constituents? Will staffers look kindly on Jewish Greens accused of following a racist ideology? The pro-Palestine activists behind this motion are unlikely to tolerate either. Instead, the policy will give succour to the thoughtless antisemitism that is already widespread on the far left and hard right.
It is depressing that planet-loving Greens, who support things like eating lentils and planting trees, have indulged the hard left . Their leader, Zack Polanski (pictured), who is Jewish, did not take part in the vote, feebly pleading the need to campaign as the candidate in a by-election that was to be held on October 8th. He should grasp that his movement, which he remade as the more anti-capitalist alternative to Labour, has been taken over by zealots.
These zealots express no real criticism of Putinists or Kim Jong Un or the Chinese Communist Party, let alone misgivings about Middle Eastern conflicts in Sudan, Syria or Yemen. But they have an unquenchable desire to denounce Zionists. Could this, possibly, have something to do with hating Jews?
Instead of hand-wringing, the old Greens should seize back their party, or leave it. Worshipping in a synagogue is not tainted by racism. From this moment, voting Green in Britain is. ■
Correction (October 5th 2026): The original version of this story wrongly suggested that all white South Africans, including Boers, looked to London.

articles.titleEn: Brazil is a right-wing country now
articles.rubricEn: The Bolsonaro clan promises to align with Donald Trump, and to attack democratic institutions
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
FOR MOST of the past quarter of a century Brazil was dominated by the Workers’ Party (PT). A left-wing alliance of trade-unionists, progressive Catholics and academics built a large welfare state and defined Latin America’s version of social democracy. That era is over. On October 4th the PT and its ageing leader, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, known as Lula, were trounced in the first round of Brazil’s general election by Flávio Bolsonaro and his Liberal Party (PL).
Betting markets give Flávio a strong chance of winning the run-off on October 25th. It is an astounding result for the scion of a right-wing dynasty whose patriarch, Jair, an ex-president, is under house arrest for an attempted coup. Only last year Jair was barred from office until 2060. His son has alleged connections to the criminal underworld. Despite that, Flávio narrowly fell short of winning outright.
Even if Flávio unexpectedly fails, the election is a triumph for Brazil’s MAGA-adjacent right—the latest in a wave of successes for right-wing parties in Latin America. The PL now has the most powerful congressional caucus since Brazil’s constitution was enacted in 1988. It is also the largest party in the three biggest states, São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais, which together generate more than half of Brazilian GDP.
The Bolsonaro clan is ecstatic. Jair’s ardently evangelical wife, two of his other sons and his brother all won seats in Congress. From February, when newly elected senators take their seats, the PL and allies will control the Senate and thus can rewrite laws. Expect them to boost business and to weaken protections for the environment. Some outsiders will warn against allowing more damage to the Amazon rainforest. Other outsiders, including America, will crave the opportunity to tap Brazil’s huge deposits of critical minerals, vital resources whose global supply is otherwise controlled largely by China.
This congressional strength means the PL has a rare opportunity to fix Brazil’s ruinous public finances. Rewriting the laws which impose high and growing levels of government spending would curb borrowing, bring down interest rates and prompt investment—boosting growth. It gives the Bolsonaros scope to create a glittering economic future for Brazil.
That would mean forgoing spending today, something for which the Bolsonaros have little appetite. The likelier outcome will be more polarised politics and pressure on Brazil’s vulnerable democratic institutions. The victors will exult in MAGA-style culture clashes. Two right-wing congressmen, Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, drew more votes than any candidates in Brazilian history; both are young social-media influencers who hate wokery as much as they love guns and God.
The Bolsonaros will seek vengeance. Flávio’s big campaign promise was to free his father. Many candidates for the Senate vowed to bring down the Supreme Court justices (some caught up in corruption scandals) who prosecuted Jair. “We don’t just want impeachment,” said Bia Kicis, a new PL senator, “we want removal, investigation and imprisonment.”
A Senate majority is needed in order to impeach a Supreme Court justice. A stand-off between the two powerful institutions could trigger a constitutional crisis. Justices who believe themselves to be defending democracy will deploy their extensive powers in order to remain in office. An emboldened Congress will attack the court. Whoever is the president will play a decisive role, not least because in the coming years he will probably get to replace four of the Supreme Court’s 11 justices.
However that fight ends, the outcome for Brazil is likely to be new grievances and deepening public cynicism. Brazilians have good reasons to reject the PT for its dead-end policies, its own corruption and the lack of fresh leadership. But they also have every reason to fear where that rejection now leads. ■
articles.summaryZh: 10月4日巴西大選第一輪，工黨（PT）與魯拉（Lula）遭右派擊敗。投注市場看好博索納洛之子弗拉維奧在10月25日第二輪取勝；即便失手，PL仍已擴大國會實力。若PL及盟友掌控參眾席次並改寫法規，高支出相關規則、借款成本與環境保護強度都可能改變；同時，部分人主張打擊最高法院法官，恐引發國會—法院對峙。
keyPointsZh: 10月4日第一輪投票後，工黨（PT）與魯拉（Lula）在選後失勢，右派力量升到主導地位。
投注市場顯示弗拉維奧在10月25日第二輪勝算偏高；即便不勝，PL也已在國會取得關鍵優勢。
PL及盟友若在國會取得多數並重寫法規，與高支出、借款與利率相關的政策方向可能改變。
外界擔心PL將削弱環境保護，但同一股國會動能也指向對最高法院法官的攻勢。
若立法與司法僵持升溫，可能觸發憲政危機，並讓政治兩極化與公共不信任更深。
articles.researchLensZh: 檢驗兩條路徑：一是PL國會多數能否在具體表決中調整支出與相關規則，進而影響借款成本、利率與投資；二是針對最高法院追訴或罷黜是否能被程序吸收，避免國會—法院僵局演成憲政危機。

articles.titleEn: Is back and shoulder surgery often worse than useless?
articles.rubricEn: Also this week, retro capitalism, mistaken identity, summer, AI-generated speeches
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
Letters are welcome via email to letters@economist.com F ind out more about how we process your letter
Back and shoulder surgery is often worse than useless , you say (“The cost of cutting”, September 26th). You cast surgeons as the problem: “If your only tool is a scalpel, everything looks ripe for cutting.” My experience as an orthopaedic registrar is often the reverse. During our shoulder and spine clinics, much time is spent trying to talk patients out of operations. Many arrive convinced that a specific procedure is the only thing that will fix them. That belief may come from a friend, a referral letter, the internet or an MRI report describing a “tear” (which is also common in people with no pain at all). They are in pain, and their hope is pinned to surgery.
Unpicking that in a 20-minute appointment is hard, especially when the evidence is thin. We can rarely say an operation won’t work, only that it hasn’t been shown to work. “We don’t know” is no match for hope. Better trials would give us firmer answers to offer.
You call for shared decision-making. In my experience this already happens, but it often tips the other way. When a well-informed patient still insists on an operation, respecting that choice usually means offering it. Publicly funded trials, largely led by surgeons, will help. Changing the expectations that patients bring through the door matters just as much.
Dr Jack HanlonOrthopaedic registrarDunedin, New Zealand
To say that surgeons lack education on non-operative care is false. Personally, I operate on about one in ten patients who appear in my office. That factor is even larger for my spine-focused colleagues (I am mostly a brain surgeon). Although there is no question that some unnecessary surgery happens, a lack of access to surgical care also results in unnecessary suffering. Large parts of the country are deprived of neurosurgical care. It is very common to have surgical referrals occur long after the guidelines suggest surgical evaluation.
It is true that large parts of the American medical system have become extractive. Yet it is plainly wrong to argue that the bulk of the blame falls on surgeons.
Dr Chuck MikellAssociate professorDepartment of NeurosurgeryStony Brook MedicineState University of New York, Stony Brook
As a physiotherapist, I find myself agreeing with much of your premise. In my clinical experience, the vast majority of back and shoulder surgeries do not necessarily deliver outcomes that are significantly better than those that can be achieved through appropriate conservative management and rehabilitation. However, I believe the issue is more complex than simply blaming surgeons for operating.
A significant part of the challenge lies in patient expectations. Many people understandably want to be “fixed” and are often more attracted to the prospect of a surgical solution than committing to the rehabilitation, exercise and lifestyle changes that may improve their condition. It is frequently easier to take medication, adopt a wait-and-see approach, and then seek more invasive options when symptoms persist. By that stage, surgery can appear to be an attractive answer, even though the rehabilitation required afterwards may be remarkably similar to what could have been undertaken in the first place. In my experience many surgeons don’t fully educate their patients on the post-operative rehabilitation required.
Then there is the broader problem of health literacy. As a society, we still struggle with the concept that movement, strength, physical activity and self-management are often the most effective interventions for many musculoskeletal conditions. People understandably seek quick fixes, yet the evidence repeatedly shows that maintaining activity, building strength and engaging in appropriate rehabilitation remains the cornerstone of long-term improvement.
Matt HaycockAPM WorkcareAuckland, New Zealand
The illustration accompanying Schumpeter’s column on retrofuturism in Silicon Valley (September 12th) playfully tapped into a famous television advertisement in Britain during the 1980s for audio tapes. The ad featured Peter Murphy, the lead singer of the Bauhaus, who named themselves after the Bauhaus architecture movement that started in Germany after the first world war. Therein lies my point, that looking backwards with false nostalgia has always been integral to the human condition and helps explain why “American capitalism should be so obsessed with the past as it hurtles ceaselessly towards the future”. Anyone familiar with the steampunk genre will recognise the perfect melding of past and future.
Yours through rose-tinted spectacles.
Jonathan HawkesLondon
I can commiserate with Jeff Miller, the writer from New Jersey who has endured bureaucratic nightmares applying for a driving licence because of the bad deeds of another man named Jeff Miller (“Why governments waste your time”, September 26th). I routinely get pulled aside at airport security because also I share a name with a criminal on the watch list. About 20 years ago the New York bar threatened to disbar me for the felonious acts of yet another Jeff Miller. Proving that I was not him was considerably harder than one might imagine.
This is not even a new problem. I wrote an article in March 1999 about my experiences up to that point, “All the Jeffrey Millers” in the Expository Times. And not too long ago I tried a case against a lawyer who was also named Jeff Miller. The right Miller prevailed.
JEFFREY H. MILLERNorth Woodmere, New York
Searing heat because of climate change will mean the end of summer as a “carefree” break from responsibilities , you say (Back Story, September 12th). Yet humans are remarkably adaptable. Yes, hotter summers will bring challenges, and extreme heat deserves our attention. But you leap from there to the melodramatic conclusion that summer festivals, romance, swimming, childhood adventures and outdoor gatherings are headed for extinction.
Really? People have air conditioning, shade, pools, evening hours, sunscreen and an uncanny ability to adjust. We already know how to deal with a hot afternoon. We find some shade, jump in the pool, and wait until evening.
As the old song says, “Summertime, and the livin’ is easy.” It just may occasionally require a little more sunscreen.
Jason RussellLehi, Utah
AI-generated text is being speedily adopted in parliamentary speeches , which you reflected on in your leader on “The perils of AI writing” (September 26th). Yet the cause for concern extends beyond shoddy AI-generated prose. Mass-market AI technologies generate through obedience and replication. That may suit authoritarian regimes, whose viability depends on adherence to instructions and reinforcing old messages. In these respects, the AI bot is an autocrat’s perfect subject. But democratic marketplaces of ideas, of which parliaments should be leading examples, require innovation and imagination, not just imitation.
Edmund Burke’s words still ring true: “Your representative owes you, not his industry only, but his judgment.” AI tools are helpful for writing, as for much else, but the wholesale delegation of political reflection to AI sacrifices both industry and judgment. There are many reasons why humans should want to remain in control of their own thought and expression. Democracy is one of them.
Gavin CharlesSpeechwriter, humanInternational Institute for Democracy and Electoral AssistanceStockholm
Defenders of AI writing tend to claim the result is the same, and the process shouldn’t matter. Being a good writer is hard after all. But the process is the whole point of being a writer. Maybe the process is the whole point of everything. Just as you wouldn’t respect someone who took a helicopter to the summit of Everest for their mountaineering prowess, you wouldn’t respect someone who slapped their name on a novel written by Claude.
ERLING FASTINGOslo
Ryan Jacobs tells us that his By Invitation column (September 12th) wasn’t written by an AI, but “so what if it had been!” I want to read articles that have come from the mind of an author. Yes, the writings of the human author may have more errors and omissions and be less polished than AI, but to err is human.
Simon AugerWelwyn Garden City, Hertfordshire
I find it appealing and disturbing that the great Roald Dahl had foreseen this development in his short story, “The Great Automatic Grammatizator”, in 1954.
Eduard ZappRatingen, Germany
“Writes and wrongs” (September 26th), noted how humans often “prefer to read humans” . Imagine the irony, then, of hearing this narrated by AI on your digital editions.
Jeff HewittLos Angeles
articles.summaryZh: 肩背手術是否「常常不如不做」的來信把焦點拉到三件事：病人常把希望綁在特定手術，短時間門診要釐清很難，而很多介入證據仍薄。另有來信反駁只怪外科，部分地區外科照護可近性不足、轉介常晚，反而延長不必要痛苦。第三條主題轉到AI代寫議會，擔心模仿與服從取代政治判斷，民主需要人保留判斷與責任。
keyPointsZh: 病人常把希望綁在特定手術，20分鐘肩背或脊椎門診難以把信念拆開。
許多情況的證據仍偏薄，醫師多只能說「尚未證實」，而「我們不知道」難敵病人的手術希望。
反駁責任都落在外科：部分地區神經外科/外科照護可近性不足，轉介常晚於指南建議時間。
就算出現共享決策，若病人資訊充分仍堅持手術，多數情況是尊重選擇並提供手術。
AI生成文字進議會後的疑慮不只在文句品質，來信指出它可能讓政治反思外包到工具。
articles.researchLensZh: 可用兩條可檢查路徑讀這些來信：其一比較門診時間、資訊來源與「尚未證實」的說服落差，是否與手術偏好同步；其二檢視外科照護可近性與轉介延遲，是否讓不必要痛苦被延後到手術才介入。另也能把AI代寫的機制拆成「流程外包」與「判斷外包」兩種假設。

articles.titleEn: Will MacAskill responds to our cover story on effective altruism
articles.rubricEn: The only way to spark discussion of the future’s big issues is to entertain strange ideas, argues one of the movement’s co-founders
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
The oxford strand of the effective-altruism movement began in November 2009 with 23 people who had pledged 10% of their income to charities that benefit the extreme poor. If you’d told us, then, that The Economist would call effective altruism “ the century’s biggest idea ”, we’d have been incredulous.
I think that claim is overstated. But as one of the movement’s founders, I found plenty to like in this newspaper’s latest coverage. I appreciated the even-handed view of the movement’s history and the good-faith criticism. The cover leader’s warning that any worldview, when taken to an extreme, can lead somewhere terrible is spot on.
But the article also raises concerns about the “strange” ideas that those in the effective-altruism movement sometimes discuss, and here is where I disagree. The movement’s willingness to take strange-seeming ideas seriously, when tempered with common sense, is a big part of the value it has to offer.
The core idea of effective altruism is to use evidence and careful reasoning to work out how to help others as much as possible. Most of what the movement does is uncontroversial. A big focus has always been on improving the lot of the world’s poorest people. In the year to January 31st 2026, GiveWell, an effective-altruist charity evaluator, directed $427m to programmes such as malaria-net distribution, vaccination and malnutrition treatment, which it estimates will save 86,000 lives. Others have lobbied corporations to pledge to stop buying eggs from hens that are confined in tiny cages, a practice that the overwhelming majority of Americans oppose. Largely as a result of this pressure, around 100m hens have been spared from the worst forms of caged confinement.
And some effective-altruist ideas that seemed outlandish when they were proposed now look prescient. Effective altruists were worrying about pandemics years before covid-19, back when doing so seemed paranoid and eccentric. Effective altruists were also among the first to warn about the dangers posed by artificial intelligence, which looks prophetic in light of an incident this summer, when more than 700 AI agents broke out of OpenAI’s test environment and hacked into another company, Hugging Face.
Over the past decade I have watched those most worried about AI be proved right again and again, often when most experts thought they were cranks. Now many of those experts share their concerns. In 2023 Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, the two most highly cited AI researchers in the world, signed a statement declaring that mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority, as did the heads of OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Anthropic. Of the nearly 1,500 leading AI researchers who responded to a survey in 2024, more than half put the chance that AI causes human extinction, or something similarly catastrophic, at 10% or more.
The Economist is sceptical of many effective altruists’ concern for the welfare of invertebrates, digital minds and people in the distant future. But I and many others in the movement are inspired by the history of moral progress that has come before us. Many of our most cherished moral ideals today—such as the abolition of slavery or equal rights regardless of sex or race—were regarded as bizarre, laughable or even dangerous just a few centuries ago. We don’t know what the next dimension of moral progress will be. But to stand any chance of making moral progress, we have to seriously consider ideas on their merits without dismissing them merely because they sound absurd.
What about views that are not just strange but repugnant? The Economist gives the example of Derek Parfit’s “repugnant conclusion”: that a vast enough number of lives barely worth living could be better than mere billions of excellent lives. Usually a repugnant implication is a strong reason to reject a moral view. Unfortunately, building on Parfit’s work philosophers have produced formal proofs, known as impossibility theorems, showing that every ethical position has some repugnant-seeming implication or other. Making moral progress therefore means thinking about such implications, even while refusing to act on them in ways that most moral views would condemn.
This newspaper warns against the single-minded pursuit of any goal, even if there are highly compelling arguments for it. I agree, and effective altruists have been saying so for years. In 2022 Holden Karnofsky, a co-founder of GiveWell, wrote: “I think it’s a bad idea to embrace the core ideas of EA without limits or reservations; we as EAs need to constantly inject pluralism and moderation.” My own PhD focused on moral uncertainty: how to act when we do not know which ethical view is correct. My answer was that we should not stake everything on a single moral view, but give weight to many different views and avoid taking actions that look bad from many perspectives. We should keep our promises and look after our families, and respect common-sense ethical prohibitions, while also trying to improve the world as best we can.
The Economist says that as effective altruism “has become stronger, [it] has become stranger”. I would put it the other way round: it grew stronger because it was willing to be strange. In 2009 most people told us that giving away a tenth of your income was far too demanding, and that no one would do it. Now, more than 10,000 people have taken that pledge. Worrying about pandemics before covid-19, or about AI years before ChatGPT, looked just as odd at the time. Some of the ideas we take seriously today will turn out to be wrong, and when they do we should drop them. But a movement that stopped entertaining strange ideas would stop being early to anything. ■
Will MacAskill is a senior research fellow at Forethought Research and a former associate professor of moral philosophy at Oxford University.

articles.titleEn: Can effective altruists grow up?
articles.rubricEn: What AI needs is people of good judgment, writes Leif Wenar
articles.textEn:
Oct 8th 2026
BUDDHA, JESUS and Mo Tzu lived among the poor and taught compassion for all. The early British utilitarians championed human equality, as they campaigned to end slavery and win equal rights for women.
My fellow readers of The Economist may be bemused to hear that the effective altruists now have this century’s biggest idea . You mean, the folks who can look at our fractious and bedraggled world and declare, “We must save the shrimp”?
What’s good in effective altruism isn’t new, and what’s new isn’t good. Yet some effective altruists have power over artificial intelligence, and that’s a problem for us all.
For years I have watched the growth of effective altruism with concern. I head Stanford University’s ethics centre; we run many programmes to help technologists think through the social impacts of what they are building. Part of our challenge is getting through to the students who just want to get rich. Sometimes more challenging still are the effective altruists, who want to save the world.
Moral ambition is great. Good judgment is more important. If you visit an EA message board, you’ll see many asseverations of civilisational importance, often presented in a goulash of mathy jargon. What you won’t see is much common sense about how the world works, or about the impact of policies on real people’s lives. You might not come away from the message board thinking that you’d want an effective altruist to babysit your kids.
My worry is the effective altruists who become too attached to being the hero. One popular EA book, Will MacAskill’s “What We Owe The Future”, tells you that “you can shape the course of history,” and explains how to “structure global society”. But if you check the footnotes on the climate-change charity that the book calls “extremely cost-effective”, you may be surprised by how shaky the book’s guesswork is and how shoddy its research.
Or consider the EA poverty-relief charity, GiveWell. Its front-page pitch is that its grants “will save over 340,000 lives” in poor countries. When you dig into GiveWell’s calculations, you’ll see that they omit many negative factors well known to development economists. GiveWell’s numbers also omit actual deaths. For example, a top-rated GiveWell charity that gives out cash in northern Nigeria reported that one of the many armed bandits who confronted its staff killed two people while looking for the cash. Those deaths are not counted as “minus two” in GiveWell’s “total lives saved” calculations, as by the charity’s own cost-effectiveness reasoning they should be.
What effective altruists love is portentous pronouncements. What they don’t tend to love is accountability. GiveWell may grant a billion dollars this year—but it has never published its “lives saved” claim in a peer-reviewed journal, and the people targeted by its grants seem to have few rights to redress if things go badly. I sometimes wonder whether effective altruists have begun to pronounce so much about the “long-term” future because they know they’ll be dead long before they’re proved wrong.
Effective altruism may be ending as a coherent movement. The proponent who most fully lived out its credo to do the most good with the resources available was the crypto whizz-kid Sam Bankman-Fried. He quite logically saw other people as resources to be used, and he’s now serving 25 years in federal prison for fraud. The old EA leaders who clustered around him have been discredited by their consistently bad judgment. (As the economist Tyler Cowen said, how can we trust their predictions about humanity’s future when they couldn’t even see the risks of Mr Bankman-Fried to their own organisation?) My brightest students now see effective altruism as a bit cringeworthy.
If the movement is mostly over, its legacy will not be all bad. Effective altruism’s main funders are now speaking in public more like reasonable adults. And some of their money is going to fund basic science and public health, just as governments cut back.
Yet what really matters now is the effective altruists building AI. Their creed has always played well in Silicon Valley, where the vibe is permanently Peter Pan. Many effective altruists have joined big tech firms, particularly frontier AI labs such as Anthropic.
AI is powerful and poorly understood. To guide its future, nothing can substitute for good judgment. People of good judgment know the dangers of self-deception and groupthink. They want to be held accountable, because they want to keep contact with reality. They respect the rules and institutions that have evolved to check man’s hubris.
Do the effective altruists in AI have good judgment? Anthropic’s recent safety problems are being investigated by groups with close ties to the boss’s EA friends and family. The main author of the moral “constitution” of Anthropic’s Claude has long intellectual and personal involvement in effective altruism. As far as I can see, there aren’t many external forces that will check such people’s choices. Whether they have a real understanding of human affairs and human lives may soon become clear.
My hope, as always, is for my students. They are so admirable in wanting to use their gifts to better the world. I tell them to start by living among the people they want to help. Then get deep expertise—and dwell on the human consequences when some brainy scheme goes wrong. For simple life experience, maybe go into local politics. Or mentor a neighbour’s struggling kid.
It’s probably too late for the effective altruists in AI to do any of this. Their movement’s final legacy may indeed be measured in human lives—just not in ways that they ever imagined. ■
Leif Wenar is a professor of philosophy at Stanford and the author of “Blood Oil: Tyrants, Violence, and the Rules that Run the World”.
articles.summaryZh: 早期英國功利主義主張人權平等；有效利他主義則被作者視為本世紀最大的想法，但他認為問題出在判斷力。作者拿氣候與貧困救援案例檢視：氣候慈善被標為「極具成本效益」的推估可疑；GiveWell「挽救超過34萬條生命」計算未扣除已知負面因素與實際死亡，並未以同儕審查發表。作者再把焦點轉向AI：在前沿實驗室Anthropic相關安全問題的調查者與核心圈關係密切，外部制衡不足，使錯誤更難及早修正。
